speechtext: On the Orders of the Day:

Mr. Speaker, I wish to call the attention of the Government to a most important and urgent matter. I am informed from reliable sources that the ice jam on the St. Lawrence is much deeper this year than ever before. At Cap Rouge, above Quebec, there is a gorge, and I am informed the ice has frozen 40 feet deep, and that the *water behind has risen 6 feet higher in some places. There is an ice barrage. If this barrage is not immediately broken up there will be serious floods from that point up to Montreal. We had ice-breakers that were built for that purpose. I understand that the "Earl Grey," the "Minto" and the "John D. Hazen" were sent to Russia in 1915-1916 and 1917.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. The hon. gentleman is beyond question bringing forward a subject of public importance, but he should not attempt to enter into any argument. If he will state the ground work and put his question, he will be quite in order.

The "Montcalm" is at Halifax and I understand the "Lady Grey" is not powerful enough to break the ice there. I am informed that unless dynamite is used to break the ice very serious floods will occur with resulting damage. What I wish to know is if the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Ballantyne) is aware of the facts, and what steps he intends to take.
Hon. C. C. BALLANTYNE. The hon. member for Chambly-Verchferes (Mr. Ar chamhault) was good enough yesterday to give me notice of the question he has just asked. I am afraid that the information that has reached the hon. member is not accurate, and I shall be very glad indeed to give the information that the' hon. gentleman asks for. First of all I wish to say that the first part of the winter was, not very cold, and no ice bridge formed on the St. Lawrence up to Nicolet Traverse (a distance of 90 miles above Quebec), until the last week in January. The ice jammed several times during the winter at Cap Rouge-the Quebec Bridge site-which is considered the key of the ice situation, but was successfully broken up by the ice-breaker " Lady Grey." With no ice bridge formed at this point, there is no fear of disastrous floods occurring above. The channel is now clear of ice up to a point near Portneuf, 35 miles

above Quebec, where the "Lady Grey" is working to-day and is making good progress.
I will not take up the time of the House by going into further details except to say that the conditions this year, I am happy to inform the hon. gentleman, are not much different frqm those of former years. The "Lady Grey" hopes to reach Cap Charles, 50 miles above Quebec, very shortly. In regard to the "Montcalm," I think hon. members are aware that first of all she had to go to Belle Isle to take the place of the steamer "Arranmore" that was wrecked, and to relieve the lighthouse people there. She afterwards had to go to the assistance of the Canadian Government steamer "Canadian Spinner " that was stuck in the ice below Father Point. After releasing that steamer she proceeded to the Magdalen Islands carrying provisions for the distressed people upon those islands. Owing to the severity of the weather and the thickness of the ice she was delayed a month in making that voyage. She returned to the city of Halifax requiring repairs, especially propeller blades, but owing to the wreck of the steamer "Bohemian," she had to go to her assistance. The "Montcalm" is now in Halifax and will go on the-dry-dock as soon as possible. I do not anticipate any serious results from floods this spring-no one can accurately tell-but I am pleased to say that the "Lady Grey" is working so well and-that the ice bridge is broken.

speechtext:
. ADDRESS IN REPLY.
Consideration of the motion of Mr. Hume Cronyn for an address to His Excellency the Governor General in reply to his Speech at the opening of the Session, and the proposed amendment of the Hon. Mackenzie King, thereto resumed from Monday, March 8.

Mr. Speaker, at the outset I desire to associate myself with the congratulations that have been offered by hon. gentlemen who have preceded me in this debate to the mover and the seconder of the Address in reply to the speech from the Throne. If I do not dwell upon the speeches of these two hon. gentlemen, or upon those of other hon. gentlemen who have followed them in this discussion, it is because I have a good deal to say on other subjects and I do not want to occupy the time of the House at undue length.
Let me, then, Sir, at once begin by implementing a promise that I made to this House some four or five months ago. It will be. recalled that in September last, during the session that was then in progress and while I was absent from Canada, the President of the Privy Council (Hon. Mr. Rowell) delivered a speech which he and his kept press were pleased to describe as a reply to a speech that I had made about eighteen months previously. It will be further recalled that when I returned to the city I spoke in this House on a question *of privilege, and as the rules of the House prevented me from saying all that I wanted to say I gave the House an assurance that .1 would return to the subject at the next session of Parliament. That, Mr. Speaker,
it is my purpose to do in extenso this afternoon.
Before dealing with what the hon. gentleman (Mr. Rowell) said last session it is desirable that the sequence of facts leading up to his speech should he first presented to the House. Let me then state briefly what had occurred prior to September last. During the last general elections when the anti-Laurier, anti-Quebec and anti-Catholic madness was at its height, the President of the Privy Council fanned the flames of sectarian hate iand added fresh fuel to the fire by a speech which he made at North Bay on December 6, 1917. In the course of his inflammatory harangue the hon. gentlemen indicted the people of Quebec for their alleged lack of sacrifice, and he then made an attack on the members of the Religious Orders from France who had been in Canada and whom he falsely said had not gone back to help their Mother Country in the war. As reported in the "Toronto Globe" the hon. gentleman, after denouncing the attitude of the Quebec Nationalists towards the war, said:
In this attitude they were undoubtedly encouraged and abetted by the members of the Religious Orders from France who found an asylum in Canada and used that asylum to undermine Canada's strength in the struggle.
Believing this statement to be made with knowledge of the facts, and that it was true, many newspapers and speakers who were supporting Union Government used it throughout the country, and in this way spread the flames which the President of the Privy Council had deliberately kindled. A short time after the election the President of the Privy Council was written to and asked to give the proofs in support of his attacks on the French Religious. His reply was a brief letter in- which he said he was investigating the facts. In other words, Mr. Speaker, he admitted over his own signature that although he had made a wholesale charge of treason against a body of men several weeks previously, he did not know whether the charge was true or false; -but the elections being over, and his purpose accomplished, he was going to take time to inquire whether his statement was true or false. I do not pause here, Sir, to use the only terms that would fittingly describe the self-confessed turpitude of the hon. gentleman-in fact I need not do so in view of the judgment the public has already pronounced upon him. In addition to the written request that I have mentioned, the hon. gentleman was publicly challenged by two newspapers-the Catholic

If I had known of the position of those members of the French clergy I should have paid a tribute to them.
. The Catholic Record of January 4, 1919, dealt with the hon. gentleman and his Bowmanville speech in the following article:
Mr. Rowell vs. Mr. Rowell. .
In our comments last week on Mr. Rowell's charge against the members of French religous orders living in Canada we took the report of the Free Press as quoting his very words so far as he touched, in his Bowmanville speech, on his famous-or infamous-accusation. The Free Press report we find was incomplete.
Before us now is the Globe's full verbatim report of Mr. Rowell's Bowmanville address, and we shall quote his every word of explanation or justification.
Our readers will have noted that we have always confined our comments on Mr. Rowell's North Bay speech to this single charge against the French religious orders. Cleverly enough, perhaps, for the audience, as well as that portion of the wider public to which he addressed himself, Mr. Rowell first appeals to anti-Bourassa and anti-Quebec prejudice, reiterates his general charge against the clergy of Quebec, deliberately and dishonestly transfers some of the very words of his particular charge against the French religious orders to the general charge against the French-speaking clergy of Quebec:
"The substance of my statement about the French-speaking clergy in Quebec was that the majority of them' were supporters of Mr. Bourassa'in his attitude on the war, and that in the course they were pursuing they were undermining Canada's strength in the struggle
The words we have italicized referred, in Mr. Rowell's North Bay speech, solely and exclusively to the members of the French religious orders who had found an asylum in Canada. It must be admitted that Mr. Rowell is a
good "mixer"-when he has reasons for not being straightforward.
Then the sometimes Liberal leader poses theatrically as the bold and fearless champion of free criticism of any class of citizens.
"If their objection was to my discussing the question at all. then I can only say that this country does not and will not recognize any immunity of the clergy from just and fair criticism of their acts as citizens or residents of Canada."
As no one ever hinted at jOX thought of claiming any such immunity the speaker delivered a knockout blow to this straw man which he had set up to show his prowess-and his courage.
"Fair and just criticism"-that is an important limitation to all criticism. It is fair and just criticism to quote,-in Mr. Rowell's own words,-the most serious accusation ever made against any class in Canada's population; to point out that if true the Government have a duty in the matter that cannot be shirked without such moral cowardice and betrayal of trust as would brand them as accessories after the fact to the alleged monstrous abuse of hospitality charged against the immigrant French religious; to demand, therefore, that the allegation publicly made by a public %man be substantiated ; or if made under misapprehension of the facts or misinformation, then for the sake of decency, honour, truth and justice, public and private, that the charge be withdrawn, the amende honourable made, and the injury repaired.
Mr. Rowell makes a high patriotic virtue of his long silence in face of the peremptory challenge to prove or retract. He brings in Mr. Bourassa's name at every turn: "Mr. Bourassa and those who think with him" is his favourite way of using the proverbial herring.
"While the war was on," asserts this high-minded patriot, "I ignored all these attacks." Yes, just such "attacks" as the Kaiser repelled when he inaugurated his war of self-defense! Mr. Rowell is even less frank than the Kaiser. The patriotic and long-suffering Liberal-Unionist leader conveniently forgets that it was he who made the attack, a wanton attack, an attack which he has never justified, against a whole class of Canada's population. He gently and virtuously insinuates that he has been wantonly attacked and plainly boasts that it was from patriotic motives alone he remained silent. Oh Spartan patriotism!
So far as Mr. Bourassa and the clergy and laity of Quebec are concerned they have their press, their full representation in Parliament, and are well able to take care of themselves. We have never troubled about them; Mr. Rowell is as disingenuous here as elsewhere in insinuating that it is only sympathizers with Mr. Bourassa and his Nationalist party who called him to account for his public accusations. Mr. Rowell of course knows better; but he is playing to the gallery.
The charge which we challenged Mr. Rowell to prove was this:
"In this attitude," added Mr. Rowell, "they were undoubtedly encouraged and abetted by the members of the religious orders from France, who found an asylum in Canada, and used that asylum to	undermine Canada's strength
in the	struggle."	.This	is a specific	accusation	against thereligious from France; it is a sweeping charge	without	any	reservation	whatsoever
against these men, all of them or at any rate as a class. If any doubt remained as to the general application of this sweeping charge Mr. Rowell cleared the minds of his hearers and readers most effectually by adding:
"It Is a misfortune that they did not follow the example of the priests of the Catholic Church in France, who threw themselves into the struggle of their people to preserve their national existence, and by their courage and sacrifice won for themselves a new place in tne hearts of the French people."
Challenged to substantiate so grave a charge Mr. Rowell remained silent; confronted with the statistics adduced iby Mr. Murphy in Parliament Mr. Rowell was dumb.
These statistics proved incontrovertibly that the maligned French religious who found an asylum in Canada not only emulated the priests of France, but by their courage and sacrifice, by their unselfish devotion to their beloved France whence they had been exiled, they wrote the most sublime chapter in the sublime record of patriotism during the Great War. We reprint in this issue that portion of Mr. Murphy's speech which dealt with these heroic dead and no less heroic living Frenchmen to whom Canada will ever have been proud of having opened wide her hospitable gates. Their glorious record cannot be read and reread without a thrill of pride by every Catholic, by every Canadian.
Nevertheless these slandered dead and slandered living heroes Mr. Rowell allowed to rest under his baseless calumny for a full year. At 'last in his Bowmanville speech he makes this allusion to them:
"In order, however, to make political capital and stir up religious and racial feeling against Union Government, it is suggested that my references covered the French reservists who were members of religious orders, and who, when called to the colours by their Government, returned to France and fought as members of the French army. My references were not to men who had gone forth to fight but to men who stayed at home, men who were in the province of Quebec during the war, supporting Mr. Bourassa. Of the men who went forth to fight none can speak in too high terms."
And this_ is all that Mr. Rowell feels called upon in honour and justice to say in explanation or justification of his wanton and unwarranted attack on the gallant religious, " a body of men," to quote Mr. Murphy when marshalling the facts to rout Mr. Rowell's slanders, " whose courage, devotion to duty and self sacrifice in the present war stamp them as worthy to follow in the footsteps of that noble band of French missionaries who first made this land known to Europe and blazed the way for its colonization and development."
And the reason that even this tenuous, disingenuous, quasi-retraction, quasi-justification was so long delayed was that Canada's part in the war might not be impeded!
Note the impudent charge and the base appeal in the opening sentence; and then in what immediately follows:
" The trouble is, not that I misrepresented anybody, but that I told the truth about the situation then existing in the province of Quebec. An explanation of the campaign of misrepresentation now being pursued by Mr. Bourassa and those associated with him in this province is that they hope by representing that their faith is attacked, and by posing as defenders of that faith, to unite behind them in
fMr. Murphy.]
one party, for political purposes and political action, all those who share their religious views."
Dr. Johnson is sometimes quoted in a more comprehensive sense than he intended when he said that patriotism is the last refuge of a scoundrel; but that honest and sham-hating old Briton could find to-day in Mr. Rowell's speech an apt illustration of his meaning. " Patriotism " and prejudice, partizan, racial and religious, are the last refuge of Mr. Rowell.	.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. There is an imputation in the latter portion of the letter editorial, or newspaper extract from which the hon. member is quoting which he might not himself make in the ordinary course of debate. The hon. member may go no further in reading from an extract than he could go if the remarks were his own. I sincerely hope that the hon. member will, during the further course of his remarks, adhere more closely to the amenities and the technicalities, if I may so term them, of debate.

Anything which in your judgment, Mr. Speaker, is objectionable in the editorial I quite agree should be excised. The editorial then proceeds:	-
Mr. Rowell's charge a year ago was plainly, unequivocally, directly, against the French religious resident in Canada, and against them as a class without qualification or reservation.
Now he has the effrontery to say that " in order to make political capital and stir up religious and racial feeling against the Union Government it is suggested that my references -covered the French reservists who were members of religious orders and who, when called to the colors by their government returned to France and fought as members of the French army."
When Mr. Rowell meets Voltaire in the Elysian fields the famous French infidel will greet the Christian statesman from Canada as a man after his own heart-" l'Audace l'Audace, toujours PAudace ! "	-
In the first place few if any of the slandered religious were reservists. They were not obliged to return and fight in the French army-, as Mr. Rowell insinuates, though he dare not say so outright.
Mr. Rowell knew this. Mr. Rowell knows that it required a special treaty to enable the United States, after entering the war and put-ing conscription in force, to reach American citizens subject to the draft who were by accident or design in Canada or Great Britain. Mr. Rowell knows that with Ireland exempt from conscription Great Britain could not reach the tens of thousands of Englishmen subject to the draft who sought refuge in Ireland during the war.
Mr. Rowell knows that the French government, which had exiled the men whom he maligned, had no jurisdiction over them in Canada to compel them to return and fight in the French army.
If Mr. Rowell had told his audience that every single man of military age and fitness of that class which he had slandered had, in spite

of any feeling of resentment he may have felt at being expatriated, gone freely back to fight for France, that a score of them had laid down their lives in that cause which he had accused them of undermining, that military honors and military orders had recognized the valor and gallantry of those who still lived, the honest feeling of even that partizan and misinformed gathering would have found expression in applause and cheers. Then he might, in the contagion of that honest and honourable and manly feeling, have found it in his heart to admit that he was ignorant of the truth when he spoke a year ago at North Bay. But, like many other politicians, Mr. Rowell has too low an opinion of the sense of decency, the sense of honor and justice, the manliness and mental [DOT]capacity of the common people if he does not realize that in honestly acknowledging his error he would stand in their estimation of mind and heart in a place which he has chosen to abdicate.
Some families gave their every member capable of bearing arms to the cause now crowned with victory. Not one of these exceeded the record of the French religious resident in Canada.
By their action at the beginning of the war in rushing to the colors and giving a tremendous impetus to Canada's effort, a magnificent inspiration to Canada's loyalty, the British-born who had chosen Canada as their home won for themselves undying honour and gratitude.
The British-born as a class, magnificent as in their record, can not equal the sublime record of the men whom Mr. Rowell accused of monstrous abuse of Canada's hospitality and of undermining the cause for which they were ready to die.
At the conclusion of his recital of the evidence which crushingly refuted Mr. Rowell's charges, Mr. Murphy on the floor of the House of Commons thus summoned their author to
retract:
" If the hon. gentleman's statements were not made for a wicked and a malicious purpose, then by every standard of public and private honour he is required to retract what he has said, to offer an apology to the living and to make reparation to the memory of the dead."
Mr. Rowell's friends can hardly be proud of the way he has attempted to measure up to the standards of public and private honour.
Upon reading that editorial, a Toronto gentleman with whom I was not then acquainted wrote me in these terms:
Toronto, January 7, 1919. The Hon. Charles Murphy,
Ottawa.
Dear Sir,-I read an article in the Catholic Record which was a summary of your reply to the Hon. N. W. Rowell's shameful allegations regarding the French Religions. I had not read his speeches but was so disgusted, although not a Catholic, at his want of fairness, I immediately sat down and wrote him a letter, a copy of which I enclose herewith.

Much less may they be used by quoting some person outside of the House. I must ask the hon. member to delete those portions of the letter.

Very well, Sir. The enclosure that accompanied the letter which I read is as follows. It is a copy of a letter that was sent to the President of the Privy Council:
Toronto, January 7, 1919. The Hon. N. W. Rowell,
Dear Sir,-I came across the enclosed article in the Catholic Record this evening, and if the speeches in which you made the accusations referred to are correct, I am amazed, shocked and grieved that a man occupying the position in Canada you do could be wilfully guilty of such calumny. Prom the article containing the refutation of your charge, it appears you are challenged to give proof of the truth of your wicked allegations, and you remain silent. Shame on you! How can you ever hope to be great?-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member cannot shield himself behind any lemark made by some person outside this House. What he may not say himself, he certainly may not quote.

I am not trying to
shield myself behind any remarks made by anybody in or out of the House, and I think I may appeal, Sir, to your knowledge of me to justify that statement. I do not want to use in debate any language that is not in accordance with the rules of debate, and if in your judgment Sir, anything contained in the letters that I have read should not be repeated, then they may be deleted from the copy.
Thus matters stood until last session, when, during my absence and while the debate on the Address was in progress, the President of the Privy Council for the first time in the House professed to deal with my speech delivered eighteen months previously. What the hon. gentleman said in the House was largely a repetition of what he had said in his Bowmanville address of December, 1918, and before I deal with certain specific utterances of the hon. gentleman, I want to point out that neither in his Bowmanville speech nor in his speech of last session does the hon. gentleman dispute the correctness of the following charges contained in my speech of March 19, 1918:
1.	That his support of the Ross Government entailed no sacrifice on his part, but on the contrary resulted in his securing- control of the reorganization of the Clergue industries at the Sault, and that he derived therefrom the profits that I described.
2.	That while the hon. gentleman acted as Provincial leader, there was a fund of about $3,750 raised to enable the hon. gentleman and his press agent to go on a Cook's tour to the battle front.
3.	That in his North Bay speech of December 6, 1917, the hon. gentleman garbled the facts relating to the Conservative alliance with the Nationalists of Quebec in order to conceal the fact that his present leader was in active personal alliance with the Nationalists in 1911.
4.	That he had sent as his agent to the city of London, Ontario, Colonel F. H. Deacon to induce a prominent Liberal of that city to desert the Liberal candidate by offering him as a bribe the Chairmanship of the War Purchasing Commission.
5.	That he deputed another Toronto gentleman to interview various Liberals as to whether
.they thought the public would stand the appointment to the Ontario Supreme Court Bench of a member of the present Union Government.
6.	That he sent a third Toronto gentleman to eastern Ontario to urge Liberal candidates to desert Sir Wilfrid Laurier, and that this emissary pointed out the advantages by which such treachery w'ould be awarded.
7.	That as charged by the Toronto Telegram in its issue of March 14, 1918, Mr. Robert A.

Mulholland, who had been nominated for the House of Commons in Durham county was bribed with a seat in the Senate, to make way for the hon. gentleman as a candidate in the county of Durham.
That is the indictment which in his two-speeches the hon. gentleman has not dared to challenge. It is too late for him to do so now, because no credence would be given to any belated statement he might, now make. With reference to these unchallenged charges, I have only to observe that many a man has forfeited his position in society on a much less serious indictment than the one which the hon. gentle' man has allowed to stand against him.
Now' let me examine what the hon. gentleman pretended to explain or refute in
.	his speech in the House last
4 p.m. September. Here is what he said about his North Bay charge against the members of the French religious orders (unrevised Hansard, September 17, 1919):
Will the minister cite the figures which were given by the hon. member for Russell as to the number of members of each religious order who crossed over and fought?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
My hon. friend simply anticipates the point I am coming to. At the time I spoke at North Bay I was not aware that -the French law of compulsory military service covered members of the French-speaking clergy of military age who had come to Canada, and who remained citizens of France; that they were obligated by this law to return to France for military service; and that those who were physically fit, and were not exempted temporarily or otherwise, did return to France when called by their government to do so. As I did not know this, I could not specially refer to their service, but my attitude to all who went forth to fight was clearly shown by my reference to the clergy of France. If I had known of the position of these members of the French clergy, I should have paid a tribute to them.
Further on he is reported to have spoken as follows:
Had I known that the law of military service had applied to those men and that they had gone forth to fight, I should have paid a tribute to them with greater cheerfulness than I paid the tribute to the French clergy in France.
Still further on, he is reported to have said:
I do not question the figures set out by the hon. gentleman in his speech, as illustrating the part which those men took in the struggle.
With that tissue of amazing evasions, and the hon. gentleman's failure to do what any other man in Canada would have done under similar circumstances, the Catholic Record, in its issue of October 11, 1919, deals in this fashion:

The Honourable Newton Wesley Rowell, President of the Council, has ^t last summoned up courage to refer on the floor of the House to a subject that affects his honour as a public man, his conscience as a private individual, and his personal reputation for truthfulness, decency *and fair dealing.
It is worth while recalling and setting forth in all its naked malignity the foul and unfounded charge which Mr. Rowell made against a body of men whose record in the war compels the grudging admiration of even Mr. Rowell himself. The enormity of the original and still unretracted charge and Mr. Rowell's shiftiness and evasion demand, even at the expense of brevity, a clear and full restatement of the question at issue, and an analysis of Mr. Rowell's explanation or palliation or whatever his latest pronouncement may be called.
In the course of a speech delivered at North Bay, December 6, 1917, after discussing the attitude of Quebec Nationalists, lay and clerical, Mr. Rowell added :
"In this attitude they were undoubtedly encouraged and abetted by the members of the religious orders from France, who found an asylum in Canada ahd used that asylum to undermine Canada's strength in the struggle.''
No charge of graver or more menacing import was ever preferred against any body of men in Canada; and this charge was publicly preferred by a man prominent in Canadian public life.
It was promptly and peremptorily challenged ; it was never substantiated; it was never withdrawn. It still retains, after Mr. Rowell's recent speech in the House of Commons, all its importance, all its implications, all its menace. - Its truth or its falsity floes not and can not lessen its tremendous import or alter the fact that it was made by a responsible public man now holding a high position in the Government of Canada.
If the charge were true then the Government was bound to stop this, monstrous abuse of Canadian hospitality, and by interning or deporting the ingrates prevent further undermining of Canada's strength in the struggle in which we. were then engaged ; nor, if true, can the Government evade its plain duty in the premises now that the war is over. To maintain its truth is to point out inexorably that plain governmental duty; to admit its falsity lays on Mr. Rowell, if he desires to retain his position of leadership in Canadian publjc life, the duty of clearing himself from the imputation of being a slanderer and a coward. It will be a bad thing for Canada and a worse thing for Mr. Rowell if he be allowed to escape the responsibility and evade the duty of making good his hideous accusation, or of retracting it, admitting his misinformation and making the amende honourable like an honest and honourable man.
In his recent speech in the House, which in so far as it deals with the question in issue we reproduce on page 5, he does neither the one thing nor the other; he advances not a shadow of proof of the truth of his charge, but he does not withdraw it. He writhes under the lash of Mr. Murphy's facts and figures with regard to the French religious; he makes an oblique admission that these figures prove the class he had branded as ingrates, who shamelessly abused Canada's hospitality, were "gallant men who left Canada and went overseas to fight for the cause of liberty," but he does not withdraw the charge that they "used their asylum in Canada to undermine Canada's
strength in the struggle." It is a difficult feat of shiftiness and evasion; but Mr. Rowell accomplishes it. Still one can see that he is not proud of his performance and one can admire the prudence of selecting a time when Mr. Murphy was out of the House and out of the country ; and when the rules of debate preclude all possibility of reply this session.
Mr. Rowell is progressing. On the 17th of last December, at Bowmanville, nine months after Mr. Murphy's crushing refutation of his charge against the French religious resident in Canada, he deliberately transferred the very wording of his charge against these French religious to make it read as though it applied to the French-speaking clergy who were supporters of Mr. Bourassa. That was crude work for an artist in evasion. Mr. Rowell has evidently come to be ashamed of it. In the House he read his infamous accusation verbatim. But as he comes to his reference to the priests of France he interrupts himself to exclaim:
"I am accused of belittling the work of the priests; I am magnifying the work of the priests."
Now, that is less clumsy than the Bowmanville method; but not less disingenuous. "I am accused," says this eminent patriot and long suffering, pious Christian, "of belittling the work of the priests." No, Mr. Rowell, you are not accused of anything. You, Mr. Rowell, made an infamous accusation, you admit you made of it; that accusation was proved up to the hilt to be a foul and baseless slander. You admit that, too, in a half-hearted way; you dare not deny it. You are the accuser. You pretend to deal with the accusations you made and you whine or boast-"I am accused," Then you glory in the tribute you paid to the priests of France as showing your breadth of mind and freedom from bigotry, when you know that you referred to the priests of France solely for the purpose of making their brother French priests in Canada stand out in odious contrast.
Mr. Rowell concludes his tribute to the priests of France by saying: "No one can speak disparagingly of the work of those men at that time." In. what did the conduct of the priests of France differ from that of the French priests who had found an asylum in Canada? In no single particular, save tliat the patriotism of those gallant men against whom Mr. Rowell levelled his false and foul accusation of shameless ingratitude to Canada and treason to France, stands out in higher relief than even that of their brethren of France. Those resident in Canada had that magnanimity of patriotism which impelled them, despite the fact that they were despoiled and robbed and expatriated, to go back and fight shoulder to shoulder with the priests whom Mr. Rowell professes so much to admire.
Does "the magnificent service of those gallant men" shame Mr. Rowell into withdrawing his charge? Not at all. On the contrary. These are his own words:
"At the time I spoke in North Bay I was not aware that the French law of compulsory military service covered members of the Frenchspeaking clergy of military age who had come to Canada and who remained citizens of France and that they were obligated by this law to return to France for military service; and that those who were physically fit, and were not exempted temporarily or otherwise, did return to France when called by their government to do so. As I did not know this I could not specially refer to their service. .	.	. Had I

known that the law of military service had applied to those men and that they bad gone forth to fight I should have paid a tribute to them. .	.	."
Magnanimous Mr. Rowell!
With "damned iteration" and awkward repetition Mr. Rowell seeks to convey the impression that some of these men "who were not exempted temporarily or otherwise" went back to fight for France because they were compelled by French law and the French Government to do so.
This is a clear case of deliberate suggestio falsi made with malice aforethought.
Mr. Rowell knows, as everybody knows, that the exiled French priests resident in Canada were beyond the reach of legal compulsion and beyond the jurisdiction of the French Government. These men whom Mr. Rowell accused of using their asylum in Canada to undermine Canada's strength in the struggle went freely back to France to take their heroic part, yes, to die in that very struggle. But' Mr. Rowell " did not know," he " was not aware" dr he "should have paid a tribute to them." Yet now that he does know, he still has the infinite meanness of spirit to suggest a new falsehood while failing to retract the old false accusation.
Could any one in Canadian public life other than Mr. Rowell be guilty of this:
"I have no hesitation in saying that if the general expression I used hurt the feelings of any in that I did not recognize the fine service of the men of whom I did not know, I would be the first to withdraw any such suggestion. I recognize the service they rendered. But when my friends say that I have attacked the Catholic Church I say there is no foundation whatever for that statement."
In the very pretence of dealing straightforwardly with the specific and definite charge against the French members of the religious orders he flounders into this rambling profession of ignorance, withdrawal of the "suggestion of his general expression," and denial that he attacked the Catholic Church.
But he allows the definite and specific charge to stand.
"I do not question," says Mr. Rowell, "the figures set out by the hon. gentleman in his speech as illustrating the part which these men took in the strugglebut he does not withdraw the charge that these same men used their asylum in Canada to undermine Canada's strength in the same struggle.
"Again I repeat," said the conscientious and truth-loving President of the Council, "my references at North Bay were not to the men who had gone forth to fight, but to the men who stayed at home, men who were in the province of Quebec during the war supporting Bourassa but he offers no suggestion of proof or ground for suspicion that of the religious whom he maligned as a class the members who stayed at home because of military unfitness were a whit less enthusiastic in the cause than their militarily fit brothers who fought and died in the struggle.
Should some unscrupulous politician for sordid purpose accuse certain families, whom he disliked, of shirking and slacking during the Great War; nay, should he go further and accuse those families of treason and sedition, traducing them where they were not known; and then should some well-informed friend confront the traducer with incontrovertible proofs that every single member of every slandered family was serving at the front, some of them having already given up their lives, what would happen?
	.
Amongst people with instincts of decency and fair play the traducer would be called to account. Suppose in a sanctimonious, self-sacrificing way he explained, that he did "not question the figures," and that he "did not know that they were obligated by the law of compulsory' military service," had he known "he would have paid .them a tributeand professing again his ignorance of the record of these families, expressed his willingness, if any one felt hurt, "to withdraw the suggestion of his general expression." Why, such an unscrupulous politician would be hooted down by his very friends and made either to proive his charge or withdraw it.
But a (Christian statesman may do just that sort of thing when he traduces the members of religious families, and poses as a martyr while doing so.
In his speech in the House of Commons Mr. Rowell has not substantiated his infamous charge; he does not question the accuracy of the figures which are its crushing refutation; but he has not the honesty or manliness to withdraw it. Mr. Rowell's position no honest or self-respecting man can hold. No public man can be allowed to hold it without degrading the standards of Canadian public life.
After that masterly analysis of the hon. gentleman's performance in connection with his base and unfounded charge against the living and the dead members of the French religious orders, there is nothing left for me, or for any other hon. gentleman who might be disposed to defend the living and the dead members of these orders, to say. In his speech in this House on the I7th September last the hon. gentleman put up a number'of straw men so that he might display his' prowess in knocking them down. One of them was that I had said that he had received moneys from the Secretarial Fund. I never said anything of the kind. In support of his assertion the hon. gentleman said that I had received letters of protetst from Liberals in Ontario asserting that my statement was untrue. Out of the hundreds of letters I received in approval of my speech of March 19, 1918, there were two in which it was mentioned that I had been in error in saying that the hon. gentleman had been paid out of the Secretarial Fund. One of the writers was Mr. Bowman, the former Liberal whip in Ontario, whom the hon. gentleman mentioned in his speech of September last. Upon receiving Mr. Bowman's letter, I wrote him on the 7th May, 1918, as follows :
"Let me point out that you have fallen into the error that a number of others fell into, namely, that you have interpreted my statement as being one to the effect that the gentleman referred to shared personally in the fund mentioned. I did not say that. My information was derived from three contributors to the fund, and, therefore, I was too well informed to make any such statement as the one you seem to think I did make. This correction of your misunderstanding should be made as early as pos-

sible, and that is why I am sending you this line."
What I made plain in that letter to Mr. Bowman, and what I said in this House, I repeat, namely, that the secretarial fund was raised to guarantee the hon. gentleman against any loss while engaged in his work as provincial leader. Briefly stated my argument was that in the field of provincial politics, as in other fields, the hon. gentleman had made no sacrifice because this secretarial fund had provided the money to defray the expenses of his work which otherwise he would have had to pay for out of his private means. I am going to prove by evidence that not even the hon. gentleman would controvert that what I said was absolutely correct. I hold in my hand a document with this heading:
Mr. Rowell's Secretariat, Third Annual Report.
November 1st, 1914, to October 31st, 1915.
It bears at 'the end of the signature " Main Johnson, private secretary/' I will read a few extracts from this report:
To the Committee:
Gentlemen,-I beg to submit the report ol Mr. Rowell's secretarial office for its third year.
1.	Private Secretarial Work. One of the principal duties of this office from its inception has been to do private secretarial work for Mr. Rowell in connection with the various phases of his public work. A new aspect has been given to this activity during the present year by Mr. Rowell's speeches on the war, and his visits to all parts of the country in connection with recruiting meetings. The private secretary accompanied Mr. Rowell, for example, on his visit to the Canadian Westv this summer and the office has been kept busy securing and keeping material for Mr. Rowell's use in his addresses.
In addition to these special features of the work, the secretariat has continued to do the ordinary, daily work of a political private secretary's office, both during the session of the Legislature and during the rest of the year as well.
2.	Publicity. A considerable portion of the work has consisted in complying with the request of newspapers that we keep them supplied with reports of Mr. Rowell's speeches on the war.
Then there is reference to the Liberal Club Federation of Ontario and after mentioning that this federation had been formed in 1913, the report proceeds:
The Federation has adopted as its motto the word "service"

I would like you to note that, Mr. Speaker, because I shall refer to it several times in my subsequent observations:
The Federation has adopted as its motto the word " service," a choice which has aroused much favourable comment in the press of the province.
And listen to this, Mr. Speaker. In view of -the denial of the hon. gentleman,-just listen to this paragraph:
The Liberal Club Federation has its own officers and is entirely independent of the Liberal Party or its organization. The secretarial office, however, acts in co-operation with the Federation as its business office, and the private secretary assists the officers in their activities throughout the province.
And then the gem of the lot is in the concluding paragraph, No. 5.	" Staff " is the
heading:
The office staff remains as in the two previous years-two stenographers-one for Mr. Rowell, who does Mr. Rowell's legal and political work and whose remuneration is divided between this office and Mr. Rowell's legal firm, and a stenographer for Mr. Rowell's private secretary who does political work exclusively.
Now, that report, Mr. Speaker, proves several things. In the first place, it proves to the hilt my assertion that the Secretarial Fund was for the purpose of guaranteeing the hon. gentleman against any loss while engaged in his work as Provincial header. In fact, the last paragraph of the report shows' that a portion of the fund was even used to assist the hon. gentleman in Ips private legal work. That alone, Sir, should dispose of all further pretentions about " sacrifice." What further does the report prove? It proves to the hilt my assertion, *which the hon. gentleman pretended to dispute, that the organization of which the hon. gentleman was the Provincial head was separate and distinct from the Liberal Party, and was designed to advance not the cause of Liberalism but the "uplift" fads of the hon. gentleman himself. The adoption of the word "service" as the motto of the so-called Liberal Club Federation makes it clear that it was intended that the Federation should be a kind of glorified Sunday School with the hon. gentleman as its teacher, and not a political, organization to advocate or press forward Liberal principles. And what else, Sir, does this report prove? It proves that the Secretarial Fund was used largely to advertise the war speeches of the hon. gentleman, and that he did not hesitate to use the war and all connected with it for his personal glorification. Other public men in this country did their duty quietly and at their own expense, but the hon. gentleman had his war activities financed by special funds and advertised by a special staff. More sacrifice, Mr. Speaker!
In his speech of last September the hon gentleman denied that Sir Joseph Wesley Flavelle had contributed to the Secretarial

Fund, because he said, and mark the reason, " the fund was a Liberal fund and Sir Joseph is a Conservative." But we all know, Mr. Speaker, that as between commercialized Christians a little thing like that does not stand in the way. However, the fact is that my information on that subject came from two prominent gentlemen in Toronto whose veracity and good faith I have no reason to doubt, and as they have not corrected their original statement, which I repeated, I must continue to rely upon it. But even if my informants placed iSir JSseph's name on the wrong list of contributors, that would not -be surprising in view of the number of funds raised for the purpose of assisting the President of the Privy Council to make sacrifices.	[DOT]
I have spoken of the Secretarial Fund, and the fund raised to send the hon. gentleman and his press agent on a Cook's tour to the battlefront. My further information is that there were at least two other funds into which the hon. gentleman dipped. One was a Prohibition Fund to which very generous subscriptions were made. Several of those whose names have been given to me are represented to have subscribed in amounts that reached four figures. Now, I have been told that for his services as a Prohibition speaker some years ago, the hon. gentleman was paid out of this Prohibition Fund. Then I am informed there was another fund, a campaign fund, raised by his friend Colonel F. 1?. Deacon a little over five years ago, and that subscribers to this fund in the city of Ottawa were told that it would amount to $25,000 and that it would be used to assist the hon. gentleman in his public work. Possibly Sir Joseph Wesley Flavelle's name should have been placed as a subscriber to either of these two latter funds, but if any error of that kind was made the hon. gentleman could easily rectify it by giving the House a complete list of the subscribers to all the funds from which he has benefited together with the amount of their contributions. That, Mr. Speaker, would stop all controversy and besides it would be illuminating-very illuminating, Sir, I can assure you.
Now, Sir, although the hon. gentleman has lived, breathed, and had his being in funds of various descriptions, he was not content with that; and his frugal mind, constantly running in the direction of sacrifice and service, suggested to him that a Cabinet Minister might also become a tax dodger and no one would be any the wiser. Sir, let me expose to you how he,

as a Cabinet Minister, tried to work this little game of the tax dodger. An item in the Toronto press in October, 1918, tells the first part of the story. It was this:

Hon. N. W. Rowell Claims Exemption Because No Longer Resident.
Hon. Newton Wesley Rowell, President of the Council in the Dominion Government, is appealing to the Court of Revision against an income assessment of $5,000. He claims that toeing no longer a resident of Toronto the assessment should toe cancelled. The Assessment Department contends that Mr. Rowell secures the income from his law practice in the city, and is therefore liable for income tax.
That is the first part of the story; the second part of the story was supplied here at Ottawa. You will observe that the newspaper item states that the hon. gentleman appealed against his income assessment of $5,OCX) in Toronto because he was no longer a resident of that city. In other words, he took the position that as a Cabinet Minister he was a resident of Ottawa. Now at the time that he launched this appeal in Toronto, both his salary as a Cabinet Minister and his sessional indemnity as a member of Parliament were exempt from taxation in Ottawa under a special agreement that then existed between the Government and the local municipal corporation. The result, Mr. Speaker, therefore would be that if he escaped taxation in Toronto on the ground that he was living in Ottawa, he would escape the payment of taxes in both cities. The publicity given to the hon. gentleman's Toronto appeal apparently killed it. In any event, the papers were taken off the files in the Toronto City Hall so that no record would remain there of this remarkable act of sacrifice and service on the part of the President of the Privy Council. And ,by the way, as I see my hon. friend the Minister of Finance in his seat, I would suggest to him that before we are put to the trouble of getting a return brought down in the House, he would make examination and find out What kind of Government income return his colleague the President of the Privy Council has made.
Now, Sir, it is a singular fact that'the individual who is most careful about his own money very often displays the utmost recklessness in spending other people's money. That is particularly true of the President of the Privy Council. His abnormal craving for notoriety, combined with the pushfulness that distinguishes the commercialized Christian, has resulted in the wasteful expenditure of enormous sums of

money since he came to Ottawa. The public records contain some items, others have not yet been made public, but the character of them all may be seen by running over a few of those that have come to light.
According to a calculation made by the Toronto Telegram in its issue of March 14, 1918, the capital value of the life interest in the seat in the Senate, acquired by the candidate who made way for the President of the Privy Council in the county of Durham, amounts to $50,000. The payment of that sum the hon. gentleman saddled the country with in order that he might get into Parliament.
A second obligation of the same kind was imposed on the country last year when the President of the Privy Council had appointed to the Senate another gentleman who had been rejected in turn by the Liberals, by the Conservatives, and by the United Farmers of his own county. Thus, according to the calculation of the Toronto Telegram, another $50,000 charge upon the country must be credited to the hon. gentleman.
Speaking in the House on March 27, 1918, the right hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster), in reply, I think, to the then leader of the Opposition, said that the Food Controller's branch was in the hands and under the direction of the President of the Privy Council. Up to that time the cost of the department averaged close to $200,000 per year, and the Farmers' Sun has described it as the most useless as well as the most costly of all the commissions that had been appointed by the Government.
Within a few weeks of assuming office the President of the Privy Council summoned a women's conference here at Ottawa. In due course the women delegates came to spend an afternoon, and were received by the hon. gentleman. There is no record of whether they put in the time crystal gazing or denouncing cigarettes, but it is on record at page 875 of Hansard for 1918 that the country paid $4,427,91 for that afternoon tea.
As an offset to this conference and just to show his impartiality and versatility, the President of the Privy Council next summoned a conference of organized labour. The delegates came at the appointed time and met the hon. gentleman, and for the afternoon of mutual improvement the country paid another $4,427.
Then, Sir, you have heard of the Department of Public Information. That -was a " Puffery Bureau," operated' for the especial benefit of the President of the Privy 16
Council, and down to the 30th of September last it had cost the country $168,000. That amount, Sir, must have been' greatly increased since September, because to the expenses of the office here must be added the expense of opening up and maintaining a similar office in New York.
Another of the hon. gentleman's fads was the Repatriation Committee. To give it an air of usefulness and respectability, there was attached to it an advisory committee of the Great War Veterans' Association. The gentlemen who' composed this advisory committee endeavoured to give the President of the Privy Council and his colleagues the point of view of the returned men through a series of recommendations on a large number of practical subjects, but when they found nothing was done they resigned on October 29 last, and in their letter of resignation they said:
To our regret and disappointment the greater part of these recommendations have been ignored or only partially considered. Had these matters been dealt with in a statesmanlike manner the present Parliamentary Committee would have been unnecessary, and the unrest among returned men,-the direct result of inaction and half conceived measures,-would have been prevented. Even after the Parliamentary Committee met and the facts had been presented to them its recommendations are apparently such that we are constrained to regard them as unsatisfactory, and we are therefore placing our resignations in your hands, once more as a protest against the inadequate measures of reestablishing the man from the battlefields of Europe.
(Sgd.) "William D. Tait,
R. B. Maxwell,
David Loughnan."
Now, Sir, up to the 29th of October last, the date of the resignation of the Great War Veterans' representatives, the Repatriation .Committee had cost the country $194,309.08, and no doubt 'that amount also has been increased since that date.
Another creation of the President of the Privy Council was the Canadian Official Record. This publication was used as a medium for boosting the Government in general and the President of the Privy Council in particular. Its contents were largely reprints of articles that had appeared in other publications, and so indefensible was the expenditure of public money on such a sheet that Government newspapers like the Toronto News and the Ottawa Journal made strong protests against it. However, in less than eleven months the President of the Privy Council made this country pay $40,134.36 for this toy of his.
Then, Sir, the President of the Privy Council went into the moving picture busi-

ness. Although the Department of Trade and Commerce has a splendid outfit for the production of moving pictures, and has expended upon it and its Publicity Bureau a sum that must now approximate $100,000, the President of the Privy Council insisted' on attaching to his Department of Public Information another moving picture outfit. According to a return brought down in the House, the hon. gentleman after paying $5,000 in connection with moving pictures, entered into a contract for one year with the Pathescope Company of Toronto for producing other moving pictures, to be approved by him, and he is paying the company $50,000 for their year's work. It is significant of the flouting of Parliament in the matter of public expenditure that that $50,000 payment is to be made out of moneys provided by the Demobilization Appropriation Act of 1919. In that way the transaction would be covered up and thus escape criticism in Parliament. Now that it has been exposed it will, I hope, open up a field of work for those who believe that the Government should practice economy.
In regard to this moving picture business the Farmers' Sun a short time ago drew the attention to a Government expenditure of $504.80 for bacon-hog moving picture films. Now, Sir, that is a suspicious looking item.
Explain.

At once it raises the question of whether Sir Joseph Wesley Flavelle, through his fellow Christian the President of the Privy Council, has succeeded in getting an advertisement for his bacon at the public expense. That will also bear investigation at the hands of those who believe that the Government, particularly at this time should practise economy. In view of this indefensible waste of public money the "Farmer's Sun" is moved to. say: " But still we, the common people, are adjured from Ottawa to 'produce, produce; and save, save.' Isn't it about time Ottawa itself set an example in economy?"
Now, Sir, if we pursue a little further our scrutiny of what the President of the Privy Council has been doing here at Ottawa it will be plain that, in his case at all events, appeals for economy will fall upon deaf ears. He believes in bolstering up his political fortunes at the country's expense, and there is no field in which he is not prepared to make a new venture, regardless of the cost. You will recall, Mr. Speaker, that not long ago the hon. gentleman announced that the Canadian people were suffering

from neurasthenia, and as his colleagues were insensible to this national affliction he took it upon himself to act as national physician. Accordingly he established a new Department of Health at an initial cost of .;$66,000 and put himself at the head of it as Dominion Physician-in-Chief. This was too much even for Toronto, and, as if to ridicule the minister's new pose, that city at once proceeded to develop an outbreak of smallpox. This lack of appreciation by the city in which he had tried to dodge his taxes must have astonished the minister, because even though he may have consulted all the pharmacopoeias in the Toronto Star office and the Methodist Book Room, he did not emerge from either place with any remedy .adequate to meet the new smallpox situation. In fact, while he was trying to think up .something that would make his new Health Department function, the health authorities [DOT]of the ctiy of Montreal first, and later those of the province of Quebec, issued regulations forbidding any person coming from Ontario to enter the province of Quebec unless proof of recent vaccination could be furnished. This was done, of course, purely as a measure of self-protection, but in view of the hon. gentleman's record and temperament nobody need be surprised if he should issue an order in council declaring that after careful analysis his Health Department has found that the action taken by Quebec is a dangerous symptom of French-Canadian lese-majeste, and that to prevent, its becoming contagious a new branch will be created to deal with it exclusively.
Mr. Speaker, not only has the hon. gentleman taken our national health under his wing; he has done likewise with our national morals. He is not only the national physician; he is also the national big policeman. If we will not be good, he will throw us all into jail; and for this purpose he has organized a new police force. This he did by prying loose the Dominion Police Force from his easy-going colleague the Minister of 'Justice (Hon. Mr. Doherty) and then merging it with the Royal Northwest Mounted .Police force under a new name. The combined force, according to an official announcement handed out by the minister, is to consist of a mounted section and a dismounted division. The duties of the former were defined in this official announcement in these words:
The mounted section of the force will be extended in its operations to the East, so that a series of detachments will be available in all the Provinces for the enforcement of Federal laws and also to assist the Provincial authorities at any time.

Mr. Speaker, when I read this language I was astounded. It was such a plain intimation of future encroachments upon provincial rights and suggested so many possibilities of stirring up trouble in the proy-inces of Quebec, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island, that I wrote the premiers of those provinces directing their attention to the announcement the minister had given to the press and inquiring in each case if the province had asked for the assistance of this new " Rowell Police " or if any situation in which these police would be required was likely to develop. The replies from the provincial premiers were to the effect that their provinces had made no request for the new police; that they were not aware of any situation in which the services of these police would be required, and that, speaking generally, the provinces were able to look after their own affairs without any outside assistance. The reply from Sir Lomer Gouin, Premier of Quebec, states the case so admirably that I will read it:
Office of the Prime Minister,
Province of Quebec.
Quebec, February 4, 1920. Honourable Charles Murphy, M.P.,
46 Elgin Street,
Ottawa.
Dear Mr. Murphy,-I have your letter of the 31st ultimo, in which you are so good as to-call my attention to the official announcement of the merging of the North West Mounted Police and of the Dominion Police.
You ask me if I can let you know whether any request was made on behalf of this province, at any time, for the services of this new police force and, if not, whether any condition of things exists, or is likely to exist, that will make it necessary for us to call in its assistance.
In answer, I have to state that we made no request in connection with police assistance to the Federal Government and that we do not anticipate that any condition will arise necessitating our having recourse to the Federal Police.
I must add that I felt an astonishment equal to your own when I read the announcement you refer to as I have always considered that police matters, in the province, are within the exclusive attributes of the provincial governments as being a part of the administration of justice, of municipal and local matters in the province.
Mr. ROBERT H. BUTTS (Cape Breton South and Richmond): Will my hon. friend read the reply made by Hon. George Murray, Premier of Nova Scotia?

I would like to oblige
my hon. friend but I prefer to read the reply which I am now reading to the House.
I have grave douhts as to there being any jurisdiction at all in the Federal authorities in
this connection. Some time ago Lord Rosebery stated something which I believe has its application here. The Imperial Government had advertised the sale of a part of his property which it had used during the war, without in any way consulting Lord Rosebery in the matter. The latter, on seeing the advertisement, gave out to the press that the Government and its Commissions had so frequently and to such an extent encroached upon the rights of private individuals during the war that it probably had come to think that these rights existed no longer. I am inclined to balieve that the numerous encroachments upon Provincial rights and powers of which the Federal Government and its Comrriissions have been guilty during the last four or five years have also given them the idea that Provincial rights exist no more.
I can assure you that we feel capable of coping unaided with every thing that occurs in this Province in the way of administration of justice and the protection of the life and property of its inhabitants, and that we are perfectly secure in the opinion that nothing will occur that will be beyond our powers.
Believe me.
Yours faithfully,'
Lomer Gouin.
Of course, there is another purpose for which the new police force could be used. While the hon. gentleman remains at the head of the force, it can be used for raids on private houses, colleges, and libraries, that may contain books or papers objectionable to the hon. gentleman or his friends. In point of fact, that very thing has been done in several parts of the Dominion in a way as high-handed and unjustifiable as if the Kaiser himself was directing the raids. Yin this point, the Grain Growers' Guido made a few timely observations. In a recent issue, that paper said:
The people of Canada will not be true to their instincts, their traditions, and their just rights, as a free, self-governing people, if they do not demand, and insist upon getting, an explanation from Ottawa, in regard to the arbitrary proceedings that have taken place recently, months after the cessation of hostilities, in the invasion of private houses, colleges and libraries, under the provisions of an order-in-council framed explicitly for war-time conditions, the seizure of books and papers, and the sentencing of individuals to terms of imprisonment for having in their possession literature under the war-time ban of the censorship.
In Alberta, and in 'Ontario, these searches, arrests, confiscations, and punishments have been carried out in a manner which would- have been more in keeping with the old methods of the old autocratic regime in Russia than with the institutions of government in this free country.
But, Sir, the invasion of private rights has not been restricted to the cases referred to by the Grain Growers' Guide. Of late, a new line of activity has been opened up for the new police force which apparently has instructions to make war on women

whose political opinions do not happen to please the President of the Council and his friends. The latest instance of this kind that came to my notice happened in Toronto, an dthe particulars of the incident are set out in the following letter:

Toronto, Feb. 25, 1920. Hon! Chas. Murphy, M.P.,
Ottawa.
Dear Sir:-I am sure that you will be interested to know that we have got as far as the Dominion Mounted Police.
Our first intimation of this was that the T.M.C.A. refused us a room. The President, the Secretary, and I, called to see the man in charge, and to ask why-since many organizations have meetings there-the Daughters of Canada were excluded.
He told us that a man had called from the .Mounted Police, armed with some newspaper clippings ( !) and asked for the address of our officers, as he was going to take action against us for disloyalty. Our Corresponding Secretary Mrs. Stevens, then went to the headquarters of these Police, and found an Englishman, Inspector Bates, in charge. She demanded his authority for interfering with our organization, and asked to see the newspaper clippings. He told her that they had been passed on. She could get no further information. I can't help wondering if they were " passed on " to the minister whose special brand of courage is attacking women from afar off.
Yours truly,
(Signed) Christine Ross barker,
Treasurer D. of C.
Making war on women! Imagine what a degradation that must be for the gallant members of a force with the magnificent record and the world-wide reputation of the Royal North West Mounted Police. As the Ottawa Citizen, in its issue of February 6, said:
Changing the name of the Royal Northwest Mounted Police to the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, or the Dominion Mounted Police, does not necessarily mean that law and order is being promoted. Royal Northwest Mounted Police is a name known and respected in every part of the world. When a man joins the Royal Northwest Mounted Police, he becomes conscious of having to live up to the traditions and reputation of the force, created by half a cenury of service on the side of law and order. Mr. Rowell's new police begins without any such name, and with nothing very inspiring at its political head. When the present government, itself governed by fear, gives place to government with confidence in the good sense of the Canadian people, the Royal Northwest Mounted Police should have their honored name restored to them.
Not only should they 'have their honoured name restored to them, but they should be returned to the work which they have done so long and so well. To use the phraseology of the Ottawa Citizen, "the good sense of the

Canadian people" will commend any action of this Parliament that will restore the Royal North West Mounted Police force to the enviable position it occupied in our national life before the President of the Privy Council succeeded in pulling it down from its high estate.
The hon. gentleman poses as an exemplar in so many lines, and by reason of that so often assumes the right to set standards for other people, that a few minutes may be profitably, employed in examining the kind of an example he sets the public in the matter of loyalty to his own colleagues. Last year, during the debate on the Budget, we had the spectacle of the hon. gentleman conveying to the House and to the country the intimation that his former colleague, the ex-Minister of Agricutlure (Mr. Crerar), had taken in Council a position on the tariff inconsistent with that which he afterwards took in this House. Up to the time the President of the Privy Council made his appearance in Dominion politics, the proceedings of Council were regarded as secret, and the members of Council were regarded as being bound by their oath of office not to reveal them. Only certain decisions of Council were made public, and those only in an official and a well-understood way; but the hon. gentleman, with that fine sense of honour that distinguishes him from common folk introduced a startling innovation when, in replying to the speech on the Budget of his former polleague the ex-Minister of Agriculture, lie gave the House and the country plainly to understand that the attitude which the ex-Minister of Agriculture had taken in Council, where all that is said and done is of a confidential end secret character, was at variance with the attitude which the ex-Minister of Agriculture took later in this House. This is what the President of the Council said. I quote from Hansard of June 12, 1919, page 3407:
Every man must exercise his own judgment on an important issue like this and I have the greatest respect for the judgment and sincerity of my hon. friend, the member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar), but I say to the House and to the country that if I was prepared, as all my colleagues were, to support the Finance Minister in- coming down to this House during this war year without any revision of the tariff, I do not believe that I am absolved from, supporting him when he has revised the tariff in a measure according to the lines that I desire.
Hon. members will note the oblique and tortuous way in which the President of the Council, in the words which I have just qiioted, put his former colleague the ex-

Minister of Agriculture, who was known to favour tariff revision, in the position of having first agreed in Council that there should not be any revision of the tariff in 1919, and then of having' later opposed such a revision as he desired when it was brought down in the House. The President of the Privy Council did this knowing that the only way in which the ex-Minister of Agriculture could refute him would be by disclosing what that hon. gentleman had said and done in Council, and the President of the Privy Council knew perfectly well that as an honourable man the ex-Minister of Agriculture would make no such disclosure. So, relying on the sense of honour of his ex-colleague, the President of the Privy Council in violation of his oath of office did not hesitate to place his former colleague in a false position before the House and the country.
The precise character of the offence committed by the President of the Privy Council will be made more clear if I read that portion of the oath bearing on this matter, which he took as a Privy Councillor. The oath was in these terms:
You Newton Wesley Rowell do solemnly promise and swear that you will serve His Majesty truly and faithfully in the place of His Council in this His Majesty's Dominion of Canada, ydu will keep close and secret all such matters as shall be treated, debated and resolved on in Privy Council, without publishing or disclosing the same or any part thereof, by Word, Writing, or otherwise to any Person out of the same Council, but to such only as be of the Council.	.
That is the beginning of the oath which is taken by all Privy Councillors, and which the President of the Privy Council took when he tvas sworn in as a member of that Council, and it was in violation of that part of the oath which I have read that he made the statement in the House [DOT] to which I drew attention a few moments ago. I have only to observe further, Sir, that even if the intimation given to the House by the President of the Privy Council about his colleague's attitude in Council were true, that would not justify this breach of the spirit and the letter of his oath of office.
Now let me recall the attitude this same hon. gentleman has displayed in the House and iu the country towards his colleagues the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty) and the late Minister of Customs, now the Secretary of State (Mr. Sifton). These two hon. gentlemen represented Canada at the Peace Conference. The President of the Privy Council was not there, although he and his kept press made frantic efforts to induce
the right hon. the Prime Minister to send him there. When the Peace Treaty was signed, it was the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty) /and the then Minister of Customs (Mr. Sifton) who signed it on behalf of Canada, but when anything is to be said about the Peace Conference or the Peace. Treaty or the League of Nations the President of the Privy Council, who was not at the Conference, and who did not sign the-treaty,. coolly elbows his two colleagues out of the way and tells the House and the-country what was done at the Conference, what the Peace Treaty means, and particularly what the League of Nations means. There, Sir, you have another example of the hon. gentleman's modesty and of his fine regard for the feelings ol his colleagues -of his always doing that which will promote harmony in the Cabinet and in the Government ranks.
In'case some one might be tempted to say that an Opposition member should not complain if the President of the Privy Council is acting in the way I have described, let me point out that I am not complaining; far from it, I am simply drawing attention to what is going on.
We had* another example of the hon. gentleman's loyalty to his colleagues and his fine regard for their feelings when the Grand Trunk Bill was under discussion last session. The Minister of Railways (Mr. J. D. Reid) and the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Meighen) had charge of .that measure, but on a number of occasions the President of the Privy Council shoved them aside and took the conduct of the Bill out of their hands. That was particularly the case on a memorable evening when, after the hon. member for Cape Breton North (Mr. McKenzie) had moved an amendment to the second reading of the Bill, the President of the Privy Council struggled with his colleague the Minister of Railways for possession of the floor. The incident is embalmed in Hansard of October 21, in these few lines:
