President of the Privy Council next displayed his loyalty to his colleague the Minister of Labour by going down to Washington and usurping his place there at the International Labour Conference. Incidentally, he found time during the Conference to make a trip from Washington to Detroit, at the public expense, 5 p.m. I have no doubt, for the purpose of addressing a Y.M.C.A. conference in the latter city. He is reported by the Toronto Globe to have said when speaking at Detroit :
No nation can go out to the other nations cf the world as a Christian leader until it establishes social justice within its own boundaries. We have not achieved social justice. We have not succeeded in amplifying the ideal of human brotherhood sufficiently to entitle us to be spiritual leaders.	*
He must have had an access of modesty that day. He continued:
I think quite probably there will be some funerals in both your country and mine before we accomplish that.
As you will observe, Sir, the hon. gentleman's remarks at Detroit were somewhat doleful, and they have a sound like that which a person makes when he-is preparing a soft spot for himself to fall on. In point of fact, that is just what the hon. gentleman was doing. He spoke at Detroit shortly after the Ontario elections, and as the county of Durham, which he represents. in this House, by way of a senatorship in another, had just elected a Liberal and a Farmer as its provincial representatives, he felt it was high time to begin practising his political swan song, and so he began at Detroit with this reference to funerals. He added another verse at Port Hope, and of that I shall speak a little later.
Meanwhile I want to deal briefly with a few of the hon. gentleman's other activities which have combined to create confusion in the public mind. The misleading propaganda in which the President of the Privy Council habitually indulges has been given free rein in connection with his utterances about the League of Nations and the eight-hour day. Although it has taken the United States Senate many months to discuss the Covenant of the League of Nations, and the obligations that the United States will as-sulne if the Treaty is adopted without reservations, the Parliament of Canada, after a superficial and brief discussion was induced, chiefly by the hon. gentleman to swallow the Treaty and Covenant and to reject the eminently proper amendment proposed from this- side of the House by the hon. member for Shelburne and

Queen's (Mr. Fielding). Since that time the President of the Privy Council has adopted a truculent attitude towards the United States, and in addresses before various clubs has laboured to create the impression that principally through his efforts Canada has assumed the moral leadership of this continent, that the United States Senate in not swallowing the Treaty and the League of Nations with its eyes shut has forfeited public respect, and is derelict in its duty towards other entente nations, and that the chief, if not the only objection of the United States Senate to the Treaty was the number of votes given to Great Britain and the Overseas Dominions.	I
Just to illustrate the difference between such a dabbler in world politics as the hon. gentleman and a man of trained experience and sound judgment in international affairs,
I am going to refer you to a notable article in the North American Review for January last written by the Hon. J. M. Beck who was deputy attorney general of the United States in the Qai'fiokl Administration. Mr. Beck has delivered many important addresses in Canada and he was well known here as a staunch friend of the Allies long before his country entered the war. Mr. Beck's article begins with a reference to the traditional policy of the United States towards world politics and after recalling an unsuccessful effort that was made one hundred years ago to have the United States join a European League of Nations, Mr. Beck points out that under the American constitution no official, however great or illustrious he may be, could commit the United States to any treaty obligation except upon the concurrence of two-thirds of the Senate. Mr. Beck then recalls the storm of protest throughout the United States with which President Wilson's announce: ment that he was going to Paris was received; the refusal of the American people [DOT] in the State elections of 1918 by a majority exceeding 1,000,000 votes to grant the President an unlimited moral authority to commit them to any peace programme; the formal notice given by more than one-third of the Senate on the return of the Piesident with the first draft of the Covenant of the League that it would not be accepted by the American people, and the fatal blunders that were made by the European nations in not heeding these notices and warnings. Notwithstanding these blunders and the Senate rejection of the Peace Treaty on account of the League of Nations, Mr. Beck declares that

" the Anglp-Freneh-American entente is not dead " and that " the best hope of the world for the preservation of a just peacp lies not so much in the League of Nations as in the spirit of mutual co-operation between the members of the great alliance which called it into being." In final explanation of the attitude of the United States Mr. Beck says:
It is now obvious that the United States while willing to he the helpful friend of her sister democracies was not disposed to be a partner of a large number of nations, some democratic and some autocratic and with some of whom she has scant sympathy.
Throughout the article there is but one allusion to the votes allowed Great Britain and the overseas Dominions and that is made merely for the purpose of explaining that the multiplied vote of the British Empire was desired by the Overseas Dominions rather than by England. Mr. Beck makes it clear that the action of the Senate was in no way influenced by these votes or by other alleged considerations but that it was based upon constitutional principles and upon the broadest grounds of patriotism because the covenant would permanently affect the destinies of the American people. He adds that a majority of the American people take a just pride in the fact that the Senate " refused to permit its high prerogative to be defeated by that which was virtually a policy of coercion." For us Canadians that article in the North American Review is full of significance. It shows how careful our neighbours to the south are about entering into foreign engagements of any kind and how rigidly opposed they are to the surrender of any constitutional privilege they rfow enjoy. In a word, iSir, the article is instinct with the spirit of a people who are free and who are determined to remain free without giving offence to any other people enjoying the same freedom.
If, in conjunction with that article, there be borne in mind first, the testimony of William C. Bullitt before the foreign relations committee of the United States Senate to the effect that Secretary Lansing had said in Paris that if the United States knew what it was being let in for it would never ratify the Treaty; secondly, the recent statement of Mr. Asquith during the Paisley election that the peace arranged at Versailles was a bad peace, and, thirdly, the still more recent statement of Earl Curzon that the Peace Treaty will have to be rewritten, that it was never intended to be permanent-if, I repeat, these
things be borne in mind, is it not about time for the Canadian people to call a halt to the wild capering of the President of the Privy Council through the mazes of the Treaty and of the League of Nations and that they read for themselves what men who understand both the Treaty and the League of Nations are saying about them. In any event, Sir, should not Canada be as little disposed as the United States, in the words of Mr. Beck, " to be a partner of a large number of nations, some democratic, x some autocratic and with some of whom she has scant sympathy?" The future of this country, like that of the United States is on this continent. That being so, I ask why should Canada be less careful than the United States in committing herself to foreign engagements of which she knows nothing? Why should this Parliament as the guardian of Canadian interests allow herself to be stampeded in the dark in reference to such vital matters as the Treaty and the League of Nations when eminent jurists on both sides of the Atlantic make it plain that neither is what the President of the Privy Council says it is.
Let me make a few observations in reference to the hon. gentleman's performances in connection with the eight-hour day. Having elbowed his colleague, the Minister of Labour out of the way and assumed the role of labour leader of the Dominion, the President of the Council then put himself forward as the leading authority on the eight-hour day and the forty-eight-hour week in this country. More than anything else, his speeches created the impression in the public mind that the Peace Treaty made or would make the eight-hour day obligatory in the countries which signed it. The Treaty does nothing of the kind. The Treaty only sets forth as a principle that the eight-hour day should be a " standard to be aimed at," the inference being that it should be adopted by a country when the economic conditions of that country justified such action. Beyond that the language of the Treaty does not go. The pretensions and performances of the President of the Council in reference to the eight-hour day received some attention at the hands of a newspaper which is a supporter of Union Government. In its issue of December 19 last the Montreal Gazette said editorally .
Mr. ROWELL'S MISSION.
Having committed the Canadian Government to the principle, if not the practice, of the eight-hour day, at the Washington Conference, Hon. Mr. Rowell is now engaged in discussing the matter with the Canadian pull-

lie. A reversal of this procedure would have been more in harmony with the theory of responsible government. Mr. Rowell's ministerial record does not reveal him as a consistent apostle of that theory, and it is due as much to his instrumentality as to that of any other member of the Administration, that responsible government has so largely given place to Cabinet rule in this country. Mr. Rowell spoke for the Canadian Government at the Labour Conference in Washington. He did not speak there for the Canadian people nor for Canadian labour. He was quoted as stating that the matter was one to be determined by the Government, and having enunciated that progressive principle, he announced his support of the eight-hour day convention.
A little later the same article reads thus:
The reduction of the aggregate hours of labour means a reduction in the amount of work done. Experience has by actual demonstration shown that to be the case. Yet Mr. Rowell talks in the same breath of the desirability of the forty-eight hour week, and the necessity of increased production. It would be difficult to imagine two more inconsistent propositions, and yet Mr. Rowell presents them as complementary.
Further on the article says:
Some further effort might probably be made toward a declaration in definite terms as to the exact nature and scope of the conditions attached to the acceptance of the eight-hour day. What limitations were made, and how far do they go? Is it proposed to apply the so-called principle of the eight-hour day to the basic industry of Canada, that of agriculture? Are the fisheries to be operated on an eight-hour day basis, and is the forty-eight hour week to prevail in the great lumber industry? These are all seasonal occupations, carried on under conditions which do not lend themselves to the operation of an eight-hour day, or, if at all, only at enormous additional cost, which must-be borne by the consumer. As against this increase in the cost of production there is, of course, the alternative of a reduction in the production itself, again with its burden of higher prices to be paid by the consumer.
Take agriculture as an example. It is hardly necessary to state that a reduction in the agricultural yield means higher prices for the amount actually produced. The eight-hour day in agriculture would inevitably reduce production, unless more labour is employed, and more labour, if it can be secured at all on the farm, means increased cost of production, which the consumer must pay. The question as to the practicability of applying the eight-hour day to farm work was answered only a few days ago in Toronto by J. C. Dixon, of Warfield, presiding as master of the Dominion Grange. It would mean, he said, that the people would have to pay 30 cents a quart for milk, $2 a peck for potatoes, $5 a bushel for wheat, and $1 a pound for butter, and would "come nearer to jarring the Canadian people back to a level of common sense than anything else that could possibly happen at present." If the eight-hour day means this in agriculture, how is it to result differently in other industries? Does it not mean reduced production, or the maintenance of production at greater cost, and increased prices to the public either way?
Slo much, Sir, for the vapourings of the President of the Privy Council and the mis-flfFt. Murphy. 1
apprehension which he has created about the terms of the Treaty relating to the eight-hour day. What has happened in this regard furnishes another proof of the mistake Parliament made by allowing itself to be hurried into ratification of the Treaty before examining and discussing its contents in detail.
Mr. Speaker, apart from anything the Treaty may contain, if you want sane leadership in Canada on the question of an eight-hour day you can get it from the National Trade Unions in the Province of Quebec. There was -a labour convention held in Three Rivers in September last, which was attended by delegates representing sixty-three National organizations and 30,000 workmen from all parts of the province. The convention adopted a number of resolutions of the most practical character. Here is the resolution that was adopted with reference to hours of work:
The Convention expresses the opinion that any provision enforcing a fixed number of hours for the legal working day is arbitrary, unwise and inopportune, but it maintains that the length of working, days should be such as to give the workman a reasonable time to recuperate, to perform his duties as husband, father, citizen, and Catholic, and to do justice to the reasonable obligations of commerce, industry and finance.
A report of the convention contains this summary of the discussion about the eight-hour day:
"We see no advantage," declared some of the speakers, "in legalizing a uniform eight-hour day for trades requiring little effort and carried on under favourable sanitary conditions. On the other hand, we find the same eight-hour day excessive for other very exhausting trades practised under most distressing conditions. Instead of claiming an arbitrary regulation which ignores obvious differences, we lay down the principles governing the whole question and let the various trades conform to those principles according to their respective needs."
"Less working hours and a higher salary is all very well," remarked a speaker, "but if every one does less and earns more, the cost of living will go rising and where will it stop? Then what about the poor devil who belongs to no union and can get no increase? Will his condition improve?"
Thus you see, Mr. Speaker, that the labour unions of the province of Quebec keep in mind not only the welfare of their own members, but also the welfare of those workers who are^not represented in unions. While doing th'is for the workers, they acknowledge their duty to do justice to the reasonable obligations of commerce, industry, and finance.
Mr. Speaker, is it any wonder that, industrially, Quebec has become the admiration and the envy of this continent, and the one

province in Canada where foreign capital seeks investment? Is it any wonder that a man who knows the conditions in Quebec as Sir Andrew MacPhail does should speak of that province in these terms:
" Quebecers were referred to as Canadians and there was nothing more true. It was very significant that the spirit of Quebec governed Canada, and without that spirit Canada could not be governed.
" The people had inherited the qualities of their forefathers, and these qualities, which had kept France to the fore in Europe had also kept Quebec in the lead in Canada.
**. It was the spirit of Quebec that made of the province a paradise of common sense, of political wisdom and of personal liberty. If that spirit could be maintained, Quebec would be the last refuge of civilization on the continent."
Mr. Speaker, no more deserved tribute wras ever uttered than that paid by Sir Andrew MacPhail to the spirit of Quebec. Splendid at all times, that spirit has been particularly splendid during the past two years and a half. Reviled, insulted, and outraged on behalf of Union Government. Quebec went quietly and steadily upon her way. In less than eighteen months after winning a criminally conducted election. Union Government was on its knees to Quebec praying that some of its public men would join the Government and save it from destruction. What a spectacle, Mr. Speaker, was presented last summer when the head of the Union Government, the right hon. the Prime Minister himself, and his new Minister of Finance, went sailing up and down the St. Lawrence river calling at every other wharf and beseeching one French Canadian after another to enter the Government and save the country. But the men of Quebec were true to the spirit of Quebec; and as their province had gained in national fibre and in national respect by resolutely refusing to have anything to do with Union Government, they could not be coaxed, bribed, or cajoled into an alliance of any kind with the vilifiers of their province, their race, and their creed. , And so, Sir, they remain aloof and apart from this Union Government conserving their strength for the day upon which the spirit of their province will be triumphantly justified by the defeat of the cowering politicians who let loose the floodgates of passion and prejudice, and who to-day cry aloud to be saved from the ghosts of their own raising.
Mr. Speaker, we hear from time to time a great deal of talk about the need of unity in this country; we have heard during this debate declarations of that kind
from the hon. member for London (Mr. Gronyn), from the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Whidden), and from other hon. gentlemen. As I listened to these hon. members I could not help reflecting that they were somewhat late with their appeals, and that there would have been more point in those appeals if they had been made, for instance, two years ago last December, while, the general election was in progress. As the result of that election the present Government attained office. This Government is called a Union Government, but Sir, it has destroyed every vestige of unity in this country. How could it be otherwise when the head of the Government is a gentleman who, a little over two years ago, used language in this House calculated to incite returned soldiers to turn their arms against those who dared oppose him and his policy? So that there may be no doubt of what the right hon. gentleman said I will quote his exact words. They will be found in Hansard for 1917 at page 2195. He then stated:	.
If what are left of 400,000 such men come back to Canada with fierce resentment, and even rage in their hearts, conscious that they have been deserted and betrayed, how shall we meet them when they ask the reason? I am not so much concerned for the day when this Bill becomes law, as for the day when these men return, if it is rejected.
That is the language used by the Prime Minister, and its meaning admits of no doubt. Naturally, with such a man at the head of this Government national unity is an impossibility. But, Sir, it is doubly impossible when the aims and objects of a body from which the right hon. gentleman derives his chief support are made known. That body is the Orange Order of Canada; and I propose to disclose to the House and to the country the kind of contribution to national unity that this chief prop of Union Government has been making.
Mr. Speaker, if I were to quote statements about the Orange Order made by persons not members of the Order it' might be objected that such statements were prejudiced or were incorrect or unreliable, because made by persons without actual personal knowledge of the aims and objects of the Orange Order. In order that no such objection may be urged, I propose letting the Orangemen speak for themselves, and I am going to read from a circular which carries the names of the leaders of Orangeism in the province of Ontario. The circular is self-explanatory, and while I will not read the whole of it on account of its length, I will be pleased when I am through with it

to hand it over to any person who may be desirous of seeing all that it contains. It has to be kept in mind, Mr. Speaker, that I am about to quote from this circular for the purpose of making it clear that while the sentiments that find expression in its pages are held by any considerable number of our people, and are sanctioned by any government in this country, national unity is a hollow phrase and a mockery of existing political conditions.
The circular, which might well be termed "A Canadian Hymn of Hate" begins in this fashion:
(Strictly Confidential.)
To be referred to or read only within the tiled doors of lodge, chapter or preceptory, and must on no account pass out of your possession.
Report of the Joint Legislation Committee of the Orange Order.
70 Dewson street, Toronto, Ont., March 1, 1918.
Dear Sir and Brother,-As soon as you receive this copy of the report of the Joint Legislation Committee, will you very kindly return a note acknowledging the receipt. This is very important, as w'e are anxious to know that the document comes into the right hands. A stamped addressed envelope is enclosed for this reply.
A further report will be presented to the coming session of the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of British America at its meeting, in Charlottetown, Prince Edward Island, next July.
Our financial year ends on March 31, and the report will be issued shortly thereafter.
I am, faithfully and fraternally yours,
Signed W. BANKS,
Secretary-Treasurer.
R. W. Sir and Brethren-Your Joint Committee on Legislation beg leave to report as follows:
The black clouds of war still overshadow God's beautiful world, and the bloodthirsty and impious War Lord of Germany continues, with the aid of his willing and equally guilty satellites, to pollute the earth, to break every promise, to boast in his sinfulness that he is God's representative on earth, whereas we know he is the Devil's most faithful ally.
Then they come down to matters more prosaic:
At our last meeting we reported that the Premier, in answer to our urgent request for compulsory military service on the draft principle, had said if an emergency arose he would not hesitate to follow such a course.
We continued our effort for this military service law, and shortly before the Military Service Act was introduced into the Commons a deputation from our committee which went to Ottawa, were assured that a measure of compulsory military service would be introduced, and this has, of course, now become law. ******
We have renewed our request for the exclusion from Canada of all evil-disposed and disloyal people wrho may desire to enter our Dominion

from the British Isles or other lands, under whatever name or disguise they may assume.
We have asked for the exclusion of alien enemy immigrants, for the refusal of land grants to all alien enemies, and we are pleased to report that by instructions to the customs officers, immigration officers and land agents, our requests along these lines are being carried out.
Naturalization of people from alien enemy countries is at a standstill, and the War Elections Act was passed, as we urged it should, by which alien enemies in Canada were almost entirely disfranchised.
Acting in hearty co-operation, as we always do, our own Order, through its M.W. Grand Master, Dr. Ellis, and the Royal Black Knights through their Grand Master, Bro. A.A. Gray, issued an appeal to both memberships to use every legitimate means to secure the support of the members of Parliament in every constituency for the Military Service Act and the Wartime Elections Act. We must see to it that the safe-guards of this Election Act are not thrown away when the war is over.
I commend that to your notice, Mr. Speaker, in view of the new franchise Act we are promised.
We are urging the Government to see to it that people who, by reason of peace treaties at the close of the war may be entitled to come here from alien countries, should not be enfranchised at all, and that under no circumstances shall their descendants, or the descendants of people of alien enemy countries now naturalized here be enfranchised until they can read and write in the English language and until they sign a document agreeing to obey our laws, learn the English language, have it efficiently taught in their schools, and to forfeit all their property and civil rights and be liable to deportation on conviction of failure in these matters.
/ ******
We congratulate the Ontario Government-
Of course, this was drafted, Mr. Speaker, long before the recent Ontario election.

on its new land regulations, which provide against any alien enemy or miljtary shirker securing lands in New Ontario, and for the first time in the history of this Dominion it is made part of the contract for securing the land that the would-be settler agrees to forfeit his claim if he disobeys the military and other laws of the Dominion, and if he refuses or neglects to have his children educated thoroughly in English, or disobeys the school laws, or other laws of the province.
With Bro. the Hon. G. H. Ferguson, as Minister of Crown Lands-
There no longer, Mr. Speaker.
-with R. W. Bro. Dane as Commissioner for these new lands, and W. Bro. W. D. McPherson Chairman of the Soldiers' Aid Commission, which is helping to settle soldiers in the North, we hope soon to have the disloyal French Canadian element on these new lands in their proper place.

We must not, however, stop at this. We must now begin a systematic campaign for the inspection of every convent, nunnery, monastery, anti other secret places, places men and women are immured. We must demand legislation for the registration of every inmate, for the registration of all births and deaths, for the notification of every removal from one institution to another, for the absolute prohibition of the removal to places outside of this province of any inmate of these institutions, and for the holding of an inquest in case of every death in these places, as is necessary in the case of the death of any other prisoner.

Now is the time to act, and to act persistently and continuously, until we win.
In spring and early summer there . were rumours that in some Romish centres arms were coming in and drilling taking place among Romanists. We immediately started searching investigations, and the Provincial Government employed secret service men also to investigate. The Dominion Government, at our request, also investigated.
And then, iMr. Speaker, listen to this.
No definite case was found, but there is an almost absolute certainty that these investigations put an end to any action Rome had planned for causing trouble here. The Dominion Government insists now on knowing the actual contents of packages, cases and other articles coming here from the States, as Britain does on all shipments from there.
Once again we desire to impress upon all officers and members the wisdom of doing everything possible to assist our returned soldiers. Our secretary has had scores of cases, in which our Orange members at the front have asked that their children, their wives, and their parents, be looked after. Some cases were very sad. In every case prompt attention was paid and many letters of grateful thanks have been received. Our secretary is a member of the Ontario Soldiers' Aid Commission, and is thus better able to attend to those cases. He has now the names and addresses of over 15,000 returned Ontario soldiers,

Possible voters, you see, Mr. Speaker. (Reading):

and in the course of the next few months
he intends supplying every County Master with the names and addresses of these men in his county, so that those eligible can be induced to join the lodges in their respective localities. The entrance fees in such cases might be entirely abolished or reduced to a minimum.
The advisability of getting these men to join our ranks has been made perfectly obvious by the results of the general elections. It seems to us that parties are so changing that this Order, if our leaders are far-seeing and wise, will become the governing force in Dominion affairs, gathering to its side all loyal Englishspeaking and Protestant people. Very, very few Roman Catholics will aid us,

key to its policy to-day as it ever was in the days that are past. Hence, Sir, I unhesitatingly affirm in this House that in the return of the Liberal party to power lies the hope for national unity in this Dominion of Canada.
Much of the discussion, Sir, to which you have listened in this debate has centered on the amendment moved by the honi. leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King). That amendment calls for a dissolution and an election. Speakers on the Government side of the House have challenged the arguments advanced from this side in support of the amendment.. I now propose to offer them an argument used by a member of the Government which, in my judgment, affords the strongest possible - justification for the amendment of the hon.-leader of the Opposition.
Not long ago, the President of the Privy Council made a pilgrimage to the town of Port Hope. He spoke there, and he proved the case of the people against Union Government more convincingly than even an opponent of the Government could have done. In effect, the hon. gentleman told the people of Port Hope that he knew that Union Government was singularly unpopular everywhere, and then he proceeded to state the reasons for this unpopularity. Why, Mr. Speaker, he should have sought any reason beyond his own presence in the Government is something the ordinary man cannot understand. However, he did give another reason-the most extraordinary one a Canadian audience ever listened to. The Government's unpopularity, he said, was due to its shining virtues as reflected by its administration of public affairs.
Now, Sir, here is a distinct admission by the most moral member of the Government, that it no longer possesses the confidence of the country, and that it. is merely holding on to office in the forlorn hope that something may turn up. In our political history never before has a minister of the Crown said publicly and so distinctly, that he knew that he and his colleagues were hanging on to office in defiance of the will of the people they are misgoverning. How his colleagues must have blessed him for that speech ! It gave their whole case away. It placed them in the position of men who are too good for this world, and not yet ready for the next, and, as you know, Mr. Speaker, such ethereal, creatures as that are liable to be roughly handled by the sinners who constitute the great majority at election times. No wonder, then, that the Toronto Globe and other papers like it are telling the Government to get

out -to dissolve and hold an election. It is because this feeling is so widespread that I regard the amendment placed in your hands as most timely, and it is my intention to support it with my vote.

Hon. NEWTON W. ROWELL (President of the Privy Council):	Mr. Speaker, this
House was called for the despatch of public business, not to give an opportunity to an hon. member to gratify his personal spite as against another member of this House. Hon. gentlemen have left their homes, from the Atlantic to the Pacific, and have come here to transact the nation's business in the hour of the nation's need; yet this House spent the entire afternoon in listening to an address from an exPrivy Councillor, the whole subject of which was simply to gratify an apparently unsatisfied personal animosity against a member on this side of the House to whom he attributes some responsibility for the disappointment of his political ambitions in the year 1917. I had hoped, Mr. Speaker, if it were my privilege to take part in this debate, to discuss some of the important public questions now before the people of this country and demanding the consideration of the House. I deeply regret, as I am sure you all regret, that by reason of the character of the address delivered by the hon. member for Russell (Mr. Murphy) it is necessary for me to take up some of your time at least in dealing with the matters which he has mentioned. I may, however, say that I think hon. members are to be congratulated on the fact that there is only one member of the House, who would make such an exhibition of himself as did the hon. gentleman.
I rise to reply to the hon. member not because the statements he made this afternoon demand an answer at my hands, nor to satisfy the members on the other side of the House nor on the Government side. The unsympathetic manner in which the remarks of my hon. friend were received by his own colleagues on his own side is the best evidence to the House and the country that the men who know him best trust him least. Nor is it necessary that I should reply to the remarks of the hon. member to the people who know me in this province or throughout the Dominion of Canada. My record in the public life of

this country is a sufficient answer to what the hon. member has said. Nor is it necessary that I should rise to reply to the people of this country who know the member for Russell. His record and his conduct are a sufficient answer to his own accusations. I rise because there are some people, no doubt, in this province and in this Dominion who may not know either of us, who may not know the record of the hon. member or of myself as well as the member's of this House do, and by whom, therefore, my silence might be misconstrued if I did not pay some attention to the hon. member.
Every man recognizes that the good opinion of decent, honourable and public-spirited citizens is one of the most valuable possessions that any man can have-a priceless possession. Every man recognizes and values the good opinion of his fellow-citizens. But there are some men-and the members of the House will recognize them -whose hostility and opposition constitute the greatest compliment that can be paid to a man. I congratulate myself on having earned the hostility of the hon. member for Russell.
The hon. gentleman started out by telling us that he delivered a speech in this House in 1918. He did. He made an even worse exhibition of himself in 1918 than he did to-day. He made it at a time when this country was in the midst of a war; he made it at a time when this country required to combine all its energies and resources to back up the men overseas and to help to win the war. He made an inflammatory declaration and appeal in this House, not for the purpose of backing up our men overseas, not for the purpose of uniting the people of Canada in support of the war but for the purpose of dividing the people of Canada. If the hon. member had expended one tithe of the energy in helping Canada to prosecute the war and defeat the Germans that he has in his speeches attacking me he would have been rendering a real service to Canada.
The hon. member said that he rose in the House on that occasion before six o'clock and that, due to the courtesy of the Speaker and the leader of the Government, his speech was adjourned until the House resumed in the evening. That is perfectly true. I was here up to six o'clock but I was not here in the evening for the reason that I have stated before, but I repeat that the hon. member knew when he rose that he was going to spend a great part of his time in a personal attack upon me and yet he had neither the manliness
nor the courage to give me notice of the fact so that I might have an opportunity of making answer in his presence and in the presence of hon. members of the House to the false statements that he was about to make, statements which he knew to be false when he made them. He said that he expected that I would rise in my place to a question of privilege when I returned to the House. Well the hon. gentleman had the opportunity last session of rising to a question of privilege in order to attempt to reply to me?

I will deal with my hon. friend in time; do not worry. At that time I inquired of the Speaker of the House and I found that the rule is perfectly clear, that a debate once closed cannot be reopened during the session, and that when a debate is closed it cannot be referred to in a subsequent debate. So it is clear that I was precluded by the rules of the House from dealing with the matter on that occasion. The member for Russell said my colleagues " let the debate go by default." My colleagues reported to me-hon. members in the House will appreciate the reason-that in view of the inflammatory character of the appeal made by the member for Russell their view was that if a reply was made in the same spirit it might involve an acrimonious racial and religious controversy in' this House which would greatly aggravate the conditions in Quebec at that time; and it was their desire to avoid that. They permitted the debate to close in my absence, and I was a victim of the situation; I was unable to reply on that occasion.
My hon. friend has stated that although I did reply in December, 1918, in Bowman-ville, and in September, 1919, in this House, I only dealt with some of the accusations he made, and the other accusations [DOT]still stand undenied and unanswered. Mr. Speaker, that statement by the hon. member is but another evidence of his recklessness in regard to the truth. Let him turn to my address delivered at Bow-manville-he has a copy of it-and he will find that I said I was taking up but a few of the idle and false stories that had been circulated as samples of the character of

the whole; and speaking in this House last session I dealt with the matter in the same way. My hon. friend will find on page 415 of the Unrevised Hansard of 1919 this statement:
I will not trouble the House with the other petty matters mentioned in the speech of the hon. member for Russell. They are as misleading and as false as the one with which I have dealt.
Yet in the face of these statements in both speeches, the hon. gentleman rises in the House this afternoon and tells hon. gentlemen that I did not deny his statements. I have practised in the Courts of the Province of Ontario for almost thirty years, and I speak with a consciousness of what I am saying when I state that in all my experience of witnesses in the box I never met one more reckless as regards the truth than the hon. member for Russell.
iMay I now take up some of these other matters. I will not take up the time of the House to go into them all; I will just take a few .more samples so that hon. gentlemen may see the character of the statements made by the hon. member for Russell.
The hon. member started off this afternoon by saying that I bad not answered the charge he made out that I had served the Ross Government for profit, or had found it very profitable to become solicitor in the re-organization of the great Soo Corporation. In the statement which he made on that occasion he said that in the course of four or five years I had added to my personal earnings, or profits a sum over $100,000. Well, Mr. Speaker, when I read that, it reminded me of the story of the death of Mark Twain. The report of Mark Twain's death was cabled across the sea and when the newspaper reporter went to his residence to inquire__ about it he was shown into the presence of Mark Twain himself. Asked about the truth of tihe rumour, Mark Twain said the report of his death was greatly exaggerated. The statement of my hon. friend is greatly exaggerated. I do not recall at the present time what the fees of my firm were during those years, but I will say to the hon. member that the greater part of those fees were not earned because of political association with the Ross Government or any other Government. My firm were appointed counsel to the Soo Corporation in July, 1904. The Ross Government went out of power in January, 1905, and when there was a Conservative Government in power in the province of Ontario, the greater part of these fees were earned by my firm as counsel for

the Lake Superior Corporation. From the very fact that the Government had guaranteed a loan of $2,000,000 that company did have fairly close relations with the Government. In some respects it was dependent on the Government's good will; and I am not violating any confidence, I am simply stating a fact, when I say that when the Government of Sir Ja/mes Whitney came into power, Sir James thought the position of solicitor for the corporation was a political appointment, and he sent to the president of the corporation the name of a Conservative lawyer in the city of Toronto whom he desired to have substituted for myself as solicitor for that corporation. Although the company was to some extent dependent on the Government they said "the choice of our counsel is a matter for the board of directors of the corporation. We are satisfied with the service that is being rendered and we intend to continue the same counsel." So, notwithstanding the representation of the Prime Minister of Ontario my firm was continued as counsel for the Soo Company. Now, if .my hon. friend had said that in the practice of my profession, I could earn $25,000 .a year I am not prepared to deny it. The fact is that I could .in the practice of my profession earn that amount but I would, Mr. Speaker, like to ask this:	If I could earn that amount in
my profession and I came down here to serve my country at $7,000 a year, what evidence is that of my desire to profit at the expense of my country?
The hon. gentleman seemed to attach great weight to the fact that when I made a trip overseas some political friends contributed to the expense, and I think he mentioned in that connection three thousand and some odd dollars. Well, that again, like the report of Mark Twain's death, was greatly exaggerated. The amount was not so large as that, but it is true that some of the Liberals of the Province of Ontario did provide the bulk of the expenses of that trip. Why did they provide it? They said they believed I could do more valuable work in recruiting throughout the Province of Ontario if I had the opportunity of coming in touch with the actual conditions at. the front-seeing the men in the trenches and the work they were doing, and then come back and appeal to my fellow citizens to support them. The only contribution I made was giving my time, I took it away from my profession-and the consequent loss such as any man must meet in absenting himself from his profession-but the expense was paid in that way. My only regret is that

some of the friends of the hon. member for Russell did not do the same thing for him. If he had seen the conditions overseas-the actual need of reinforcements to fill up the ranks of our gallant men and of making every effort to support them in their struggle against Germany, it is incredible to me that the hon. gentleman would have taken the course which he afterwards did in reference to the war.
The hon. gentleman also says that I sent a friend of mine, Colonel Deacon, up to bribe a citizen of London to desert the Liberal party on the promise of a position as Chairman of the War Purchasing Commission. That is just as false as the other statements of the hon. member for Russell. What are the facts? The hon. members oi this House know the character of the War Purchasing Commission. Membership in it was not a position of emolument, it was an opportunity for service. The members of that War Commission were not paid a salary, they gave their services in an honorary capacity. When Sir Edward Kemp was appointed and went overseas as Overseas Minister of Militia there was a vacancy on the Board. It was not the position of Chairman because it was understood that Sir Hormisdas Laporte, who had rendered such splendid service would be made Chairman, but it was dhe position of one of the members of the Commission. What did I do? I am glad my hon. friend from West Lambton (Mr. Pardee) is in the House.
I consulted my hon. friend from West Lambton (Mr. Pardee) as to who in his judgment would be the best man to select from among the business men of Western Ontario who were Liberals as a member for this board. We discussed the matter together and agreed upon three names, as my hon. friend will remember. The first was Mr. Gordon McGregor, of the Ford Company at Windsor, the other was Mr. Gartshore of the MoClary Foundry Company, London, and the third was Mr. Little of the Robinson, Little Company. My hon. friend and I agreed that if we could secure any one of those men as a member of the War Purchasing Commission-not in an office of emolument, but without emolument the Government and the country would be fortunate. I first asked Mr. McGregor if he would accept a position on that commission. He was not a supporter of this Government; on the contrary, he supported my hon. friend from North Essex (Mr. Kennedy), and if the latter gentleman was in the House he would tell us so, I have no doubt. Mr. McGregor 17
was not asked if he would support this Government or not; he was asked if he would be prepared to serve Canada in that position. After giving the matter due consideration he was compelled to decline owing to urgent business demands. Then we approached Mr. Gartshore, who declined to serve for a similar reason. The third gentleman to whom the hon. member for Russell referred this afternoon was then offered the position. But the circumstances stated by him this afternoon in connection with that offer I can only characterize as a yarn concocted out of whole cloth. The sole object which animated my hon. friend from West Lambton and myself was to get one of the best possible Liberal business men in Ontario to take that important and responsible post in the public service.
Then the member for Russell referred to another matter. He stated that I had not answered his charge that my place in Parliament was practically bought by offering a seat in the Senate to the Hon. Senator Mullholland. I am sorry that my hon. friend is not in the House to-night. " He who fights and runs away may live to fight another day." But, Mr. Speaker, I desire to place my answer on Hansard so that he can read it if he will not hear it:	If
after the bluster of the past two years of what this giant would do to me if he had an opportunity, he has done his best this afternoon, I am prepared for him to return to the attack as often as he likes, but I can assure the House that anything he can say will be as false no doubt as the statements he has already made.
I would like to ask my hon. friend (Mr. Murphy) if he were present what he would say to these parallel cases:	When the
hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding) joined the Cabinet of the late Right Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier Mr. F. G. Forbes was the member for that constituency and was appointed to the Bench in order that Mr. Fielding might have a seat in this House. Would the hon. member for Russell say that Mr. Fielding bribed Mr. Forbes in order that he might get a seat in this House, or that the late Right Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier bribed Mr. Forbes for the same purpose?
When the late Hon. A. G. Blair entered the Government he had no seat. Did Mr. Blair or Sir Wilfrid Laurier bribe Mr. E. G. King, the then member for Sun-bury and Queen's who resigned in favour of Mr. Blair, by a seat in the Senate. Will hon. members on the other side suggest that when Hon. Mr. Templeman came into

the House Mr. George Riley from Victoria, B.C. was bribed because he retired and was given a seat in the Senate in order to provide a place for Mr. Templeman? When the Hon. Mr. Graham entered this House did he bribe Mr. Derbyshire the member for Brockville to make way for him by the promise of a seat in the Senate? Did the late Bir Wilfrid Laurier bribe Mr. Derbyshire by a similar promise? When the Hon. Senator Beith did not accept nomination in Durham in 1904, but gave it to Sir Alan Aylesworth, was he bribed to do so? It is true he was not appointed to the Senate immediately, and some of his friends thought he was passed over, but in due time he was appointed. Will my hon. friends opposite suggest that Senator Beith was bribed? Then came a change of Government and Sir Robert Borden came into power. Dr. J. W. Daniel retired from St. John, N.B. and was made Senator to make way for Hon. J. D. Hazen; and Mr. George Taylor retired from Leeds to make way for my hon. friend, the ex-Minister of Finance (Sir Thomas White); and Mr. George Gordon retired from Nipissing in order that the late Hon. Frank Cochrane might become Minister of Railways, were these members biibed to give up their seats? No hon. member w'ill make any such suggestion. Every hon. member knows that it has been the custom and tradition in both political parties when an hon. member makes way for a Cabinet minister to recognize the public spirit of that member by appointment to the Senate or to the Bench, or to some other suitable public position.
Now, my hon. friend may say that that is not a wise policy nor a good practice. Well, if he will advocate a reform of the Senate and a complete change in the method of appointment, I for one will support him. Mr. Speaker, I am one of those Liberals who believe that the Liberal Party failed in its duty while in power in that it did not carry out its pledge to reform the Senate. I still believe that the Senate should be reformed and made more representative of the sentiment of the people, and I stand on the policy upon which the Liberal Party stood during all that period.
But the crowning piece of casuistry, Mr. Speaker, of which the member for Russell has been guilty is his reference to the " Secretarial Fund." Let me read to you, Mr. Speaker, the exact statement made by Mr. Murphy in the House in 1918 with reference to that fund. He then said:
Now, Sir, what happened when the hon. gentleman entered the provincial field of politics?
[Mr. Rowell-I
With his usual presence of mind he arranged with his friends to form a committee for the purpose of raising a fund to guarantee him against any loss while engaged in his work as Provincial leader. Mr. A. E. Ames, of Toronto, was chairman of the committee, and in addition to Sir Joseph Flavelle, the contributors included several other Toronto gentlemen. The fund itself was called the " Secretarial Fund," and I am informed that it varied in amount from $9,000 to $11,000 a year. Again, the exact amount raised in any one year is immaterial ; the point it establishes is that as Provincial leader the hon. member for Durham was protected against any sacrifice while he retained that position.
I appeal to hon. members, just -as I did last September, what meaning did you take out .of that statement; and what meaning did the hon. mfember for Russell intend that you should take out of that statement? Exactly the meaning that you and the people of this country took out of it, namely, that out of that fund moneys had been paid to me to compensate me for my loss of time, in connection with my work as Provincial leader.
The hon. member for Russell referred to the letter he wrote to Mr. Bowman, Chief Liberal Whip. Why did he not read the letter he received from Mr. Bowman? Mr. Bowman is a supporter of my hon. friends on the other side of the House. When he read the statement by the member for Russell, knowing how false it was, although he was not a political supporter of mine, he felt compelled to enter his protest against such a false statement. It was the same with contributors to the fund. Let me read a letter, Mr. Speaker, that the committee got from one of the most distinguished Liberals and one of the most influential supporters of my hon. friend the leader of the Opposition, in Eastern Ontario. His name is known from one end of the province of Ontario to the other. What did this contributor say in his letter to Mr. Ames, the chairman, in reference to this matter? I quote:
- After being in the South the latter part of the winter, I have read the speech of the Hon. Mr. Murphy on my return home, and, amongst other things in his attack on Mr. Rowell, I note with considerable interest and surprise that he states that the Secretarial Fund to the extent of nine to eleven thousand dollars a year was paid to Mr. Rowell.
The member for Russell did not say that, but that (was the inference that was conveyed and the inference that this contributor to the fund drew from the hon. gentleman's remarks.
As I know, you were chiefly instrumental of raising this Fund, and I think were the Treasurer. I would ask if Mr, Murphy is right in this. I cannot conceive that such a thing is possible, for, when I was asked to subscribe to this Fund, I was not only told it was a Secre-

tarial Fund, but actually for the purpose of paying Mr. Howell's secretarial expenses, such as secretaries, postage, etc., etc.
While Mr. Rowell will wait his own good time, I have no doubt this point is one he ' should not fail to take up on the floor of the House, and, in the meantime, as a subscriber, I would like to know if Mr. Murphy is wrong.
Now, the member for Russell said this afternoon that in his letter to Mr. Bowman he had said that he did not say I had shared .personally in the fund mentioned, but that it was to guarantee me against loss. Well, if it was to guarantee me against loss it meant that I (would have to take money out of the fund, because I was losing in the practice of my profession on account of the time that I was giving to the work of leader of the Opposition. But I want to- take the statement of the hon. member as it stands. According to his own admission he knew that I had not received one dollar out of that fund; yet he came to the House of Commons and with deliberate ingenuity frames a statement conveying a totally false impression and framed it in such a way that he thinks he can crawl out from responsibility When it found out. Mr. (Speaker, the man who with cool calculation, deliberately surveying a situation, believes that it is to his profit to lie and does deliberately lie', open and above-board *and is prepared to take the consequences if he is found out-we may have' no respect jfor that man, but we do not despise him. But the man who toy ingenuity conveys an equally false impression and does it in such a way that he thinks he can escape the .consequences otf his falsehood, that man adds to the "sin of falsehood that of cowardice.

Well, if it afforded him any comfort I am glad, because so far as T was concerned it was of interest to me, and I am glad he has drawn attention to it. But the point which I desire to draw particular attention is the reference in the report to the Yojang Men's Liberal Federation. The hon. member referred to that organization as being wholly independent of the Liberal party and conveyed the impression that that was the organization of which I was the head in connection with the work of the provincial Liberal party. If that is his view he is wholly mistaken. That organization was a federation of the young Liberal clubs of Ontario. The leader of the Opposition knows of the organization; other hon. members on the other side know of it. It was independent of the actual political organization, for this reason: The young Liberals of Ontario, the members of these clubs, desired to have freedom to express their own opinions on public issues. I believed that it was in the public interest that they should have that freedom; they preferred independence to any association with the political organization. But the point to which I particularly wish to refer is this. The hon. member said that the motto of this Young Liberal Federation was "service," and he seemed to get a great deal of pleasure out of repeating that word. He said it looked as if this was the organization of some (Sunday school class having no relation to the Liberal party. Mr. Speaker, it is because a section of the Liberal party of Ontario, the section which could be influenced by the member for Russell, had wholly lost the spirit of service and were in politics as part of the game and for what they could get out of it, that the Liberal party received such a crushing defeat in Ontario on more than one oc-

easion. My hon. friend should learn the meaning of the word "service." I say it to the credit and the honour of the young men who were members of these clubs and who had as their motto the word "service" that when a few months later war broke out and the call went forth for young men to volunteer, the ranks of these clubs were depleted because of the numbers of their members who, inspired by the spirit of service, went forth to fight for their country. I can only regret that the member for Russell did not even during the course of the war learn the true significance of the word "service."
The hon. member made light of what he called the "Sunday school idea of service." Well, if that be the Sunday school idea of service, then I stand in this House for the Sunday school idea of service; for it is only the spirit of service that can save the country in such an hour as this, just as that spirit saved it in the critical days of the war. It was because that spirit of service did not animate the member for Russell and others that when the critical hour came and members of the Liberal party and others had to decide whether they would choose the ideal of service-service for the men overseas; service to their country-service to the cause for which we were fighting -there was a cleavage, and the men who stood for service joined together in the formation and support of Union Government. I do not wonder that the hon. member for Russell does not care for the word "service," neither voluntary nor compulsory, neither civil nor military.
The hon. member for Russell said that there were several other funds. I think, if I recall aright, there were two he mentioned; the prohibition fund and the campaign fund of 1914. Well, his knowledge is somewhat better than mine. So far as I am aware, there was only one fund, the prohibition campaign fund of 1914, which was the one fund for the two purposes, because that campaign was fought on the issue "abolish the bar." The hon. member for Russell said that he would like to see a list of the contributors to that fund. I have never seen the list myself. The fund was raised by a provincial Liberal committee in Ontario and was administered by them in connection with the campaign of 1914; but I can tell you this, Mr. Speaker, because it came to my knowledge, that while other Liberals in the city of Ottawa contributed to that fund and their names will be found on the list, the name of the hon. member for Russell will not appear there, for he declined to give a contribution to assist the provincial Liberal party in its campaign of 
"abolish the bar" in 1914. Therefore, I was not surprised when, in the June session of last year, we came to vote on the Government Prohibition Bill, the hon. member for Russell led the Opposition in rising to oppose the resolution which- the Prime Minister moved in the House. Perhaps that is another reason for his opposition to me, namely, that he does not agree with my views on that issue as he does not on some other issues. He suggests that I received some compensation at some time out of the prohibition fund. Here he makes a direct statement. Well, that is equally false with the other statement. I never received a cent of compensation, direct or indirect, out of that fund nor out of any other fund for my personal service at any time whatever. I never received a cent of contribution for any address that I made on that question or on any other question at any time in my life. I am glad to say that I have always been able to afford-if you care to put the case on that ground-to render a .measure of service in the causes in which I believe, without accepting any compensation for my service.
My hon. friend next finds something in which he takes a great delight. He says: Now, I have this man; he is a tax evader, and he says that I appealed from taxation in Toronto because I was living in Ottawa and-my income as a Privy Councillor would be exempt in the city of Ottawa. If a Privy Councillor's salary was exempt under the law why was I not entitled to the benefit of the exemption. My recollection, however, is that the matter was taken up while I was in England by my office and they lodged the appeal, but may I add I did not know at that time that, under the agreement with the city of Ottawa, a Privy Councillor's salary was exempt from taxation. I do not believe it is a sound principle that either a Privy Councillor's salary or a Civil Servant's salary should be exempt from municipal taxation, and I am glad that I am a member of a Government which has negotiated with the city of Ottawa a new agreement whereby that exemption has been wiped out. No longer will a Privy Councillor's salary be exempt from taxation.
My hon. friend devoted much time to my North Bay address. I dealt with that .matter at the last session of the House, and it is not my intention to-night to go over the matters I then discussed. Hon. members who wish to see my statement can find it in Hansard as of that date; but there are just one or two observations I wish to make in view of the remarks of the hon. member for Russell to-day. The hon. member stated

that he had a letter that I had written to somebody, I think, he said in the month of January, 1918, in which letter I, in effect, admitted that I had made a statement without any knowledge of the facts and that I was only then proceeding to investigate the facts. I am sorry the hon. member did not produce the letter, and he did not tell us to whom the letter was written. So far as I can find in my records, I can only locate two letters written about that time. It may be that either or both of these letters have come into the hands of the hon. member for Russell. If they have, I only regret that he did not read either or both of them to the House. But just to see what I did say on that occasion in reference to this matter, permit me to turn to one of these letters, because my statement on this point does not materially differ in the two letters. I received a letter which enclosed a clipping from my North Bay address, and I was asked as to the correctness of that statement, the writer stating that I had many Roman Catholic friends and he was sure I did not desire to say anything disrespectful to my Roman Catholic friends. I replied:
I realize that many of my best friends are Roman Catholics, and I should deeply regret saying anything that would hurt their feelings, and particularly anything that was not fully warranted by the facts. I think the extract quoted hardly gives a fair view of what I Aid. I enclose herewith the context so that you may see just what I stated. If I am incorrect in the statement I should be very glad to know it, but my statement was based upon information received during the past two or three years from sources which I believe to be absolutely reliable. The position, which I was informed the members of those Orders took, was that this war was a judgment of Heaven against France for her apostasy from the Church and for the manner in which she had treated the Church.
Then, in discussing the matter further, I said:
I shall make further inquiries about the matter and see what the result is.
If the hon. member for Russell had either of these letters before him, he had before him the statement that what I said at that time was based on information which I had received during the past two or three years, but in view of the letters which I had received that I purposed making further inquiries in respect to the matter. I only want to add this one further word in reference to it. As I saitRin the House last session, and as I said in Bowmanville the year before, at the time I spoke, I did not know that members of religious orders had gone over to France to fight in the war. I said that, had I known that, I would have paid
them the tribute that I did to the other clergy of the Roman Catholic Church and which was undoubtedly their due. My view -and a fair reading of my statement will show it-was that I was not referring to the men who had gone overseas but to those in the province of Quebec who had remained behind. But I said then, and I repeat now, that if my language was capable of the construction that it applied to the men who had gone overseas, I regret it, because I would be the last man in the world to say anything disrespectful to or anything other than the warmest word of appreciation of men who had gone overseas to serve their country as these men did. But I should like to add this one word, that I am sure it is a matter of regret to all. the members of the House that, with these magnificent examples before him of heroic patriotism on th- part of members of religious orders in Quebec, the hon. member for Russell (Mr. Murphy) did not become a veritable Peter th Hermit, going from one end of the country to the other to rouse the people to follow the example of these men who went overseas. Unfortunately, Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Russell only magnified their service and their sacrifice when he thought he could gain some political advantage and kudos for himself at the expense of a political opponent.
I shall not attempt to follow the hon. member through all the meanderings of that rambling and lengthy address of his.; It is a case Where the mountain laboured and brought forth a mouse. But I must mention one or two other matters.
The hon. member for Russell referred to loyalty to colleagues. I could hardly believe my ears when I heard him speaking of loyalty to colleagues, and I am sure there was more than one member seated either beside him or 'behind him who must have been astonished when tney heard those words from the hon. member for Russell, Hon. members on the Opposition side are not ignorant, and hon. members on the Government side are not' ignorant of the situation that has developed. The hon. member for Russell is a veritable political Jack-the-Ripper. When he cannot find an hon. member on this side of the House on wdiorn to practise the peculiar art in which he professes to have such ski'll, he turns to hon. members on his own side of the House.. No hon. member on the other side of the House enjoys in larger measure the confidence and esteem of members on both sides of the House than the chief Opposition Whip, the hon. member for Chateau-
[DOT]m

guay-Huntingdon (Mr. Robb). Everybody knows that the hon. member for Russell has been after his scalp. Why, Mr. Speaker? Because the leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King), the Chief Whip (Mr. Robb), and the hon. member for Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe), and other hon. members on the other side of the House want to make that section of the Liberal party a national Liberal party, but the hon. member of Russell is determined to keep it merely a religious group. It is even reported that he does not stop at the Chief Whip and others but -challenges the supremacy even of the leader himself, and I have heard that the threat has been made that if he cannot have his way he may leave the party and join the United Farmers. Mr. Speaker, I do not know what crimes the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar) and the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark) and those who sit around them have committed, that they should deserve such a fate. "We all know the No Man's Land down there which they have established between themselves, and the official Opposition, and I can imagine that if the hon. member for Russell started to move his seat down that way, No Man's Land would soon be barricaded with benches and barbed wire to protect the farmers' group from receiving his assistance.

speechtext: Keep your squabble to your own end.

speechtext: That is what I am trying to do, Mr. Speaker. I am trying to protect my hon. friend from this addition to his ranks.

maintopic: DAUGHTERS OF CANADA, INCORPORATED 1919, DOMINION CHARTER.
speechtext: We do not need any protection.
