maintopic: DAUGHTERS OF CANADA, INCORPORATED 1919, DOMINION CHARTER.
speechtext:
Speaking of the question of loyalty to colleagues the hon. member for Russe'll stated-and he read into my speech a statement which is not there- that I had said or words to that effect, that certain statements made by the hon. member for Marquette in Council indicated a position which he afterwards changed. There is no such statement in my speech. There is nothing in my whole speech which would justify such an inference. The hon. member for RuSsell knows if he read Hansard that when such a statement was hinted at by an hon. member on the other side of the House, it met with a very prompt and vigorous denial. No statement made by me was a disclosure of any confidence of Council, and the hon. member for Russell must have known that, if he read Hansard.
[Mr. Rowell. 1
It is just on a par with the other matters he mentions.
His childish talk about-the Grand Trunk, the Peace Treaty, and matters of that kind I shall not go into, nor shall I attempt to follow his ramblings through various other matters that came up in the course of his speech. In connection with a number of them, there will be plenty of opportunity later on in this House to discuss the real merits of the case. There may be differences of opinion on the question of the labour clauses of the Peace Treaty. If there are, there will be an opportunity in the House for hon. members to express their honest convictions, and I shall reserve what I have to say on that subject until that occasion.
It may be that some hon. mem-9 p.m. bers on the other side of the
House have repented of the approval given to the League of Nations. If so, when the Bulgarian Treaty comes up as the -Covenant of the League is repeated in that Treaty, there will be an opportunity for my hon. friends to, express their views on that occasion. I shall, therefore, not take up the time of the House in discussing it to-day. The hon. member for Russell also referred to the Mounted Police. There is a Bill before the House, and there will be estimates, relating to the Mounted Police, and I shall be glad to discuss the whole question of the Mounted Police either on the Bill or on the estimates. There is nothing that the hon. member has mentioned that I shall not be prepared to discuss'at the proper time and give the House full information, and make a defence, so far as any defence is needed, though I think none is needed of the position of the Government in connection with these matters.
But there is one thing I cannot pass over. The hon. member for Russell referred in a sneering way to the calling together of the patriotic women of Canada in a women's conference in the city of Ottawa in the early part of 1918, when the heads of the principal women's patriotic organizations from the Atlantic to the Pacific, met in conference in -this city in order that they might devise plans for more effective cooperation with the Government in the prosecution of the war. These patriotic and public-spirited women of Canada are made the butt for the-jests of the hon. member for Russell. I cannot believe that in those jests he voiced the sentiment of any member on the Opposition side except his own.
He also referred to the calling together of the Labour Conference. We shall have

an-opportunity of discussing that question when the Labour estimates come before the House, but I want to say that the Union Government took no wiser .step than when the Prime Minister (Sir Robert Borden) included in the Cabinet one of the recognized leaders of labour in Canada and further I believe the Government took a wise step when they invited the leaders of labour from all parts of Canada to come to Ottawa for a conference with the Government in order to establish the most harmonious relations possible between labour and the Government in the prosecution of the war. That policy of co-operation with labour has 'been pursued by Union Government from the day it was formed down to this date, and I submit with confidence that the magnificent position which labour has taken in Canada throughout the war, and the comparative industrial peace we have in this country as compared with practically every other country, is in no small measure due to the really sympathetic attitude of this Government towards the cause of labour in Canada and its desire to co-operate with labour.
The member fox Russell referred to the Department of Health. The hon. member, Mr. Speaker, suggested throughout that I was unfair to the Roman Catholics and the French Canadians. What I have stated before, I repeat here to-night: I challenge any man to point to any statement I have ever .made reflecting upon the French Canadian people of this country; I challenge any man to point to any statement that I have ever .made reflecting upon the Roman Catholic church. The most important appointment I have been called upon to recommend since I became a member of the Government has been that of Deputy Minister of Public Health. Who was appointed to thait position?-a French Canadian and a Roman Catholic-not because he was a French Canadian and a Roman Catholic hut because, surveying the whole field with a dbsire to choose the best .possible .man to serve the people of Canada in that important post, I came to the conclusion that Dr. Amyot, the present Deputy Minister of Health, with -a splendid record overseas, with great professional achievements to his credit, was the best man in Canada for the post. So long as I am in public life, so long as I am called upon to administer public affairs, I shall seek in all appointments, in so far as the Government has any voice in them, and in all my dealing with the people of this country, to consider and deal
with every man on his merits irrespective of his race or religion.
The hon. member announced in opening that the reason he had made his speech was to vindicate the members of his church. I have too much respect for the hierarchy of the Roman Catholic church to believe that the hon. member for Russell had been commissioned for any such business. I do not believe he speaks with any right or authority on behalf of the ecclesiastics of that church. But I have no hesitation in saying that if he did speak with authority, there are not enough ecclesiastics in that church, or an any church, or in all the churches of Canada combined to induce me to depart from the path of duty .as I see it in ithe administration of public affairs.
The member closed with some references to Union Government and the amendment before the House. I have already taken up a longer time than I had intended and I will not discuss these matters further, except to say that Union Government was formed in an hour of grave, national crisis for a great national purpose. It was formed for the war and for reconstruction after the war as the programmes presented to the people showed. What were its achievements during the war? By reason of the strength of sentiment behind the Government, .by reason of the compulsory Military Service Act which they had at their command, they were able to reinforce our troops .at the front and keep them up to strength. Nay, .more, they were able to keep every battalion at the front one hundred men over strength; they were able to .add to our .machine gun equipment and personnel;' they were able to .add to our engineers and to all the forces that made the corps a real effective fighting unit, so that when the critical time came, when the hour struck for the great advance on the 8th August, 1918, .the Canadian armies in association with the Australian troops struck the blow, and started the .movement which culminated in the rolling back and decisive defeat of the German forces and which finally led to .the victory of the allied forces on the western front.
That was made possible by the unanimity of sentiment of the Canadian people on the war issue and by the power of the Government to secure the necessary reinforcements to back up the troops overseas. If Union Government had no other reason for its existence the achievements of our heroio troops in 1918 will s.lways .be the justification, the vindication, and the glory of the

men and women throughout Canada who formed and supported this Government.
What our troops achieved on the field of battle, our representatives at the Peace Conference secured in the council of the nations. It is a great record. It has been ably presented to the House. I wish I had had the opportunity of expounding some of its features rather than dealing with these small personal matters -which have distracted the attention of the House for the greater part of the day.
I leave the matter in the judgment of my fellow members. I would be prepared to leave it to the judgment of hon. members on the other side of the House. I leave it to the judgment of the people of this country. I claim no special virtue, no special privileges. All I can claim is that to the measure of my ability, in the hour of my country's stress and need, I have sought to do my duty as God has given me the light to see it.

maintopic: DAUGHTERS OF CANADA, INCORPORATED 1919, DOMINION CHARTER.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I desire to confine the few remarks I intend to make to the amendment moved by my hon. friend the leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) and I shall reserve for other occasions the discussion of the few subjects which are mentioned in the speech from the Throne and such other questions as are of great interest at the present time to the people of Canada. Being a man of peace, I feel still less inclined to interfere in the conflict between my hon. friend from Ruesell (Mr. Murphy) and the hon. the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Rowell). Of course, as my hon. friend from Russell has shown this afternoon, successfully, I believe, the President of the Privy Council is a man of many activities but I think that his importance does not justify my taking up any more of the time of the House in discussing his personality. May I tell him that I have read many of the speeches he made in 1917 or thereabouts. I am sure that when he recalls some of the statements he made then he would to-day rather that they had been unmade. They will stick to him. They are like the shirt of Nessus that clung to the body of Hercules and they will cling to him as long as he remains in public life in Canada.
I desire to offer to the mover and the seconder of the Address my most sincere congratulations. The hon. member for London (Mr. Cronyn) has made a speech possessing qualities and delivered in a manner we would like to admire very frequently in this House. After all, attractiveness

of speech only adds to the power and strength of argument. Many of the statements made by my hon. friend from London show that he has been rocked in the cradle of Liberalism and it is a matter of regret, and a painful sight to us, to see him in such bad company. I hope he will not remain there very long, for it is hard to compromise with the devil. As to my hon. friend from Pictou (Mr. McGregor), his wrong political principles are firmly rooted and his case is desperate, although I congratulate him for the excellence of his speech.
* The leader of the Opposition has made a case which, though we are at the end of this debate still stands unanswered. Every hon. gentleman in this House, notwithstanding denials to the contrary, knows that this amendment embodies the wishes and the practically unanimous opinion of the people of Canada at the present time. The first thing we must do to help the solution of our national problems, the first step' towards re-establishing the normal affairs of this country, is the restoration in its entirety of responsible Government and the, election of a representative Parliament. In order to be effective, in order to ensure the proper and normal representation of this country, or of any democratic country, Parliament must reflect and he the image, must return and must reflect the peculiarities of the nation: It must he the expression of the general will and the conscience of the people. Parliament is the instrument by which the will of the people is executed, therefore it must represent the views of the majority of the people; and every citizen has a sacred right to his proportionate share in the representation. When the majority in a Parliament no longer represents the majority of the people in the country, the decisions of that Parliament carry no influence and have no weight. Those principles are so elementary, they are at the basis of the proper working of constitutional government to such an extent, that they cannot he challenged; and I am sure that every member of this House agrees with me in so far as these premises are concerned.

maintopic: DAUGHTERS OF CANADA, INCORPORATED 1919, DOMINION CHARTER.
speechtext:
May I ask the hon.
gentleman if he considers that the members of the Liberal Party do not represent the constituencies which they .stand for?

maintopic: DAUGHTERS OF CANADA, INCORPORATED 1919, DOMINION CHARTER.
speechtext:
I will answer my hon. friend in a few minutes if he will be good enough to wait. Who will dare say, Mr. Speaker, that the present Government re-

presents the majority of the- Canadian people? It does not represent, it does not possess and enjoy the confidence of an appreciable portion of the Canadian people at the present time. Why, the Government which is supported by the majority of the members of this House is afraid to meet the- Canadian people. It has let, and is letting, the elections go to its opponents by default. The habits of the ostrich are instinctive in many human beings, but they have never been the means of noteworthy success. The only comfort my hon. friends opposite can derive from electoral results was in the case of Assiniboia, and they have referred to that election in most of their' speeches. Indeed my hon. friends seem to have a deplorable lack of humour. It is a piece of delightful irony to hear them mention that election as a blow at the Opposition. There was a constituency which elected a supporter of this Government in 1917 by a majority of over 5,000 votes. The Government kept that constituency without representation for a few sessions, and then when it was compelled to issue the writs it had no candidate in the field to represent its views. True, a Liberal candidate was defeated by my hon. friend from Assiniboia (Mr. Gould) who, f am told has always been a supporter of the Liberal Government. But, Sir, what is one of the main arguments which are used by the group of which that hon. gentleman (Mr. Gould) is a member? Their strongest, and apparently most effective, argument-erroneous though it be as a statement of fact-is that the Liberal party are not- vigorous enough in its Opposition to this. Government, that we have too many points of resemblance with hon. gentlemen opposite. Surely if the Liberal candidate in Assiniboia was defeated because his political views were not far enough removed from those of the members of the Government then the Government have little ground to hail his election as a victory, a moral victory, for them. Of course they are getting panicky and men in a panic grasp at shadows. Why should not my hon. friends opposite be candid and frank with themselves and members of the House? They still quote statistics of the election of 1917 to substantiate their claim that they have the support of this country. I understand my hon. friend from Leeds (Sir Thomas White) advanced this argument to support his speech yesterday. But, Sir, we are not living in 1917. We are Canadians of 1920 and we must discuss political questions and facts in the light of conditions as they are to-day.

maintopic: DAUGHTERS OF CANADA, INCORPORATED 1919, DOMINION CHARTER.
speechtext:
How many members
supporting Union Government would be elected in the Province of Quebec in 1920?

maintopic: DAUGHTERS OF CANADA, INCORPORATED 1919, DOMINION CHARTER.
speechtext:
Not one. No longer
will the Government and its supporters be allowed to evade facts and responsibilities by self indulgence in the monotonous repetition of war cries. Why did the hon. gentleman mention the large majorities secured in 1917 with the help of a doctored franchise?

maintopic: DAUGHTERS OF CANADA, INCORPORATED 1919, DOMINION CHARTER.
speechtext: And badly doctored too.

maintopic: DAUGHTERS OF CANADA, INCORPORATED 1919, DOMINION CHARTER.
speechtext:
The constituency of
Assiniboia, in 1917, gave to the Government a majority of over 5,000; in 1919 it gave not a single vote to the Government. The County of Glengarry-Stormont unanimously elected a supporter of this Government in 1917; my hon. friend from that riding (Mr. Kennedy) was elected in 1919 by, I believe, about 5,000 majority.

maintopic: DAUGHTERS OF CANADA, INCORPORATED 1919, DOMINION CHARTER.
speechtext: What was he before politically?

maintopic: DAUGHTERS OF CANADA, INCORPORATED 1919, DOMINION CHARTER.
speechtext: I know he is a United Farmer of Ontario now, but I judge by the glow of conscience which I see on his face that he was formerly a Liberal. The County of North Ontario elected the late Colonel Sharpe as a supporter of this Government in 1917, by a majority of over 1,600, in fact, he polled twice the number of votes that were given his opponent; this year my hon. friend, the new member for North Ontario (Mr. Halbert) was elected by a majority, I believe, of 200 or 300 votes.

maintopic: DAUGHTERS OF CANADA, INCORPORATED 1919, DOMINION CHARTER.
speechtext: Not quite.

maintopic: DAUGHTERS OF CANADA, INCORPORATED 1919, DOMINION CHARTER.
speechtext:
I will take off a few votes if it pleases my hon. friend. The County of Quebec East in 1917, gave 600 votes to the Union Government; in 1919 it did not give one single vote to that side, the two candidates vying with each other in their opposition to the Government.
How many hon. gentlemen opposite would be returned if the amendment of my hon. Leader were to carry? I do not wonder that the prospect of an election should be so abhorrent to gentlemen whose parliamentary life is limited by and based upon the life of this present Parliament. Three by-elections are to be held presently, and there are now Liberal candidates in the field. Has the Government a candidate in any of those constituencies? There is none in Kamour-aska at the present time. I most cordially invite my right hon. friend the Acting Prime Minister (Sir George Foster) to inaugurate in that splendid country the campaign of political education which he told us the

other night he was about to open. There are no finer and more courteous people in the world than the good electors of Kamouraska, and my right hon. friend would certainly get a fine welcome from them, though I could not give him much hope as to the degree of support they would give to his movement. The Government have no candidate in St. James at present-perhaps they may have one shortly. They have no candidate in Timiskaming, though [DOT] the Conservatives of the division have nominated a straight Conservative candidate-nobody would consent to run as the candidate of this worn-out, abnormal and unpopular Government. I have no doubt that that Tory gentleman will be defeated, but even if he were elected, would that be a victory for the Government? He does not represent the Government in his candidacy, h<j represents the party led to-day by the Hon. Robert Rogers, who said a few days ago that the members of this Government were a lot of second-hand dealers, tinkers and jobbers.
We have to come to this point, Mr. Speaker, that the Government does not replace the Ministers who are withdrawing because their successors could not be elected in any constituency, and as a result whole provinces are no longer represented in the Cabinet. The threat that this Government may hang on for another year or two years, as was insinuated by my hon. friend the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Meighen) the other night, is a challenge to the people of Canada, it is a challenge to democracy; it is a challenge to the proper and normal working of our constitutional Government- I will go a step further and say that when ministers disappear and cannot be replaced, such a threat is a challenge to Providence: And it is always dangerous, even for men stronger than my hon. friend the Minister of the Interior, to defy the Almighty.
One of the speakers on the other side stated that the question raised by the amendment was a question of " ins " and " outs." This hon. gentleman should realize that whoever succeeds the present Government-and the succession cannot be very long delayed-will have a terrible mess to clear up and that nobody is very anxious, from a personal point of view, to take the succession. This Government has made matters easy for their successors in one respect only: that in almost all fields the latter are bound to shine in comparison. But the hon. gentleman is right to this extent, that the difference in the point of view as to this Parliament having no right or mandate to exist any longer-a difference which must be very great as between mem-

bers on the.other side of the House and the members on this side of the House and the other citizens of the country-is the normal difference between the men who look on from without and those who share from within. But perhaps this attitude of the Government was to be expected. The instinct of self-preservation is strong in all created things, and governments are not more free from it than the men of whom they are composed. However, they cannot deceive anybody-not even themselves,- and their voice during this debate was rather uncertain and nervous, being at times like the voice of a scared child who in the dark forest sings in an attempt to keep its spirits up.
The hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Mowat) said that the present undeniable hostility of the people towards the Government was temporary and would soon pass away. Is this the opinion of the Government? Is this the cause of their present humiliating attitude? Do they believe that this great, steady, long, continued movement of the public mind is going to stop? Do they expect any change in the public estimation of their misdeeds and omissions? Are they waiting until such a change occurs? If so, they resemble the man in Horace who lay on the bank of a river expecting every moment that it would pass by and leave him a clear passage, not knowing the depth and abundance of the fountain that feeds the river, not knowing that it flows and will flow on forever.
I have referred to my hon. friend from Parkdale.(Mr. Mowat). I am not surprised at the stand he takes on the present amendment. Looking the other day over the files of the Toronto newspapers for the year 1917 -you will see, Mr. Speaker, that we have had so many bouquets thrown at us of late that I thought the reading over of certain literature would provide the antidote which would prevent the poison of pride overwhelming one, and I did not know at the time that my hon. friend from Russell would read his little circular this afternoon.
I happened to see a report of the proceedings of the convention which selected my hon. friend (Mr. Mowat) as a candidate for the constituency of Parkdale. There was a letter from the Right Hon. Prime Minister beseeching the good Conservatives of Park-dale to select my hon. friend; and then-one of the Ministers-I believe it was the Minister of Railways (Mr. J. D. Reid)-arose and spoke to the delegates. He told them that it was necessary in order to impress the country that this was a real Union ' Government that a Liberal should be se-

lected as the Government candidate for one of the Toronto seats. The president of the Tory Association then made a little speech. He said: All right; we are going to make the sacrifice, but remember, it is only a loan. So, valuable as my hon. friend is in this House, he is only a borrowed article. His contract will expire with the life of this Parliament, and these magnificent buildings will be deficient forever of one of their finest adornments.
Sir, as the leader of the Opposition eloquently said, we shall have unrest in Canada; peace and order will not be restored until the Canadian Parliament is brought into harmony with the Canadian people. It is indispensable to public safety that this should be done without any further delay. Everybody is longing for the time when things will come back to normal. Let us start at the most conspicuous point; let our politics, let our public life, come back to normal. This Government cannot pretend much longer to unite this country by dividing it. I do not now speak of the past. I respected the men who differed from us in 1917 through patriotic and conscientious motives; I would not have respected them if, feeling as they did feel at that time, they had acted otherwise. But I repeat, Sir, that I do not now speak of the past, and 1 emphatically state that any man who today proclaims this a Union Government is maintaining a sham and-supporting hypocrisy. Why, Sir, having arrayed province against province and race against race, they have succeeded by their disastrous policies, by violating their pledges, by breaking faith with their own supporters and dividing classes against classes, groups against groups, and occupations against occupations, in separating into fragments what was, under the illustrious leader who is now in his grave, a great united people.
No Government in the history of this country ever represented in lesser degree a united Canada. For the first time since union of Upper and Lower Canada one of the two great branches of the Canadian family is practically not represented in the administration of the affairs of the country.

speechtext: Whose fault is that?

maintopic: DAUGHTERS OF CANADA, INCORPORATED 1919, DOMINION CHARTER.
speechtext:
I will tell my hon.
friend. It is indeed a tragical joke to apply the word "Union" to the work of disruption which the right hon. Prime Minister (Sir Robert Borden) has been unfortunate enough to achieve. It has been urged by gentlemen on the other side-and I am free to admit it-that the Prime Minister has endeavoured to afford some sort of redress
to an awkward situation. But under the present. conditions, in view of the circumstances which preceded, accompanied and followed the accession to office of the present Government, no true and worthy representative of those to whom I now have reference can, with any sense of dignity, become one of its members. Some gentlemen opposite have said that the Government is not responsible for that anomaly; that those of the Canadian people who refused to elect supporters of the Union- Government cannot complain of being unrepresented. They are indeed quite right as to the utter impossibility of the people of whom I now speak electing a member of the present Government. Sir, it only goes to show that the situation is abnormal and unnatural. In order that we may resume the sane, safe and healthy conditions of our public life and of the civilization established by the builders of the country, by the great men of the past, the members of the Government must realize that they are an obstacle to our national progress and are blocking the way to the unity of Canada and to a fair and normal working out of the constitution.

maintopic: DAUGHTERS OF CANADA, INCORPORATED 1919, DOMINION CHARTER.
speechtext: Mr. Speaker-

maintopic: DAUGHTERS OF CANADA, INCORPORATED 1919, DOMINION CHARTER.
speechtext:
My hon. friend has put questions to me which are really not of sufficient importance to justify my allowing him to interrupt my remarks.
This Government was elected in 1917 for a special purpose; it has now no further mandate to carry on the affairs of the country. What is the present task of Parliament? To place the national Budget on a stable foundation; to work out new plans for the promotion .and regulation of trade; to cope with the problems of inflated currency and depreciated exchange, and to establish satisfactory working relations between capital and labour so that national production may make headway against industrial disorganization and general want. But the present Parliament was elected on an issue that had no bearing upon the work that is to be done. It has no mandate to formulate a programme or to execute one when it is decided upon. In refusing to accede to the clamour of public opinion, to the . request that they relinquish the reins of office, the members of the Government and their supporters in the House are breaking faith with thousands of electors who voted for Union Government upon the understanding and subject to the pledge that such Government was formed for one purpose and one purpose only, and would automatically go out o,f office with the coming

of peace. The Minister of the Interior (Mr. Meighen) and other hon. gentlemen to the *contrary notwithstanding, such a pledge was given on all the public platforms of the country. Even members of the Government made it clear to the electors. I have here a few statements which will bear out my contention in that respect. I take from the Globe of Tuesday, October 23, 1917, the report of a meeting in Winnipeg, at which the Minister of Immigrartion (Mr. Calder): spoke:	I am glad to see him in his seat.
Here is the report:
It was on that understanding they had come in. He was not deserting Liberalism, nor the principle for which Liberalism stands. They were not absorbed nor submerged by the Conservative party. They had simply consented to Union for the purpose of this war, and reserved their views and opinions outside of the war. Union had been achieved only by each side agreeing to sink for the time being purely domestic problems.
The Minister of the Interior spoke at that meeting, and this is what he said, according to the report in the Globe:
~No man or woman is asked to reverse or abnegate convictions on fiscal or other subjects. The accepted basis of union was the only basis on which Union was possible under present condition, and our appeal is that the people of Canada unite on the same basis on which the members of the Government have united, and get behind this union and stay behind it until it achieves its end.
In the town of Sarnia a meeting was held which was addressed by the former Minister of Public Works, now chairman of the Board of Railway Commissioners. I take the report of that meeting from the Globe of October 25, 1917. This is what that gentleman, then a member of the Government, said at that time:
This Government is formed for a definite purpose and for a definite period. I am in it as a Liberal for that purpose and for that period, and for that purpose I intend to give the best that is in me.	.
I am in the Government to do what I can toward winning the war. I went in freely, and if there are things happen of which I cannot approve I can get out just as easy. This is not a Conservative Government; it is not a Liberal Government. (Mostly Conservative, interrupted a voice). This is a war-Government. Its purpose is to carry on the affairs of this country in a non-partisan way until the war is won. After demobilization the contract is concluded, and each man can take the course he thinks best. (You'll all be Tories then, exclaimed another.)

maintopic: DAUGHTERS OF CANADA, INCORPORATED 1919, DOMINION CHARTER.
speechtext: He was wrong.

maintopic: DAUGHTERS OF CANADA, INCORPORATED 1919, DOMINION CHARTER.
speechtext:
He was wrong as regards some of the gentlemen, but I am afraid he is right as regards a few.
Does someone say I would become a Tory? asked Mr. Carvell. Well, I don't believe it.

(Laughter and renewed cheers.) There is only one thing for a man to do in a crisis like the present, and that is to do what he thinks is right.
What about the electors? A meeting, largely attended by Liberals of the province of Ontario who supported conscription was held, I think, in the city of Hamilton. I take the following from the report of that meeting in the Globe of November 3, 1917:
Ex-Mayor J. G. Kerr of Chatham introduced the following resolution, seconded by Mr. F. L. Fowke of Oshawa:-
" That, whereas since the notice calling this convention was sent out, a Union Government has been formed, in which Liberals throughout the Dominion have joined, this convention, recording its belief that the formation of a Union Government for the duration of the war was highly desirable and in the best interests of Canada and believing that thereby the share of Canada in the conduct of the present world war will be best served, and the Government of the country most effectively and satisfactorily carried on during the period of the war expresses its approval of the action of the Liberal members of the present Union Government in entering same."
The Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Ballantyne), whom, I am sorry, is not in his seat, spoke at a meeting at Hamilton. These are his words as reported in the Globe of November 23, 1917:
I prefer to take my Liberalism and my patriotism at this juncture from men like Hon. W. S. Fielding in Nova Scotia, or' men like Mr. Fred. Pardee in Ontario, together with __ every Liberal Provincial Prime Minister save one in Canada, Hon. Mr. Ballantyne declared, rather than take it from Bourassa, Lavergne, Lemieux and company. (Prolonged cheers).
I should like to ask my hon. friend from whom he takes his Liberalism to-day? Ha does not seem to take it from my distinguished friend, the hon. member from Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding). He does ,riot seem to take it from my esteemed deskmate, the hon. member for Lambton West (Mr. Pardee). Surely he (does not take it from the nine provincial Premiers who are all supporters of the leader of the Opposition. From whom does he take it? Perhaps, from the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Meighen)', whose brand of Liberalism I do not trust very much. The President of the Privy Council (Mr. Rowell) spoke at Durham, and these are his words as reported in the Globe of November 28, 1917:
" in all the many nations at war," Hon. Mr. Rowell declared, after relating a few' overseas incidents, V it has been found impossible for any people to put their own energy into the war as long as they are divided by party lines, and the whole object of the Union Government is that the nation may stand , united m this crisis. After Prussian militarism has been defeated

we can go back to settle our own domestic affairs by party methods, if we so desire."
The President of the Privy Council was
not so emphatic as the others. He is an old fox, although I do not wish to refer to the fox which had lost its tail at the battle. But I have still better documentary evidence. I hold in my hand a prihted circular which was distributed in the trenches and in all the military camps in 1917, and a copy of which was given to' every soldier who registered a vote at that election. That circular, which was sent and distributed by the Government, reads in part as follows:

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext:
Comrades, this is our election, because the only issue is selective conscription. Without its immediate enforcement there can be no rest or relief for Canadians at the front. The Union Government is neither Grit nor Tory. It is composed of the following gentlemen:
v I do not wish to read the whole circular, but I desire only to impress upon. the House the fact that every soldier was told, before he registered his vote, that there was only one issue and that was selective conscription. Thousands of electors, the young manhood of this country, voted for this Government, because they were told that the only issue was selective conscription; that it was purely and exclusively a soldiers' election held for one purpose only, and the mandate they were asked to give was for that purpose alone and would expire when such purpose was achieved. Furthermore, those hundreds of thousands df electors were not given an opportunity to vote for a man of their own Choice to represent them in Parliament; they were not afforded the advantage of voting for pien whom they considered qualified to discuss questions of interest to them and to the country. [DOT] They voted simply for a Government without any regard to the candidates. In many instances they did not know the candidates. They were asked to vote for a Government which would be entrusted with a mandate to enforce a certain war policy and nothing else. This mandate Jias expired. This policy has disappeared from the political field. Is it fair to the men who voted in such a peculiar and unprecedented way, to use and abuse for other purposes the special mandate which they gave to a special set of men, many of whom pre no longer members of the collective body for which the soldiers' votes were registered.
Sir, there are issues at hand that will cause a clear cleavage between progress
and reaction, between Toryism and reform. The very fact that the resources of Canada as a result of our war effort have been strained as they have been, and that we have a huge national debt, compels us to face grave and great problems and the two traditionally opposite sides cannot but face each other when the settlement is effected, and one or the other must give way. It is impossible for gentlemen of different ideas to agree on these great problems. They cannot sit together and be true to their principles. No gentlemen who has not altogether renounced his liberalism can remain in this Government to-day or support it. The hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Mowat) has stated that the real Liberals are on that side of the House, and he said he was saving Liberalism by remaining therms. Sir, when he makes those professions publicly before the country, while continuing to support the present Government, he is saving Liberalism in the same manner and to the same extent and degree as another gentleman, who two thousand years ago contributed to the salvation and redemption of the world by publicly kissing his Master to betray Him to the ' Roman soldiers. I am willing to admit that in the multitude of arbitrary and reactionary measures that have been passed by this Government some Liberal policies may have been adopted on minor points. It was Theodore Roosevelt who once said of an American politician, he was so wicked he could embrace a good principle if it ^helped him. On all vital issues, on all issues that had to be definite and would be controversial, we have witnessed a policy of indecision on the part of this Government. We are told that th$ country is in a state of unrest and that this is no time for change or the adoption of any definite policy. The argument was made by the hon. member for Leeds (Sir Thomas White) yesterday. Yet in 1911 when the Liberal Government sought to enact a treaty of reciprocity for the purpose of affording relief to the great farming community of this country, and went down to defeat on that issue, we were met by the cry: Let well enough alone; the country is too prosperous and peaceful for a change. My hon. friend from Leeds was a leader in that campaign, and now in 1920, when the country is convulsed from one end to the other, the very same gentleman says: Would you alter our policy in such agitated times as these? Such is the dilemma of a vicious Tory government and selfish interests-if the people are turbulent, they are un-

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
fit for reform, and if they are quiet they do not want reform. After every meeting of supporters of the Government at which policies were to be enunciated, it is officially reported that they have unanimously come to the decision that no decision should be taken. Hon. gentlemen opposite are simply asking for time. The hon. member for West Peterborough (Mr. Burnham) wrote in the Evening Journal yesterday that he was going to vote against the amendment of the hon. leader of the Opposition just for the purpose of gaining time, for he has no confidence in the Government. Ninety per cent of the political energies of the members of the Government are wasted on expedients to patch or piece out the political machine as often, as it breaks down.
The right hon. the Prime Minister (Sir Robert Borden) is sick and absent, and we all regret it. I think it was unfortunate and most unfair to charge the hon. leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) with discourtesy in alluding in his amendment to the illness of the right hon. the Prime Minister. The hon. leader of the Opposition was the first man to express the sympathy of the House with the right hon. gentleman in his illness. On the very opening day of this session, speaking right after the right hon. the Acting Prime Minister (Sir George Foster), who never said a word about the right hon. the Prime Minister in his speech, the hon. leader of the Opposition spoke as follows:
Sir, may I join my right hon. friend in giving expression to other sentiments which we experience in common on this historic occasion? It is not more a source of regret to supporters of the Government than it is to hon. members of the Opposition that the -right hon. the Prime Minister (Sir Robert Borden) is prevented, because of the impaired condition of his health, from being present at and participating in these opening ceremonies, certain, as they are, to live in the memories of all who are privileged to witness them. It is gratifying to us, as it will be to the people of Canada, to know that the change of scene and thought, and most of all, the freedom for a time, from vast responsibility, which the Prime Minister is at present enjoying, have not been without their beneficient effects; and that restoration of health, which we all hope may be speedy and complete, appears now to await him. Still, we regret his absence, and we miss his presence.
We all regret the unfortunate illness of the Prime Minister, but we shall not allow hon. gentlemen opposite, who for years have prevented the free discussion of their misdeeds and extravagant administration by sheltering themselves behind the glory and the sacrifice of our brave Canadian soldiers, to screen themselves to-day behind the weakness of a sick man. The Govern-
[Mr. E. Lapointe.!
ment has no right to exploit the illness of the Prime Minister, and they are most unfair to him when they try to do so. We all hope that his health will
10 p.m. speedily be restored, but my duty to this country compels me to state that I object emphatically that Canadian policies-the solution of reconstruction and other national problems-should also travel around the world with the Prime Minister on Viscount Jellicoe's ship, or rest with him in Florida. Canada cannot afford to waste another year, and still less two whole years.
The hon. Minister of the Interior (Mr. Meighen) asked the House the other night what was wrong with the Government and with the body politic. So far as he could see, everything was all right. The hon. gentleman has a short memory. Only a few weeks ago he went to the city of Kingston and virtually pleaded for a new alignment in the political field. Why is he advocating a new union if everything is all right today? I have in my hand the Montreal Gazette containing a report of a speech of the Minister of the Interior and it reads as follows in part:
I am asked what it is proposed to do. The air is filled with clashing demands, conflicting criticisms and contradictory appeals. One extremist calls for one thing, another extremist for another thing. The extreme labour man wants labour domination; he wants the one big union and all that it involves. The extreme protectionist wants a high tariff. The extreme free trader wants no tariff at all. The extreme Socialist wants the nationalization of everything. The extreme individualist thinks we have nationalized far too much already. The extreme farmer partisan wants an agricultural dynasty. He believes he will make this country a land of Canaan by a system of free imports, by buying more goods from others.
What I say is, let all moderate men get together. There are sane and moderate labour men, thousands of them, the vast majority. Back of this restlessness and discord we have a sane business community. We have manufacturers of moderate views. We have hundreds of thousands of steady and thoughtful agriculturists, thoughtful citizens who read from experience as well as from books, men of patriotic principles, just as big a proportion of such men as in any class in the nation. Let these men and these women get together. Let them not be stampeded. The hope of this country is to be found in such a union, and such a union is right now taking place. It will draw strength from every group. It will gain in vigour from attacks. Its numbers will multiply as the danger becomes clearer. It will hold the ship steady, and it will bring us through.
Let me ask my hon. friend what is wrong with him and his friends? Is it not enough to make angels weep to hear the Minister of the Interior classifying himself amongst the moderates of this country? He was the

father, and the godfather, of the most arbitrary and despotic legislation and Orders in Council which have been executed and enforced by this Government. He is very clever and has many high qualities, but he is the last man in the world I would trust to adopt a moderate course in the political field. Again I ask, if everything is right in the Unionist family, why form a new union, why this appeal for a new alignment? If everything is right and if nothing is wrong, why should a close friend of the Prime Minister and a strong supporter of the Unionist party, Senator McLennan, launch a new political party under the name of the National party? Why should all these gentlemen try to dress or redress, the Unionist child with more fashionable clothes?
But, Sir, the Unionist house is divided against itself. We on this side of the House are witnessing with equanimity and calmness the disintegration and decay of that unnatural organization. One part wants to remain Unionist; another wants to be purely and simply Conservative or Tory; the Minister of the Interior wants a new Union; Senator McLennan wants a National Party; and my hon. friend from Red Deer (Mr. Clark) who, apart from being a farmer, is a medical man, the other day attended at th birth of a new party under the name of the National Progressive Party. Yesterday the hon. member for Leeds (Sir Thomas White) not only attended as a medical man but was the generator and creator of a new party under the name of the National Liberal Conservative party. I shall not be surprised at all if before the end of this debate some practical joker on the other side stands up and advocates the formation of the National Liberal-Conservative, Progressive, Reform Farmers' party - they would all, except the Farmers, come from the same mother, to wit: the Tory party.
Facing all these groups and factions, fighting one another in a hopeless struggle, the Liberal party stands united, vigorous, reorganized, ready and prepared for political action. The good old cause, as our late lamented leader called it so often-the good old cause, vanquished or triumphant, insulted or victorious-is still the good old cause with us. . Liberalism is the application of the eternal principles of justice to all classes, elements, interests and trades. Liberalism means evolution, along reasonable and progressive lines. But, as Burke said, innovations are not necessarily reforms. The Liberal party holds the middle course between dangerous, violent changes that would bring disaster to our institutions and
obstinate resistance to progress and the spirit of the time. The Liberal party stands between capital and labour, between the weak and the strong, between the individual . and the corporation, between the big interests, so dear to the heart of the hon. member for Leeds, and the plain citizen like you and me, Mr. Speaker. It stands between conflicting interests and classes, it. stands between that class which is the Canadian Manufacturers Association and that other class which is the Canadian Council of Agriculture, having as its only aim and ambition to do only what is fair and just to all and to each.
All the organized forces of selfishness are attacking it and questioning its motives and its aims. The extremists dislike it extremely, and, Sir, when I hear on one hand, the hon. member for Brantford (Mr. Coch-shutt) denounce us as dangerous free traders, and on the other hand, the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark), Mr. Mussel-man of Saskatchewan, or Mr. Wood, of Alberta claim that we are only protectionists in disguise, I take it as conclusive evidence that we are discharging the true and normal functions of Liberalism holding the sane and safe middle course.
When I read in the Ottawa Journal that I am, in common with friends on this side of the House coming from the province of Quebec, a reactionary and an obscurantist, as was stated in an editorial last week, and when almost at the same time I am branded in that other Unionist Tory paper, L'Even-ment of Quebec, as being a wild radical, just as bad as my hon. friend the leader of the Opposition and almost as dangerous as my hon. friend the member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar), which is still worse, I take it as an indication that I am but a plain and unadulterated Liberal, and I do not mind the abuse.
I have just mentioned the name of my hon. friend from Brantford. The hon. gentleman in the course of his speech the other night expressed regret that I was then absent from the House, because he was anxious to know whether my removal from Kamouraska to the constituency of Quebec East has had any effect on my views with regard to the fiscal policy. I understand the anxiety of my hon. friend from Brantford; I understand why he is so nervous at the present time. He has had many events in his province lately that he does not like, things he considers as plagues- he has had a Farmers' Government, smallpox, and prohibition, and now he is threatened by a reduction in the price of

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
ploughs. He ventured the assertion that my views must be modified as a result of a change in the constituency which I represent in the House. Mr. Speaker, I challenge my hon. friend to quote one word of mine, uttered at any time, in support of an absolute free trade policy in this country. For the purpose of revenue I have always stated, and I state to-night, that we must have a tariff, and we must have it much more to-day because of the great war debt that we have to pay. But let me tell my hon. friend that he has missed his guess. I was in favour of a lower tariff when I represented Kamouraska; and I am in favour of a lower tariff when I am representing Quebec East. I was in favour of a policy that would reduce the price of ploughs to the farmers when I was in Kamouraska, and I am in favour of that policy to-day when I represent Quebec East. I was in favour of the policy expounded by my right hon. leader who is now dead, Sir Wilfrid Laurier, three weeks before his death, when he spoke before the Eastern Ontario Liberal Association. That speech on the fiscal question stands as his political will. By that policy enunciated by my late leader, and by the policy which was adopted at the Liberal Convention last summer, I stood in Kamouraska and I stand in Quebec East. I am even ready to go and discuss that policy in Brantford if my hon. friend will give me the opportunity. He may rest assured that I do not, and never will, modify my principles and opinions , according to conditions of time or place.
Now, Sir, I wish to say a word on the question of the new election law which is going to be introduced and enaeted._ The leader of the House does not like the references that are made to the War-time Elections Act. It is a worn-out subject, he says, that has been fought and discussed over and over again and should be left aside altogether. Let me tell him that the discussion of this famous piece of legislation will be of permanent interest as long as the Parliament which was elected by virtue of such Act remains in office. There is an old proverb that says, " When the spring is muddy the stream is muddy, too," and the stream in this case will flow on as long as the present Parliament lasts. All I wish to say is to express the hope that the new Bill will not reproduce and embody any of the bad features of that legislation. All British subjects by birth or naturaliza-tiono are entitled to be represented in this Parliament and to exercise all the privileges of citizenship. If you want our naturalized citizens to feel for Canada more than half

patriotism you must make Canada more than half a country for them. The monstrous doctrine of collective responsibility which makes men hate and revenge themselves not only on the evildoer or the guilty but on all those of the same name, race, or colour, was a pernicious product of the war mentality, and must be discarded and destroyed if we are to have sanity, peace and progress in this country. The question to my mind is not only one of justice; it is a question of safety. It is neither wise nor prudent to deprive any class of our population of their right to the ballot. It is cheaper, after all, to lift men up than to hold them down, and the ballot in their hands is far less dangerous to society than a sense of wrong in their heads. I hope we shall have a fair and honest franchise, followed by a fair and honest election.	[DOT]
With regard to the coming elections some hon. gentleman opposite used as a justification for voting against the amendment of my leader the argument that there should be a re-distribution before the elections take place for the purpose of giving a larger representation to the farming community of Western Canada. Those gentlemen are not serious. Firstly, such a re-distribution cannot be made before two or three years. And they do not know-have they not read in the Ministerial press, that it is the intention to do away with the custom of having a different unit of representation for the urban and rural constituencies, so that by increasing considerably the number of representatives in the cities it will be possible for them to drown the voice of the farmers? Have they still some faith in the pledges of this Government? Moreover, Sir, the estimated figures quoted by some gentleman as to the probable increase in the population of the various provinces are wholly misleading as far as Quebec is concerned, if the statistics of the Provincial Government are correct, as I have no doubt they are. The increase in the population of the province of Quebec is much larger than the figures quoted in this debate indicate, and Quebec being the pivot of the representation our fiiends from the West would not get the increase of representation which they seem to expect. You see, we do not increase our population in Quebec by artificial means such as Government regulations or immigration policies. Our process of inciease is the old law of multiplication as prescribed by the Creator. Quebec does not import her population, she makes it, and that may be the

reason why our population is sane and safe.	:	[DOT]
There is another subject I desire to refer to and which should be an additional argument in favour of the amendment before the House. A great Imperial Conference is going to take place this year for the purpose of deliberating upon and considering the constitutional relations of the Empire and the various Dominions. I submit that it is necessary that only a Government with a popular mandate,- that only a Parliament representative of the majority of the Canadian people, should be entrusted with the duty and task of representing Canada and speaking for its people at this very important gathering. This weak, impotent, leaderless Government has no right to assume to speak with the great voice of Canada at that Conference, has no right to engage our future or pledge our destinies to any extent.
Last year when speaking on this subject I strongly urged that no question affecting Canada's future should be discussed at any Conference without having been first submitted to the Parliament of Canada, and that our delegates should go to that Conference with a clear mandate and with no other rights or missions than those agreed upon and conferred by this Parliament. I am glad Indeed that the opinion I then expressed has received the support of hon. gentlemen who have spoken in the course of this debate. During the last few years Parliament has been treated in this lespect with scant courtesy. These great problems must be considered from a purely Canadian point of view. We are prepared and willing to do our part amongst the nations of the world, but our main policy is and will remain the policy of Canada first; we are and shall remain one hundred per cent Canadians, and will not allow anybody to change our status for us without our participation.
My last words, Sir, will be an appeal to all the members of this House to listen to the voice of the country which is heard from the Atlantic to the Pacific asking them to support the amendment of the leader of the Opposition. The Government has always represented itself as being a war Government-as being purely and simply a war machine. This Parliament was elected as, and has been always stated to be, a war Parliament. The war is over. The Government have demobilized everybody else; I ask them to-day to demobilize themselves.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it was not my intention to take part in this debate until the conclusion of the speech of my hon. friend the leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King), when he put his amendment and challenged the whole administration of the Government of which I have been a member since its inception in 1917.
I wish to express, in common with other speakers who have preceded me, the gratification that we all feel on coming into this beautiful building. I do not know that any higher compliment could be paid to the building or to its designers than to say that judging from the feelings of all the members and the great satisfaction they have expressed on getting into these new quarters, we all feel that we can at least enter 'a building that shows beauty and strength somewhat in comparison to the strength and beauty of the parliamentary institutions which are carried on on this north half of the American continent.
I wish also to say a word in passing in reference to the speeches of my hon. friends, the member for London (Mr. Cronyn) and the member for Pictou (Mr. McGregor), the mover and seconder of the Address. I haye been a member of this House for twelve years, and have necessarily therefore heard the speeches of a great many movers and [DOT]seconders of the Address, but I cannot recall in the whole of that time any speeches which have been permeated with a finer spirit. The address of my hon. friend from London was not only characterized by great breadth, but also by a full recognition of the problems that are facing this country to-day, and contained yaluable suggestions towards their solution, and both as to matter and manner was an admirable speech from beginning to end. I can only say that my -lion, friend "from London is a type of representative that we sorely need to have and to keep in our public life. I would not say any less than that of my hon. friend from Pictou. He gave a sane and thoughtful presentation of the problems pf war and of the problems that have come to us with the conclusion of peace, and his solution for those problems are worthy of consideration. I was particularly interested in, and I think it would be well for hon. members to read and re-read, what he had to say about the soldier questions which now confront us.
Sir, there was one thing that struck me as particularly pleasant - about those speeches, and that was their absolute freedom from political rancour; a generous spirit breathed through them. I also would like to say that it is a pleasure for this House to notice that the same generous * spirit characterized the speeches of the



leaders of that small group at the further end of the Chamber known as the crossbenchers. I heard with great pleasure my old friend from Red Deer (Mr. Clark) give that fine eulogy on the Prime Minister (Sir Robert Borden). It was not less appreciated by members on this side of the House and indeed by many on the other side, when my hon. friend from Marquette (Mr. Crerar) paid a similar tribute to one who is literally a " casualty of the war." I would like to add that it gave us all on this side gratification to hear my hon. friend from Red Deer pay that fine tribute of his to a political opponent in the old days, the right hon. the leader of the House at this present moment (Sir George Foster). He did it in a manner worthy of the best traditions of this House.	i	i
I wish, Mr. Speaker, that I could speak in the same appreciative tone of the attitude adopted by my hon. friend the leader of the Opposition. I noticed that when he commenced his speech he said:
It would be strange, indeed, if, under the spell of the noble and dignified proportions of this Chamber, we were not all impressed with the spirit of the Canadian people in rising out of the difficulties of the past.
I must confess that when he proceeded with his speech I thought he was freeing himself from the spell of the building with remarkable success, and the further he proceeded the more completely he freed himself, until when he came to his amendment he was absolutely free from any such spell.
And if I can say this of the speech of my hon. friend the leader of the Opposition, I can surely say it with greater force of that of the member for Russell (Mr. Murphy), who made one of the most extraordinary speeches that I have ever heard since ^ became a member of this House. I think the best thing to do with that speech would be to absolutely forget it. But I would call atten-' tion for a moment to his closing statement: That the Liberal party was established for the promotion of neighbourly relations, mutual respect and good-will. If that is so, I never heard a speech so singularly calculated to thwart the purposes for which the Liberal party was established.
The hon. minister (Mr. Rowell) who was the subject of that attack needs no defence from me; he made a pretty good defence for himself, I think. As one of his colleagues, I have only to say that he has the fullest esteem and confidence of his colleagues as a valued member of the Government. I would commend to my hon. friend from Russell, as to other hon. members who

are apt to indulge in rancourous debate and acrimonious personalities, the words- which I cordially endorse-with which my hon. friend from Marquette closed his speech the other day. He 6aid:
If we as Canadian citizens seek only what is good, noble, honest and true, and look only for what is best in one another, I have no fear for our future prosperity and welfare, nor need, I think, any of us.
Now, Sir, my hon. friend the leader of the Opposition is a young man and a Canadian, he has worked at industrial problems not only in this -country but in another country, and I think it unfortunate that the style of his speech should have been what it was. He seemed to have a strange misapprehension of the spirit of the last three or four years as shown not only in the world generally but in this country particularly. He seems to have forgotten that men are no longer cleaving in the selfish way they did years ago to the old party system and shouting the same old acrimonious party battle-cries. I think if he had realized that more he would have changed the tone of his address and have discarded some of the methods which characterized the unrestrained party methods of years ago. When he referred to the members of this Government as having only the desire to hang on to office, he surely must have known that he was not speaking the truth. He must have known something of the strain that Ministers have undergone during the frightful struggle of the last few years. He certainly must have known that so far as material rewards go we have had no reason to hang on to office. So that it is a matter of regret that a gentleman starting out as leader of a once' historic and still, in a sense, big party, should descend to this line of argument,-speaking of his opponents as men only capable of hanging on to office, of violating popular rights, and of banishing freedom. These are old cries that are very much out of place in these days.
My hon. friend lamented the loss of faith in our institutions 'and in ourselves that exists in 'Canada and generally throughout the world. I can only say that in his speech he himself, as the leader of a great party, adopted a very poor method of restoring it. I am not so pessimistic as my hon. friend. It is true that the millennial is not here; that the results of the war have not been as happy as they might have been in the establishment not only of a speedy peace but of something approaching a finer spirit of brotherhood all over the world. Nevertheless, while there may not be on
the part of the people the same ready assent to formulas and conventions that there was, and while there may be an impression that people are getting loose in their moorings, I as a Canadian do not believe for a moment that the millions who have gone through this awful struggle, who have displayed unselfishness and courage and self-discipline during these years of war, have faced the realities of life for nothing, nor will they fail as a great and steadying influence in our future progress.
My hon. friend did himself scant justice when he complained of members of this Government being continually away and suggested that we in Canada should primarily attend to our own affairs. He complained that a thing like the Grand Trunk agreement had not been brought down, too much .attention being given in the meantime to external matters. Well, he only had to wait a day or two before he got the Grand Trunk agreement. And surely my hon. friend of all gentlemen in this House should be the last to complain on this score. It is true that we have to attend to Canadian affairs first, but can we say that Canadian affairs are not in a very real sense hound up with world affairs at this time? My hon. friend should not 'be a little Canadian. He has been a member of different commissions. He was a member, I think, of a commission to inquire into immigration from India and the vexed problems connected with that subject. He was a member also of a commission to deal with troubles in Japan. He has spent some time in the United States studying great labour and industrial problems. He, therefore, of all men should be the last to complain. Does he say at a time when the after-problems of the war and the steps to he taken following the conclusion of peace had to be decided, Canadian Ministers were not in t.heir proper place when they were amongst those by whom the solution of these things had to be brought about? (1 think that my hon. friend has not taken very good ground on that point. If I could stretch my imagination sufficiently to imagine him as Prime Minister of this . country,-and it would be a difficult thing to do-I would think that in that capacity he would take a somewhat broader view. As one illustration of the prestige which our country has attained among the nations . of the world, I may point out that when the one representative. for the British Empire was to be appointed on the Saar Valley Commission, a body to govern the Saar Valley for a period of fifteen years, the British Government asked that Canada 184
name that representative. That suggestion has been met and a Western man has been selected, a high type of Canadian, who has since been made Chairman of the whole Commission.
My hon. friend says that we are suffering at this time from the inability of the Government to meet the needs of the country. I do not know to what extent my hon. friend has followed the problems of the last few years or the manner in which the Government has dealt with them. As my hon. friend has no responsibility so far as governmental office is concerned, he feels that he is free to criticize. But he has been a member of a government; he is now leader of an Opposition. He will appreciate that saying of M. Diderot: "II est si difficile de produire meme une chose mediocre; il est si facile de sentir la mediocrite." This Government has produced constructive legislation which is not by any means of a mediocre character. It has had to deal with immense problems and has settled them satisfactorily. At a meeting in Ottawa the other day my hon. friend welcomed the advent of women into the political life of this country, but he did not think of giving credit to this Government for introducing that great reform, the enfranchisement of women. There are other things that he might have had in mind so far as the accomplishments of the Government are concerned, but these have been so ably dealt with by the member for Pictou (Mr. McGregor.), the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster) and others that I shall not do more than touch very briefly upon them.
I should like to refer to one thing which at least many of the people are giving the Government due credit for, but which my hon. friend seems to pay little attention to namely, the exceptionally successful work initiated and carried on by the Minister of the Interior (Hon. Mr. Meighen) in connection with the settlement of soldiers upon the land. If that is not appreciated by my hon. friend, at least it is appreciated in other countries. Although the Act has been in force only one year, more than 15,000 men have been settled upon the land under its provisions; loans amounting to $57,000,000 have been approved and 35,000 returned men have received qualification certificates. Without dilating upon the subject, I may say that in what has been done in this respect we are 100 per cent in advance of Great Britain, the United States, or, in fact, any other of the countries that were engaged in the war.

My hon. friend has said a great deal about unrest. So far as I aril able to judges, there is less unrest in Canada than there is in any other part of the world. The problems that have been so acutely before the people of all countries since the war have been just as acute here, and they have been met. I say without fear of contradiction that in the volume of our trade; in the small extent to which we have been troubled by labodr difficulties; in the successful solution of such problems as the railway question and other important matters, no country in the world has greater cause for Vratitude' than the Canada in which we live.
It is interesting and not a little amusing to watch my hon. friend's attitude with regard to the Farmers' party. My hon. fiiend has shown some alarm with regain to-the formation of this Farmers' party. He says that the Liberals are not opposed to the farmers. He argued at a recent meeting that in so far as the farmers had any virtue, any qualifications such as were enumerated by the member for Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe) just now, they were in reality Liberals. Evidently he looked forward hopefully to the time when he could 'amalgamate the Farmers' party with his own. Well, I think the member for Red Deer (Mr. M. Clark) would say that a man once bitten is twice shy. He was for many years a member of the Liberal party. During all that time he preached pretty strongly the economic doctrines which he believes in-and he thought that within the folds of the party which my hon. friend (Hon. Mr. Mackenzie King) leads to-day, he was a kind of voice in the wilderness.
I do not think it is likely that he will join it in the very near future, but it is somewhat amusing to this House to see the way in which the leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) has cornered the group of cross-benchers in this particular amendment. My hon. friend, at a Liberal gathering in the city recently, challenged the Farmers' party on this motion, and on what they will do, he said, on "the fundamental question as to the attitude they will take towards the Government". He is not concerned about great questions of policy or great economic questions, but hq is deeply concerned as to what attitude they will take in regard. to the desire to put out of power the Government which is now in office. I am not surprised that the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. M. Clark) laboured somewhat in his reasons for supporting the amendment, and I would 
think his friends on the cross-benches would have been entitled to vote with the members on this side against the amendment of the leader of the Opposition. The hon. member for Red Deer had a fundamental difference with the leader of the Opposition and his party in 1917, and I can understand the reluctance with which he would join with him in any kind of a vote, much more in a vote of this sort. We on this side, much as we may differ with the hon. member for Red Deer, are never likely to forget the loyal and consistent support t that he gave to the war when he was a whole-hearted member on this side. A certain famous divine, Archbishop Magee, used to say that there were three kinds of .speakers in the world-the men you can listen to, the men you cannot listen to and the men you cannot help listening to, I would put my hon. friend in the last class, namely, those you cannot help listening to.
I should be sorry, as I think many of us here would be, to lose my hon. friend from this House. If he votes for this amendment and if the amendment were to carry and an election follow, w'e might lose him. The hon. member for Red Deer has been somewhat franker than some of his friends who are voting for this amendment. My hon. friend in his speech said:
So far as a desire for an election is concerned,	any hon. member who is pining
for an election is fonder of adventure than I am	The doctrine of self-preservation is
the first law of nature.
If I can infer anything at all from that, I can infer that my hon. friend does not want this amendment to carry, and he has a pretty shrewd idea that it will not carry. He justifies his attitude and his support of the amendment, as does the hon. member for Marquette (Air. Crerar), on grounds of public policy, namely, that the Union Government had only a mandate for the war, also that there are now before the country issues which require an appeal to the country for a fresh Government. It is not necessary for me to point out to this House, or to members who have sat in it for a long time, that this is not a mere formal vote of want of confidence, but that, as a matter of fact, it is an arraignment of the present administration and couched in language so partisan and unfortunate that* I do not wonder that the group of crossbenchers, including the hon. member for Red Deer, are extraordinarily reluctant to swallow the dose prepared for them by the leader of the Opposition.
For a short time, and hurriedly, I should like to refer to the speeches made by- the

lion, member for Marquette and the hon. member for Red Deer. The hon. member for Red Deer referred to his fellow-member as his leader. I do not know whether he is his leader or his pupil, but, I should rather be inclined to think,, the latter. At all events, they preach the same doctrine, and they justify the establishment of a third party on the ground of -their common desire for the abolition of tariffs which they saw no hope of abolishing through the instrumentality of either of the old parties. Before touching on the economic views advanced by my hon. friends of the crossbenches, I should like for a few moments to turn to what has been said as to the new farmers' political organization being a class movement and as such not in the interest of the State as a whole. This morning's paper had rather a significant item to the effect that there were seven hundred canvassers going out from the United Farmers of Manitoba to canvass the whole of the farmers of Manitoba for funds with which to carry on a campaign for capturing the citadel at Ottawa. Well, that is fairly good evidence, I think, that this is a class movement. Certainly, the dominating spirits of this movement in the West are men who have appealed to the class.to which they belonged, initially to those who are purely grain growers, and embracing perhaps a large number of those who are farmers and practically at that time all in the West, and they have used from time to time some sound arguments, some very specious arguments, and some, I think, We must admit, rather unfair and very misleading arguments in their appeal to their constituencies and in trying to point out the alleged injustices under which the farmers were suffering and the remedies which were to be applied. Political action, political methods, party organizations have been preached and practised. In Ontario, if the report is correct, methods of organization have gone so far that they have actually countenanced by prearrangement resignations in the party of those who are nominated if they should attempt to break away from the party, and the organization is to be used for the distinct purpose of aiming at control of federal affairs. In British Columbia a similar energy has been shown in the attempt to organize the United Farmers of British Columbia. This attempt has not met with quite so wide a response, and perhaps, for obvious reasons, because conditions in British Columbia in respect to matters which I have touched on, are not those of the Prairie Provinces. The president, however, of the United Farmers of
Alberta, at a convention held the other day at Victoria, B.C., made this statement, that when the United Farmers of British Columbia went to the polls as one man, they would become the economic force that nature destined them to be. It is quite evident that although differences of opinion exist, there is not the ground for the same response that was given in the Prairie Provinces. The hon. member for Red Deer the other day in his speech made this remark:
:-The farmer of all men

and particularly the Western farmers-are certainly free from any charge of selfishness in so far as their policy goes, because the first thing they ask Parliament and the Government to do is to take off all duties on the things they produce, in order that the general consumers of Canada may have the benefit of wholesome and cheap food. That is not class selfishness surely.
I am afraid I cannot follow my hon. friend in his argument. He is perfectly aware of the fact-and I am not criticising the ground upon which my hon. friends base their action

that the main product of the Western farmer is wheat which has to find its market in the world market unprotected, and it is perfectly natural for him to feel that, if his product has to meet without protection its price in the world market, everything else in the way of tax should be removed from the things he buys. You can call that self-interest or you can call it Selfishness; but what it seems to me our friends in the prairies fail to realize is this, that the abolition of tariffs goes a good deal further than this. In the West as elsewhere there are selfish and sectional protectionists; there are selfish and sectional free traders, and if men of extreme views of this kind insist on pressing their views, and could press them to a point where they would obtain power to put them into effect, they would simply jeopardize the whole state structure.
