As the ex-Minister of Finance (Sir Thomas White) pointed out in his able speech yesterday, any kind of economical policy that has to be carried into effect in this country must be absolutely national in its character, and not sectional.
What are the doctrines and political ideals which my hon. friends from Marquette (Mr. Crerar) and Red Deer (Mr. Clark) and the rest of' the cross-benchers are advocating? I shall quote the exact words of my hon. friend from Marquette so as not to be misunderstood. He said:
It will take a long time indeed to convince the farmers of Western Canada that there is any virtue in the principle of protection, especially in a customs tariff.
Further on he said this:

of the great national industries, namely, that of agriculture, in the old country. The figures that I have quoted will show not only that a tariff for revenue is in operation but that the protective principle also is in operation. Let me illustrate it in other directions. I have not time to go into the details of what has T)een done in connection with wheat, bread and flour during the past few years in England. My hon. friend of course knows that by fixing a guaranteed price of wheat for years, which is still in operation,-and a greater price is being clamoured for now with, I think, some success-and by fixing the maximum price ,of the four pound loaf at 19 cents, the British Government not only gives a protection to the farmers but gives practically a gratuity to the consumers to the extent of millions upon millions of dollars which is taken from the general taxpayers of the country. I am not criticizing their 'action or questioning the wisdom of adopting protective measures of this kind. I would venture to say that with the increasing pressure of the farming community in England ,still higher protection will be adopted. I plight point out to my hon. friend and his friends also that in their handling of the dairy products of England there has been in operation the protective principle, for which I am not criticizing them. They have had such a control of the imports from this country and such a control of the production of their own dairy industries in Great Britain that it has given, what I think they are justified in giving, such a measure of protection to the dairy industries in that country that they will not be ,wiped out and jeopardized as the whole agricultural industry was jeopardized when the crisis arose and which they had to face during the past four years in the old country. I need not point to another direction in which they have adopted the protective principle in England. I refer to the question of. livestock. Tinder the very thin disguise of a health measure one of the strongest forms of protection to the cattle industry of Great Britain has been maintained by an absolutely unjustifiable embargo against the cattle of the United States and especially of Canada where not the wildest straining of the facts could elicit anything but the cleanest bill of 'health in regard to our cattle, and in regard to which they have hardly attempted to veneer their action by denominating it as a health measure. Admittedly it is intended to be a protection to their own-agricultural interests. I do not think that in view of the facts I have stated, Eng-
land's march towards abolishing all tariffs or the element of protection of its own industries has been so rapid or complete as the member for Red Deer would have us believe.
My hon. friend referred to the victory achieved by the Right Hon. Mr. Asquith recently as a triumph of the economic principles for which he stood. I think the facts, if we knew them, would rather be that another man running in the constituency of Paisley holding the same economic principles that Mr. Asquith holds but not with the powerful personality and great traditions that pertain to Mr. Asquith's name, would have met a very different fate. I am glad, as every man is glad, that any English constituency would return a statesman who has served his country so long and so ably as Mr. Asquith has done.
I was rather surprised and a little interested when my hon. friend from Red Deer in his speech from Friday last in giving an illustration as to the evils of protection asked us to follow the example of the men in the trenches. I will quote his exact words. He said:
Let me make an appeal to these gentlemen to use all their endeavours to grow into the same stalwart type of Canadians that stood in the trenches and asked for no protection and the farmers of the West who ask for no protection.
I think that of the men whom he mentions for the purpose of illustration he could not have made a more unhappy choice than when he referred to the man in the trenches as the man who was not asking for protection. I think he would find that the man in the trenches when he was getting' the benefit of some high explosives from the German positions would send up a flare for the artillery in his rear to give him protection. Or if there was the likelihood of an aggressive movement from the German front he would want to have the protection of all the barbed wire he could get, and rightly so. What did the adoption of the helmets used in the last years of the war mean but protection? What was the object of every form of manoeuvre and device that could put the forces of the Allies in better condition than the German forces but protection, and protection of the sanest and soundest character. I do not think a more unhappy illustration could possibly have been drawn than the illustration my hon. friend advanced in that respect.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to keep the House much longer for I know the hour is late and we are shortly to vote on

the amendment before us. The farmers' party, as represented by the group at the other end of this Chamber, are apparently going to support the amendment. I can only regret it. They are certainly not going to support that amendment for the same reasons that the leader of the Opposition and his friends are going to support it, because they have not manifested any particular hostility toward the policies that were put into effect by this Government, or the principles for which this Government stands, apart from this particular tariff question. In fact I think my hon. friend from Marquette and my hon. friend whom we highly esteem from Red Deer, and their associates were with us on this side of the. House when great problems were undertaken, and I think successfully undertaken. They, I think, will not only have sympathy with the difficulties which we encountered and the way in which they were surmounted, but will admit that, apart from this particular measure of tariff reform, which they think we are not hastening to as quickly as they anticipate, they have no very strong cause for voting for this particular amendment especially in the way in which it has been framed. It is quite a different matter with my hon. friends opposite-certainly in the case of the leader of the Opposition because when addressing Liberal friends in this city the other night he put the matter this way:	"If we do not win on Parliament Hill in this particular amendment by carrying it, we will carry it from the Atlantic to the Pacific, and we expect the people of the country to rise up with us and demand that this Government get out of office." That is all he is aiming at. It does not matter what the Government has done or what it stands for-and he seems to comprehend very little of what it has * done-his chief anxiety is to get this Government out of office so that he and his friends may take its place. Well, as citing a fairly independent and pretty sane opinion from the West on this matter I might direct my hon. friend's attention, and especially the attention of the hon. gentleman who last spoke (Mr. Lapointe), for whom we have a warm regard, let me quote from a paper which has a very considerable influence in the West namely the Manitoba Free Press. In its issue of March 3 last, that newspaper says:
Members of the present Dominion Parliament were elected for a five year term, and they are under no moral obligation to vote for Mr. King's amendment providing for an early election. If a majbrity of them want an election they will, of course, support Mr. King's
resolution, and no one will question their right to make such a decision. On the other hand, if their decision is adverse, they are equally within their rights in deciding, so far as the decision rests with them, they will continue to represent their constituents for the period for which they were originally elected.
Should the House of Commons reject Mr. King's amendment, as it no doubt will, it does not follow that there will be no general election until the present Parliament completes its term. The right of the Administration to consult the electorate in its discretion is inherent in our constitution, and an appeal to the people by the Government during the present year is regarded by all political observers as well within possibilities.
A House of Commons elected during the present year, while it may be more representative than the existing Chamber, would fall far short of being truly representative of Canadian opinion at the present time. Election on the basis of the present constituencies would leave the West under represented to at least the extent of twenty members. The West has never had its full representation in the Cana-, dian Parliament. By accident or design it has always happened that a general election is held on tlie eve of redistribution, the effect of which has been to keep the western representation always far below its proper strength. Further, the cities are, under the present scheme of representation under-represented to a degree that is not longer defensible,'and it is quite clear that there must be extensive adjustments in this respect, which ought to be accompanied by the adoption of proportional representation for at least the urban areas.
It is a quite arguable proposition that upon the whole the interests of Canada will be best served by putting up with conditions as they are for another two years until it will be possible to have a proper redistribution of seats which will do the West justice; will give the cities at least a percentage of the additional representation to which they are entitled ; and will provide a more accurate method of election. With these reforms it will be possible to elect a truly representative Commons, which is not attainable under existing conditions. A general election now means that a truly representative Parliament could not he elected until 1925.
Inasmuch as it is already "quite evident that in the next Parliament there will be a contest between the policy strongly backed by the West and an alternative policy, which will draw its strength from the East, it is desirable that the West should have all the members to which it is entitled. The fact that under a proper redistribution the West will gain at least twenty more members, while the East will lose ten, may have some bearing upon the demand that is being heard in the East, and which Mr. Mackenzie King voices for an early election.
Now, Sir, in closing, ^may I say that I hold the opinion, as many people do, that the plunging of the country into a general election at the present time would not be in the best interests of Canada. In spite of what my hon. friends argue, and in spite of what they present to this House, no man would deny that under the present war conditions, with conditions such as they are economically, industrially and socially all, over the world to-day, and to a greater or

lesser extent in 'Canada, to plunge this country into the chaos of a general election would not be wise in the interests of the country or in the interests of any individual party. My hon. friends need not cherish the belief that this Government and its supporters are afraid to meet the country at any time. They are not afraid. My hon. friends seem to entertain some dissatisfaction, not only with so many Liberals joining this party in 1917, but feel an acute distress that those hon. gentlemen are still staying with the Ministry at the present time. I would like to say to my hon. friends that when this Government does go to the country my belief is' a policy will be enunciated which will not only justify the strong grounds upon which my hon. friends from the Liberal party joined the Coalition in 1917, but will also justify in the fullest way the continuation of their adhesion to this party and what it stands for before the people.
If when this Government does go to the country the people should choose to put in another Government,. I cherish the belief that whatever Government does come into power will undertake the administration of this country in the sane constitutional methods to which we here, at all events, are so strongly adhering, and that those elements which would rather reverse all the constitutional principles for which we on both sides of the House have stood for so long will have such a severe lesson taught them that they will realize that no party, however violent or however influential, can divorce from the minds of true Canadians the determination to cherish .the institutions and to maintain the constitution for which they have stood so long. However, when that appeal is made, I believe, as I stated before, that this Government, which has met the conditions of the war and the problems which have arisen out of the war with courage and success, will have no difficulty in justifying their stand to-day and in bringing back to this House a party that will successfully carry on the affairs of this country for many years to come.
Mr. ROBERT H. HALBERT (North Ontario) : Mr. Speaker, after listening to the cross-firing which we have had for several days it requires considerable courage on the part of a new member to make what is called his maiden speech. As a new member I was greatly interested in the able addresses of the hon. members who have spoken, although, Mr. Speaker, some remarks have been made -which I think in the

interests of Canada would have been better unsaid.
I was pleased with the deserved tributes paid by previous speakers to leaders, both past and present, of His Majesty's Government and of His Majesty's loyal Opposition.
The subject of the designing and carrying out of the design of this magnificent building in which we h'ave the honour to meet for the first time has been pretty well .exhausted by men capable of doing justice to the subject and needs no further comment from me. In fact, the ground has been so well covered that there is very little left to be said. The reference made to the war and the Peace Treaty and the deserving tribute paid to our boys whose manly courage and work well done overseas made the Peace Treaty possible, I am sure, Mr. Speaker, is heartily endorsed and concurred in by every member of this House; but there are some matters mentioned in the address from the Throne and in the course of this debate upon it to which I wish to draw your attention, as you will notice that some do not appreciate any too well the fact that in four of the by-elections just held the electors of all shades of politics, callings and professions, sent men to sit in the cross-benches whom they, believed would represent them and not misrepresent them; and just here, Mr. Speaker, permit me, representing, as I do, the federal riding of North Ontario, represented previously in the House by the late lamented Colonel Sam Sharpe, to pay tribute to his memory by saying that he was a man who was held in the highest esteem by the electors of his riding, revered by his men overseas and, I believe, Sir, was esteemed and admired by his fellow members of the House of Commons, of which he was a member for some years.
Reference has been made to the farmers' organization as a "class" movement and it has been said that all classes should be represented. We believe so, too, and that is why we are here representing rural constituencies. We are here, Mr. Speaker, as a protest against class rule and class legislation. The Organized Farmers stand for British fair play, equal rights to all and special privileges to none. We are here to assist any Government that will give us sane, honest, economic and progressive legislation; and Government not subservient, to the Big Interests, but truly representing the ideals and aspirations of the great masses of the people. As some hon. gentle-

men apparently do not want to believe that we are not advocates of class legislation, permit me to read one clause from our constitution in reference to that matter:
By endeavouring to suppress personal, local, sectional, national, political, partisan and class prejudices, and thereby to promote the best Interests of Canada as a whole.
Mr. Speaker, attention has been drawn to the unrest in this country. No doubt there is unrest and a great many people believe that the present Government has outlived its usefulness and would like to see a Government in power that would pay more attention to ascertaining the real will of the people and carrying it out than to territorial boundaries and winning an election. If Canadian politics are to be saved from utter disgrace and if the bloodshed which has taken place in other countries is to be avoided we must have sufficient faith to trust democracy with democratic methods. If our grievances are to be settled by ballot-which I think should be-people must be allowed to use the ballot, and, what is more, the gerrymandering of present day partyism must be absolutely abandoned. When autocracy interferes with the channels of public expression it causes unrest and invites direct action.
Canada is essentially an agricultural country. Its chief asset is the soil, the foundation upon which all the superstructure stands. While we admit that the products of sea, forest and mines are known to be great, yet the possibilities in plant and animal production far exceed them all in magnitude and importance. The products of the mines are taken, never to be restored; the forests to be perhaps partially renewed after many years; but .the farm production where intelligently carried on has been secure without depleting to any appreciable extent nature's storehouse of resources.
The manufacturing industry, it is true, has come to play an important part in the nation's progress, yet a great many of them are dependent on farming for their raw material, and a great many of them must look to the rural districts for the great bulk of the market for their finished product. Therefore, the progress in agriculture in Canada is a national concern. It affects every one, and everything possible should be done to make agricultural life attractive and remunerative so that labour and capital will be attracted to the land instead of away from it as it is at present.
Mr. Speaker, every one who has the true interest of Canada at heart desires to see
the present unrest satisfactorily settled. This can be done by an honest effort on the part of all. To my mind, one of the greatest causes of the unrest lies in our tariff laws, which affect to a very great extent the high cost of living; but, Mr. Speaker, as you have intimated that will be discussed in the Budget debate, I will not discuss it at the present time, except to refer to what has already been said with regard to re-establishment of the returned soldier.
In connection with the re-establishment of the returned soldier it has been urged that he should go on the land. We hope to see a good many returned soldiers go on the land. But when they do so they find that the tariff affects them very materially so far as the cost of the implements of production is concerned. It , has been said that a large amount of the money necessary to pay our war debt has to be taken out of the top six inches of the soil. You ask the returned soldier to go on the land and to take out of the top six inches of the soil enough to ipaf for the canned goods he eats as well as for the shells he fired when over in the trenches fighting for democracy. Well, suppose he does that for a number of years and eventually succumbs under the heavy burden, what does the tariff do then? It collects from the heirs a percentage by way of taxation even on his shroud, on his coffin, on the screw-nails that fasten down the lid of his coffin, and on the shovel with which the grave digger digs his grave. No doubt the same people who impose these tariffs may be lamenting the fact that they cannot follow him over the Jordan and put a tax on his royal robe.
With regard to the amendment of the hon. leader of the Opposition, I may say that while I do not agree with the wording of it, I shall support it because I believe that the present administration has not the confidence of the people, as the by-elections just held go to prove. If their record is as good and their policy as popular and pleasing as they would try to make us believe, they should be anxious to go to the country and get the endorsation of the people to carry on. The question is not who will be in power, but who will give the people the best legislation in the interests of Canada; and of that the people should be the judge.
Mr. Speaker, there is one other matter mentioned in the Address about which I wish to speak before taking my seat, and that is the Franchise Act. We who have been born in Canada sometimes fail, I

Mr. Speaker, I desire to make a few observations at this point chiefly because I think that my hon. friends on the other side would be disappointed if I did not. What has been
fltr. Halbert.!
said this afternoon will, I am sure, lead them to expect me to say a few words.
The attack that has been made upon the President of the Council (Hon. N. W. Bowell) was so thin, so stale, and so vindictive that it will leave no impression on the country unfavourable to the President of the Council. That kind of thing always reacts on tire man who is responsible for it, and I am sure that that will be the case in this instance.
The attack on the President of the Council was due to his criticisms of some of the religious orders in the war. As to the accuracy in detail of what he said I have no knowledge. But in support of what he said at North Bay I desire to quote a very eminent and brave French-Canadian, who for many years was a much admired citizen of my own city, a man with whom I enjoyed very pleasant social relations, I refer to General Lessard. Here is a report of something that he said during the progress of the war:	.
There is a general complaint that the lower clergy of the Province have not lent an attentive ear to the voice of the higher Episcopal _ authorities so as to bring its message in regard to the duty of the French-Canadians at the present time to recruit the race as a whole.
He pointed out the grave responsibility that the lower clergy assumed in putting a damper on the appeal of the hierarchy to its children. As far as he himself was concerned he expected a more wholehearted co-operation from the clergy in conformity with the great influence which . it exercises on the destinies of the French-Canadian. He might say the same thing about their leaders-those who directed opinion in Quebec. It was long enough that politics had been a bar to the complete spirit of union necessary to rouse up the French-Canadian people to rally to the great cause.
I	desire to read also a paragraph from a letter written to Colonel Obed Smith, a Liberal, by a French-Canadian who was serving at the front, about the time of the disturbances in the city of Quebec. It reads:	[DOT]
' The question should be handled with steel gauntlets,' he says, 1 Ignorance is rampant in my native province. The blame is on the shoulders of the Fathers of Confederation, who allowed two official languages. A dual language begets separate schools, they beget ignorance.
It may require a small army to enforce the radical changes after the war, hut we shall have it. The indifference of Quebec in this struggle will be a powerful lever in the hands of a bold leader.'
What is the name of the miscreant who wrote that letter?
The letter was given by the writer to Colonel Obed Smith.
Who wrote the letter?

A French-Canadian at the front.
Mr. ARCH AM,B AULT: Anonymous?

No, Colonel Obed Smith was a man who was serving and who had a good deal of prominence iii this country. Therefore, there is a good deal of support for what the President of the Council (Mr. Rowell) said and for which he has been criticised so severely on at least two separate occasions.
The hon. member for Russell (Mr. Murphy) produced a document from which he read a number of extracts. I am familiar with the literature of the Orange Association, and this bears none of the earmarks of that organization. I venture to say that this document from which he read was printed in either Nova Scotia or Quebec; a document something of this kind has been sent out, but to what extent it is garbled, I do not know. I can, however, say this for myself and for the names of those Past Grand Officers that appear on the document; I did not sign such a document, and I have no reason to believe that they did. As to the position taken in this document with regard to schools, with regard to the war, and with regard to the association of which I am a member, I am prepared to defend the substance of everything that appears there. I want to point out to the House that in this debate I am not the aggressor; I am doing as every true Orangeman ought to do, standing on the defensive, defending his principles and convictions as straightforwardly as it is the practice of members of the association to do. I will endeavour to do that, Sir, without saying a word that should give my hon. friends opposite who disagree with me in matters of faith any just cause for offence.
My course, since I came into this House -and this is my fourth session-has been *one of conciliation. I think I may fairly say-and my hon. friends opposite will agree with me-that I have not sought any occasion to stir up racial strife or to express any opinions that I thought might be offensive to any one of them. At the same time, I do not purpose sitting in my seat and hear the. institution with which I am connected attacked without making a reply. This document refers to the language question which has been the bone of contention between Quebec and Ontario. It arose shortly before the war and was the occasion during the war of a very serious agitation in certain parts of Ontario as well as in Quebec. The charge was that the province of Ontario had proscribed the
French language. That is not so. I have before me regulation 17 which says:
Where necessary in the case of Frenchspeaking pupils, French may be used as the language of instruction and communication; but such use of French shall not be continued beyond Form 1 excepting during the school year of 1912-13, when it may also be used as the language of instruction and communication in the case of pupils beyond Form 1, who owing to previous defective training, are unable to speak and understand the English language.
Further than that, upon a report of the chief inspector, the French language may be used for communication and instruction up to the fourth form.
I think that is a reasonable regulation, especially when we all realize, as has been admitted even by the counsel for the French-tCanadian Educational Association that, under the constitution of this country, there is no obligation upon the province of Ontario to allow French to be taught at all, and when so many believe that it is [DOT] impossible in the primary schools to teach two languages successfully.

When was that proved?
'Mr. HOCKEN: I say that is the general belief in the province of Ontario.
That is a wrong belief.

It is the belief of that
eminent Episcopal Divine,. Bishop Fallon, of London, and I am in his company when I'say that in my belief two languages cannot be taught successfully in the primary schools. We make provision in the secondary schools for the teaching of French, and practically every child that goes into the secondary schools studies French.
Has the Bishop to whom the hon. member refers ever learned French?
I have never tested him, so I am unable to answer that question.
If it is impossible in the primary schools of Ontario to teach both languages, English and French successfully, how is it that both languages are taught successfully in Quebec?

They are so much
cleverer than wre.
I think so.

Sit down. You started it;
take your medicine.

Let the hon. member
answer the question.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member for Toronto West has the floor, and I hope he will be permitted to continue his speech without interruption.
I put him a question, and I think my question is legitimate and I would like to have an answer.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
It is within
the right of the hon. member to answer the question or not, but he should at least be given an opportunity to do so.
Why not?

Behind that claim is
this: that the French language shall have the same status in every province as it has in the province of Quebec.
That is the constitution.

No. I should like to read the opinion of Hon. Senator Belcourt, who was specially delegated to prepare a reasoned opinion of the law upon the subject. He said:
The true fact, regrettable as it may be, is that for the federal domain and the provincial domain of Quebec, there is but the constitution which defines equality of both languages at the Dominion Parliament, at the Quebec Parliament, before the Federal tribunal or courts, and also before the courts of the Province of Quebec is the French language on an equal footing with the English language. Section 133 of the British North America Act which proclaims equal rights of the French and English before the Federal House, the Federal courts and before the provincial house of Quebec and the provincial courts, and in section 93 of the same Act which gives to each province the exclusve power to legislate in matters of education, constitute the sum total of the rights officially recognized in favour of the French-Canadian people of the Dominion of Canada; these are the only rights recognized in favour of our race; they are the only rights which cannot be stripped from us without the intervention of the Imperial Parliament; they are the only rights which the constitution and the law formally guaranteed to us; they are the only rights which the law will permit us to exact and about which it gives us the means whereby to exact the same.
I hope my hon. friend will accept the reasoned opinion of Senator Belcourt. That was also admitted by Sir Wilfrid Laurier.
If I understand Senator Belcount's opinio'n properly, federally speaking, the French and English languages are on an equal footing. Is not that the case?

No. They are on an equal footing in the federal courts, and in the Houses of Parliament, but not in the schools. It is just 'as well to have this matter out now we are at it. There has been a movement vigorously and energetically pressed, to surround the province of Ontario with a French population which would enable the French to secure about twenty seats in the legislature, and thus dominate the policy of the province.
Why not?

Why not resist it, if we do not agree with the principles that prevail in your province? Father Hamon, the head of the Jesuit order, has admitted that this movement is going on. He .wrote a book on French-Canadian aims and ambitions in which he said this:	.
None of the obstacles met have checked the settlement of the valley of the Ottawa and of the Province of Ontario. And yet, for the French-Canadian, is not Ontario a country different from theirs, both in religion and language, and even in polities, in that, at least, which relates to local interests? In spite of these difficulties, in spite of a tenacious English element, hostile to the invasion and seeking by all possible means to prevent it, the French-Canadian pushes towards tile end for .which he set out. The French-Canadian infiltrate themselves everywhere in those counties of Ontario which divide it from the province of Quebec, and continue bravely to march toward the West .
That is their right.

Yes. To continue:
The policy of the church is to guide the movement, plan and forward settlement, and especially the parish system, the parochial school, and the religious and national societies.
That is their duty.

Then to watch and wait for providential
developments, that she may mass and lead the people for the effective overthrow of Protestant error and paganism.
That is their hope.

The French-Canadian race is God's chosen
people to save North America and to restore its population to the bosom of the church of Rome. Is this a dream? No, it is more; it is an. everyday issue.

As far as the people of the. Protestant section of Ontario are concerned we have just as much right to oppose that
movement as the hierarchy of Quebec has to encourage and promote it?
Who is preventing you?

Nobody yet. We are doing the best we can to resist the movement, but we have not succeeded quite so well as we would like.
Mr.. CANNON: Would my hon. friend allow me a question?
Keep quiet over there.
Order.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. The hon. member for Dorchester (Mr. Cannon) has asked permission to ask a question of the hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Hocken). Had the hon. member for West Toronto retained the floor, the hon. member for Dorchester would certainly not have had that right, but as the hon. member for Toronto has taken his seat the hon. member for Dorchester is perfectly justified in asking his question.
Will the hon. member for West Toronto give me one example where the Catholic church in the province of Quebec has impeded or tried to impede any Protestant movements in the province of Quebec?
I do not live in the province of Quebec.
Happily for us.
We do not grow your kind.

In answer to my hon.
friend from Dorchester I could give many instances, and I may do that later. Just now I am trying to give my reasons why the institution which I represent as one of its officers, resists the extension of the French language into the province of Ontario, believing it to be inimical to the interests of the English-speaking people of that province, and contrary to the constitution. I am supported in that by some of the most eminent members of the Roman Catholic church. There are clergymen in this city, as well as the Bishop of London, who say that this is being done by the bishops and the French hierarchy.
There is another reason why we do not want this to go on because the aim is to extend ecclesiastical government to the province of Ontario. The province of Quebec is ruled by the ecclesiastics. The people must take their politics as well as their religion from the bishops. We do not want

that hind of thing in Ontario, because we have discovered that when clericals rule a country there is always restraint upon freedom. It is even worse, Mr. Speaker, when this restraint is imposed by the members of a faith whose religious leaders have the power, according to the belief of those who follow them, to open or close the doors of heaven. The /Protestant preacher has his own personal influence and nothing more, but the bishop of the Roman church has the sacraments and that makes a good deal of difference. My hon. friend dissents from my statement that in politics they are governed, as they are in spiritual matters, by their clerical leaders. Let me give an instance to prove my point. It is a well known fact that if a newspaper publishes matter which is offensive, or thought to be injurious to the interests of religion in Quebec, that newspaper can have the ban put upon it, and it can be closed up. It has to suspend publication. That happened to one of these papers some years ago.
How many years ago?

I cannot give you the exact year' but I remember the case very well. It does not apply to newspapers only but to pamphlets. A man cannot write a book in Quebec that declares for freedom in politics without having to take it back.

Ah; I will give you a notable instance of that. I will tell you all about it. The most interesting I have to present is that of a book or pamphlet written by the Hon. L. 0. David. The writer's object was to uphold the proposition, that the priests ought to confine themselves to the spiritual domain, and as his reason for so saying he quoted from history to show that whenever they meddled with secular affairs it was to their own hurt and that of the province. Starting by laying down "that bishops and priests are men subject to error" he went on to point out how, in his view, they erred in 1837 and at each subsequent crisis when French nationality was in jeopardy. Professedly a devout Catholic, Senator David deplored this, blaming the mistaken course of the priests to ignorance of public sentiment. "The truth," he declares, "reaches them (the priests) with difficulty through the fumes of the incense which envelops them," and he warned them to awake from their sleep of false security and escape the storm which menaced them by leaving politics alone.

The little book, which was issued in September, 1896, was condemned by the bishops in a joint pastoral in January following. After stating the book had been submitted to the Holy Office at Rome and been formally condemned "with the approval of the sovereign pontiff," the rule is laid down that no layman "has authority to judge, condemn, or approve of doctrines or writings. .	. It is, by your bishops and the
priests, who- are united with them, that you are to receive the teachings of the Holy See. . . . to be with the Pope you must not be in opposition to the bishops."
Will the hon. gentleman allow me a question?

No, not just now. The judgment against this book was that every person having a copy should destroy it and that any copies in the hands of the author should also be destroyed. Senator David said:
When I wrote the little book 1 had no idea of the storm I was raising. I thought I was doing the clergy a service in speaking out the thoughts that X could not drive from my mind. After the last general election I noticed a growing feeling against clerical interference in politics, and simply gave it publication. They may condemn me; they may excommunicate me. I cannot help that, but I shall remain a Catholic-that is my religion, and they cannot take my faith from me.
This is the significant paragraph to which I am trying to lead up. He said:
I thought when I wrote my book that, as a British subject, I had a perfect right to do so. If not, there is something wrong, for I feel that, as a French Canadian and a Catholic, I should have the same rights in politics as my Englishspeaking brethren.
A more lamentable confession by a public man has seldom been made than that he is not allowed to exercise his own judgment in writing a book criticising the political activities within his own province. If that does not prove my case that there is an ecclesiastical government in Quebec I do not know what more would be required. We do not want that in Ontario. We do not want the peculiar laws established by the church in Quebec. We do not want the tithing system. Down in the county of Prescott, although there are no such laws in this province, a county judge gave a judgment that the tithing laws of Quebec operated in the province of Ontario and he compelled a man to pay his tithe for the building of a church. That is introducing something into Ontario which we object to.

I do not think that was the purport of the judgment. It was not

that the tithing system of Quebec was in force in Ontario but it was that when a man enjoys the services of a priest he ought to pay for them.

!If my hon. friend can see any distinction I would like to know it. If this man enjoyed the services of a priest he ought to pay for, them but my point is that he should not be compelled by law to pay for them because there is no such law in Ontario and it is a law that we do not want in Ontario.
* Mr. CANNON: Will the hon. gentleman allow me a question?
No, not now.
It is significant; the answer must be hard.

It is so late that I would rather not be interrupted. There are many other things of that kind that I do not propose to go into but I want to explain why it is that we object to these things.
Now why should the French desire to engraft these laws on Ontario? It is to get control of that province. That may be a perfectly legitimate ambition; they have the right to do so if they can; but I submit that they have no right to condemn us for resisting such a policy when we do not believe in it. If the French Canadians desire that kind of Government in the province of Quebec well and good, let them have it; but they should keep it there and not try to drag it into the province of Ontario. How does it come,. Mr. Speaker, if there is not a settled purpose by powerful and wealthy organizations to get control of Ontario-why is it they infiltrate into Northern Ontario and do not go into Northern Quebec? There is a lot of good land in the northern parts of Quebec, the people of that province could go and live under their own laws and under their own peculiar institutions. Nobody in the province of Ontario has ever suggested we should go down and. interfere with their local autonomy. They can have any kind of government in Quebec that they desire, but we are not going to have it brought into the province of Ontario if we can prevent it. A prominent public man told me that he got on the Transcontinental train at Quebec, about a year ago, and it was occupied by a number of colonists and for a distance of many miles fresh colonists at intervals boarded the train.. Not a single one of them detrained in the province of Quebec; they were all billed for the northern parts of Ontario. They go 19
there to develop their own institutions and to overcome the institutions that we have established there at the present time. I repeat that the French Canadians have a perfect right to do that, they have a perfect right to go into the province of Ontario, but we have an equal right to fix the terms upon which they shall come. This policy to which I have reference is one that politicians are working out for their future aggrandizement and they are looking forward to the time when the peculiar institutions of their province will be spread over the province of Ontario.
Another matter to which reference was made in the circular in question was the war. We were aggrieved at the action of Quebec in the war, and it could not be otherwise. I am not going to rub it in, but I want to state our case. We were fighting for France as the ally of our Old Motherland, and we thought that surely the people who claim French descent, and had French blood in their veins, would do as much for their Mother country as we were doing for our Mother country. Especially, in our opinion, should that have been the case, when the very existence of France was at stake-
What about England?

-much more so than that of England. England had a. navy that could resist invasion, but the very existence of France hung in the balance in that war. And we expected our French Canadian fellow citizens to join us at least in -proportionately equal numbers to go to her defence. Now they did not do that, and it surely cannot surprise my hon. friend opposite-
Not from you.

-that in the province of Ontario, and in the cfty of Toronto, some resentment should be felt on that account. We had not, perhaps, so much right to respond to the call that was made from Europe as the men from the province of Quebec. I remember, Sir,-as I stated in this House once before-an old friend of mine, and a faithful follower of the late Sir Wilfrid Laurier as long as he lived, who used to come to my office and say that if there should be a war in which England and France would fight together that would be the thing that would unite Canada. We agreed that if such a thing should ever occur-
Were you consulted?

-that would certainly bring the two races in this country together; and if those who my hon. friends opposite represent had taken the part they should have taken there would have been in our province and in every other province, an open door to every ambition they had. Sir, in practically every home-certainly in every Orange home in Canada-there was the deepest anxiety and there were broken hearts over the boys who were fighting in the trenches, many of whom had laid down their lives in France and in Flanders. Go to the West and the records of the Institution that I, as an officer, represent, will show that in some oases practically every eligible member of the Institution in a particular section was off on the firing line. In the city of Toronto there were more Orangemen went overseas voluntarily out of approximately 30,<}00 members than there were out of the 1,800,000 French Canadians in the province of Quebec.	'
Will my hon. friend let me ask him a question?
Not just now.
How about the Orangemen who armed themselves against England before the war.
Mr. Speaker, I am discussing Canada.

Discuss the Orangemen
for a while, be honest.

I am doing so. Let me say to my hon. friend that when the war did break out in no part of the British Empire did the men respond as cheerfully and as numerously as they did from the province of Ulster.
Not any better than anywhere else.

The Ulster Brigade, and the Ulster people had nothing to be ashamed of in the war. They went out and laid down their lives just as freely as the Canadians did, and they performed good work. Mr. Speaker, I ask you, and I ask this House, if it is any wonder that men who sent their members out, as this organization did-sent more out of one city than were sent by the French Canadians out of the whole province of Quebec, numbering probably 1,800,000 of that race-is it any wonder that there should be resentment on our part, and is it surprising that sometimes strong language was used in that connection?
What about our part?

There has been a good
deal of talk about the insults that were levelled at Quebec but I do not want to go into that.
You have been into that already. Do not worry about that.

The course adopted by
the members of this institution was exactly in line with their record ever since 1912. Every time rebellion has raised its head in this country, or invasion has been threatened, the men who belonged to this organization were the back-bone of the force that put it down.

Edward Carson.
Mr. HiOCKEN:	In 1837 the rebellion in
what is now the province of Ontario was put down by the members of this Institution; and they bore a large part in the fights in 1866 at Ridgeway and Fort Erie. Yes, and they went up to Fort Garry in 1870, and in doing so they committed a crime in the estimation of my hon. friends opposite. They took their part in the fight there, and they had to go up again in 1885 when the rebellion was revived. The members of this organization went out to South Africa by the thousand in the Boer war of 1900, and again in 1914 almost to a man went to the Front, the members of the Orange order who were eligible for such service. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that men who have served Canada in that way, men who have played a noble part in the terrible crisis that we have gone through deserve respect of the country and are entitled to credit for the patriotic services they have rendered.
Why is that, Sir? Because they are trained in loyalty to the British Empire. They have in the past resisted every attempt to dismember the Empire, and they will be true to their convictions in that regard as long as they exist.
My hon. friend will remember that in some places an Orangeman is spoken of as a bigot. Nothing could be further from the truth. Orangemen are the most tolerant body of men in the world. Civil and religious liberty is nowhere so universal as in those places in which this institution is strong. In no province and city of this Dominion are the people of the same faith as my hon. friends opposite given more freedom than in the province of Ontario and in the city of Toronto. Why, Mr. Speaker, the people of Toronto contributed $260,000 to carry on the work of the Knights of

Columbus- an organization composed entirely of men of the opposite faith, and I suppose three-quarters of that sum came from the pockets of Protestants. Is that intolerance, is that bigotry? And yet such is typical of the organization.
Do hon. gentlemen forget that the Orange organization has invariably stood for its principles and convictions regardless of the personnel of our Governments? In the days of Macdonald and Cartier the Orangemen of Ontario were supporting them. Why? Because, Mr. Speaker, Macdonald and Cartier had a policy that was approved by the members of that institution-a policy for the building up of this country as a part of the British Empire, and they supported those two leaders as faithfully as did any of their fellow Canadians.
They did more than that, Sir. When Sir Wilfrid Laurier, the late leader of the party across the floor first became Prime Minister he had no stronger supporters in the province of Ontario than the members of this institution. In the City of Toronto, his opponent, the late Sir Charles Tupper, was not allowed to speak. The men who prevented him from speaking were members of the institution which I am trying to defend here to-night, and they worked energetically for the return of Sir Wilfrid Laurier and the party that he represented. They did that, Sir, because his party expressed their convictions, and they have done that in every instance from the tune the institution was founded ninety years ago to the present day.
I venture to say that had it not been for the members of this institution in the City of Montreal, my right hon. friend the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty) would not have been elected. They did not do that, Mr. Speaker, in any hope of reward, they knew they had nothing to expect from the Minister of Justice, but he stood for the things in which they believed. And I submit to this House, Mr. Speaker, that there is nothing finer in a citizen than that he shall stand for convictions that he honestly holds. If he does that he is a man to be admired; if he does not, he is not a good citizen.
My hon. friends opposite may think that the Orange order is a Conservative organization.
Hear, hear.

Well, what about their supporting the late Sir Wilfrid Laurier; what about their defeating Sir Rodman Roblin in Manitoba if the order is a Con- servative organization? Orangemen went solidly against Sir Rodman Roblin, and he admitted from the windows of his news-

paper office, the night of his defeat that his overthrow was brought about by the desertion of his old-time Orange friends. I state that, Mr. Speaker, to emphasize the fact that these men stand for their convictions as good citizens ought to.
I could go on, Mr. Speaker, if I so desired and make some reference to another organization the Knights of Columbus-an organization of just the same kind as the Orange Order.

Why don't they fuse?
Mr- HOCKEN: They are both patriotic
and religious; their only difference is in their religious faith. I have here the Congressional Record, and I find in it the oath taken by the Knights of Columbus of the third degree. I have the right, I presume, Mr. Speaker, to put this upon Hansard, but I am not going to do so.
How fickle.

I will tell you why. My friends in the Knights of Columbus deny the accuracy of this oath. I am not able to prove that it is correct, and as it is not my practice to use anything here or elsewhere unless I can substantiate it, I am going to try to convince my hon. friends that I desire to be fair with them and with all they represent.
Mr. Speaker, the Orange Order is a bulwark of the constitution-a powerful force for orderly government and evenhanded justice. The late Mr. Justice McMahon, himself a member of the same religious faith as my friends opposite, had an opportunity during the course of a trial presided over by him to have all the ritual and obligations of the order put before him, and he gave it as his unbiased opinion that any institution founded upon the principles therein stated was one that ought to be supported, and one that must be a benefit to the community.
In closing, Sir, I just want to say that if the Roman Catholic church will cease to be a political institution-will surrender its claims to temporal power and confine its activities * to spiritual things, there will be no need for the Orange Order. But until that time comes the order will exist and will grow in strength and power, because we do not believe in the union of temporal power with spiritual domination, and as long as the Vatican maintains that it has the right to rule the world, and in the final analysis to be the sole judge, it must get resistance from Protestants and from members of the Orange Order.
There are just one or two reasons why the Order should continue to exist, Mr. Speaker,

but I will only give you one reason. It is because there are such men in public life as the hon. member for Russell (Mr. Murphy).
And yourself.

Before making my argument, which will be an historical argument in favour of the early dissolution of Parliament, I wish to join the other members who have offered their felicitations to the mover (Mr. Cronyn) and to the seconder (Mr. McGregor) of the Address. But at the same time, Mr. Speaker, I must again this year protest against the seconder of the Address being 
an English-speaking rather than a Frenchspeaking gentleman. As to the other speeches made by hon. members on your right, may I be permitted to mention just a few typical remarks?
The hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Mowat) made a very frank and honest remark-the most honest, I believe, hfe ever made in this House'-when he said that the reason why he did not go back to the Liberal fold when the war was qver was because there was no coal in the bin and the larder was empty. That remark was quite superfluous; we knew all along that his reason for not coming back to the Liberal party was a "stomachal" one.
A somewhat similar typical remark, I observed, came from the member for Yukon (Mr. A. Thompson), who stated emphatically that he did not want an election. Sir, some people have an uncouth way of mak-_ ing their sores and their fears conspicuous.
The other two typical remarks to which I wish to direct attention were made by the Minister of the Interior (Hon. Mr. Meighen), and may be found on page 161 of Unrevised Hansard. The member for Marquette (Hon. Mr. Crerar) had stated that he would give the votes to aliens and make them fight. The Minister of the Interior made reference to this assertion, and the member for Marquette said, page 161:
It was the judgment of the military authorities of the United States. They enrolled these men and the casualty lists, when they came back to the United States, contained many foreign names.
The Minister of the Interior replied in this way:
I am informed on authority of, the highest character that the military men of the United States did not allow them in the front line. But I would prefer to take my example, even in matters of the late war, from the British Empire, rather than from the United States.
Very good; but not a week, a day, or an hour afterwards, but something like two minutes afterwards, the Minister of the Interior took his example, not from the British Empire, but from the United States. On the same page he is reported as follows:
The principle that the hon. gentleman attacks, right or wrong, has been more the subject of debate and has been more thoroughly reviewed on this continent than any other principle ever presented to a free, people for one hundred and twenty-five years. Its first sponsor on the American continent was the father of the American Republic, George Washington. Was he the friend and ally of special privilege and the enemy of the common people? The second statute that he placed on the statute books of the United States, after it became a nation, was a statute embodying In very pronounced form the principle that the hon. gentleman

impugns. Its next prominent sponsor (indeed very, very few opposed it), was the founder of the other great political' party in the country, Thomas Jefferson. Coming nearer to our own time, the man who laid, the foundations of the present tariff policy of the United States in general form was the man who emancipated the slaves in the United States, Abraham Lincoln. Abraham Lincoln was an adherent throughout his life to the principle that the hon. gentleman attacks. Was he either the servant or the ally of special privilege? Was he the enemy of the common people of his country? Can such an allegation be levelled at Theodore Roosevelt, whose principles were just the same?
Well, Sir, is this in accordance with the minister's previous assertion that he would prefer to take his example from the British Empire? Not quite;-but the reason is very-clear to me. In the one case it suited his argument to cite England as an example; in the other' case to cite England as an example would have destroyed his argument. So that the minister displayed his ultra-loyalism when it would be effective, but hid it very carefully away when it might have been harmful to his argument, showing the suppleness of which he is a past master.
The hon. minister also referred to his "successful" trip to New Brunswick and to the "successful" part he took in the Victoria and Carleton election. I will not chide him on the success of his trip, but I cannot let the incident pass without bringing to the attention of the House the fact that the candidate whom he, with the Postmaster General, Hon. Mr. Blondin, and the Minister of Labour, Hon. Mr. Robertson, supported, was the notorious Colonel Mel- [DOT] ville, who organized wholesale perjury during the last election at St. Johns barracks, and who tampered with the franchise in an effort to defeat the will of the electors of Chambly and Vercheres. I have nothing to add, Sir, but simply to cite the French dioton: "Dis-moi qui tu hantes,. je te dirai qui tu es."
I wish also to reply briefly to the hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Hocken):
I am informed that at the first sitting of this House in the month of March, 1918, when the hon. member did not protest in the House against the' nomination of the hon. member for Shefford (Mr. Boivin) as Deputy Speaker, he was .censured by his lodge. It is evidently for fear of being chastised again that he has tried vainly for half an hour to-night to ansvrer the grave and irrefutable charges brought forward by the hon. member for Russell (Mr. Murphy). His answers are in the same spirit as the articles written in the Orange Sentinel.
My hon. friend read a letter purporting to be from a French Canadian, an anonymous letter, published evidently in his paper to enlarge its circulation, as all letters published in that paper are. I should not say that all the letters are anonymous, because I find a letter signed very courageously by a gentleman who does not give his proper name, but signs himself " a Royal Purple Marksman." My hon. friend stated also that he never raised any race cry in this House and claimed that he was a most tolerant man. He reminds me of the ancient dragon with two heads, one blowing cold and the other blowing hot. He very seldom raises a race cry in this House, that is true but he edits a race cry in his rag. I take the edition of the 11th of March, the last number, on the front page of which there are twelve articles, every one of which, with one exception, is a race cry. The first article is entitled, " Our Point of View " and it is an attack on the French people of Ontario in regard to the school question. The second article is entitled: " Rome, the Bible and the Public School."- The third article is entitled, " Possibilities in the New Plan for Ireland'," an attack on the Catholics of Ireland. The fourth article is entitled, " The Pope and the Turk "; other articles are entitled respectively, " A Clerical Grafter ", " The Vatican Mission ", " Irish Land Purchase ", and " Evading the Facts ",-the last being an attack upon Toronto Saturday Night for defending the Irish Catholics of Ireland. I fail to understand why my hon. friend states that he is very moderate, and that he is not taking his full share in spreading racial prejudice in this country.
My hen. friend also stated that he had a great fear of the immigration of the French-Canadians into Ontario. He did not state the ground for his fear; he will not state it, but he knows it. The reason is one that was given to-night by the hon. member for Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe), namely, that the increase of our population is by nature and not by artificial processes. The fear of my hon. friend is that the love that the French-Canadians have for cradles and children might interfere with the love that my hon. friend's brothers have for kennels and Pomeranians. My hon. friend also stated, in order to show that his brothers are broad-minded, that the Orangemen elected the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty)-and I am sorry that the Minister of Justice has left his seat-in St. Anne's. I will give the House an example

of the love the hon. member for Toronto West (Mr. Hooken) has for the Minister of Justice. This is a letter published in the Orange Sentinel of January 29, page 3:
The House Leadership.
Sir,
I am sorry to read that C. J. Doherty will be House leader during the coming session. That news would be more in its place under a heading like this: "Just one more slap in the face for Protestants". Is there no other man in the Union party capable of taking Borden's place? I lost my two nearest neighbours by supporting 'Union Government when they went into power. I would do it again under the same circumstances, but under no condition could I support that party now. Who is running the country, Borden. Doherty, or the Pope? Could we expect much less from either of the latter two? Why does Borden still bend under pressure from Quebec after the rest of Canada told him at the last election that he could run Canada without the French? What did he do under conscription any more than drain the protestant farms of the last of its manhood? I do not think he will be proud of the fact or results at the next election. Remember-[DOT]
And this is probably the reason why the hon. member does not want an election.
Remember, I am not sore over having to part with a son, as I did not have any, and was physically unfit myself.
This Orange brother evidently made a tremendous sacrifice for his country. To continue:
But I sympathize with those that had sons. All this while the French looked on or hid in the timber. Why were they pardoned? Was it to cheer up the boys who fought, bled and in many instances died for them? I can't agree with you in having any further use for R. L. Borden. Give us a Leader who can stand alone, not one that looks for a prop from the French. Surely there are such men among Protestants who could fill Borden's place. Kindly enlighten me if I am on the wrong track, although all I have ever done to merit the granting of this favour, is paid my subscription (none too prompt at times) and read the paper regularly and found much information of great importance and help. Keep up the good ^yorlc according to your views. Raise the price if necessary, for I am sure no person could reasonably complain, even if we can't always see the same as you. Though not an Orangeman I fully agree with the principles.
David J. Jones.
The hon. member is responsible for everything published in his newspaper, responsible, perhaps, to Jones too, but he did not answer this letter. Let me now come to the amendment.
One reason why I rose to-night in support of the amendment of the hon. leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) was to give the House an historical argument regarding the early dissolution of Parliament. History is a subject which is

very useful to men who study political questions. My second reason is that, being a descendant of one of the first settlers of Montreal, I am very fond and proud of Canada, and I deplore the fact that some people in this country are under the impression that the history of Canada started in 1867. Some even think it started only when the Western provinces came into Confederation. I never felt so miserable as one day last year when an hon. member asked me, " Who was that man Cartier whose centenary they are celebrating in Montreal?" The period which I wish to bring to the attention of the House is from the year 1841 to 1847, covering the passing of the Act of Union of 1840 and the elections following the passing of that Act.
For a thorough understanding of the underlying currents existing before 1841 it is necessary to describe briefly the turmoil into which Canada was plunged from 1760 to 1840 by the autocratic rule, not of England, but of its governors and their entourage. In Upper Canada the autocratic creed was represented by the Family Compact, composed of men who kept for themselves all the high and remunerative positions, as well as the wealth of the country in the granting of lands and who were bitter opponents of the reformers who were preaching and figthing for responsible government. Those who wanted to protest were ostracized. Robert Gourlay was arrested in 1818 for preparing a petition to the Mother Country, and, although acquitted, and although a thorough Scotchman, he was de

 ported by the Government of that time. William Lyon Mackenzie because he had stated that " the powers claimed by the Tory executive were nearly as arbitrary as the iron rule of the Czar of Muscovy," was charged with a breach of the privileges of the House and expelled from Parliament. Five times he was re-elected by the electors of York, and five times he was forcibly prevented from taking his seat, the autocrats of that time ruling that " they could not prevent the electors from electing whom they please." Evidently they were not aware of the refinements of the War-time Elections Act, " but that they could by a mere resolution pass judgment on the eligibility of the persons elected to sit and vote." Colborne and Sir Francis Bond Head, enslaved by the elements who 1 a.m mistrusted the people, refused *	to apply the principles of responsible government, and the dissatisfaction of the masses came to a head in 1837 with the result that we all know. It brought the

Rebellion, which was crushed with unnecessary severity.
In Lower Canada the same elements were playing the same havoc with the liberties of the people. Here a population of 65,000 people were left without their leaders who, after the cession of 1760, and especially after the Treaty of Paris on February 10, 1763, went back to France, and the people were left at the mercy of greedy speculators and profiteers who were granted the lands, and who dominated and ground down the people with the complicity of the governors. In 1774, the Quebec Act, which was framed by England to redress some of the grievances of the Canadians, was jeopardized in its effects by the rapacity of the same element. The Act of 1791, framed by Pitt, created a Legislative Council and, for the first time, an elective House. But that was again nullified by the despotism of Craig and his Tory favourites who controlled the Council, and a bitter fight ensued. The war of 1812 with the United States stopped politics for a while and again, as in 1775, the French Canadians fought the Americans and saved the colony for the British Crown. The victory of de Salaberry at Chateauguay was the most conspicuous fait d'armes of the whole war. But Toryism was only sleeping, and reforms necessary to the existence of responsible government, such as no taxation without representation, the independence of the judges, the control of subsidies, the exclusion of public employees from both Houses, the reform of the Legislative Council, the responsibility of the government members to the Legislative Council, were all refused. "At last, the famous Ninty-two Resolutions were formulated, embodying all these revendications, but were unfortunately rejected and, as in Upper Canada, the only logical sequence followed, the rebellion of 1837-38, with all its immediate unfortunate results. I said " immediate " unfortunate results purposely because, although one might judge severely the actual occasion of the uprising both in Upper and Lower Canada and condemn some deeds of the patriots, no one will deny now that responsible government and the political liberties we have enjoyed since 1848 are due in great part, if not altogether, to the patriotism and courage of William Lyon Mackenzie and Louis Joseph Papi-neau. Be that as it may, these simultaneous upheavals opened the eyes of Great Britain, and Lord Durham was sent to Canada with full powers to investigate and report respecting a form of government for the provinces. His report contained a detailed statement of the causes of the rebellion, recommended the introduction of responsible government and the union of Canada under a single government. He stated in that report that the two provinces were to be consolidated with the definite purpose of submerging the French Canadian nationality and ithis was so true that in the enlightened province of Ontario to which my hon. friend who has just taken his seat (Mr. Hocken) has referred, there is a school book on the histoiy of Canada which is read probably by every pupil in the schools. It is written by W. L. Grant and at page 208 I find the following:
What remedies did Durham propose for the evils which we have described?
1.	Extinction of the French nationality.-The first was that the French Canadian language and customs must be extinguished by being ringed round with a circle of English speaking majorities.
2.	The two provinces must be united in order to swamp the French.
In the report of Lord Durham itself there is the following:
I recommend that the alteration of the character of the province ought to be immediately entered upon, and firmly, though cautiously followed up; that, in every plan which may be adopted for the future management of Lower Canada, the first object ought to be that of making it an English province; and that, with this end in view, the ascendency would never again be placed in any hands but those of an English population as means of anglicizing French Canada. I advocate the gradual sub-stiution of the English for the French language. I have little doubt that the Frenchmen, when once placed by the legitimate course of events and the working of natural causes in a minority, would abandon their vain hopes of nationality.
The French Canadians took advantage of that doubt. The same school which in 1840 wanted to deprive a large part of the French Canadian population of their constitutional rights still exists as we can see from speeches, such as that which was made by the hon. gentleman who preceded me, in the year of our Lord 1920. Let me remind these gentlemen that like the soul of France, the soul of French Canada is immortal and like all just causes the stronger the attacks upon her the stronger will remain her surviving vitality. Lord Durham failed to realize, as my hon. friend from West Toronto (Mr. Hocken) fails to realize, the permanence and virtue of our nationalism. He returned to England and Poulett Thomson, who later became Lord Sydenham, replaced him as governor. He was entrusted with the duty of having the Act of Union ratified by the Canadians. It had passed the British Parliament but
